Whence in the epistle to the Hebrews the Apostle says: [[Heb 12:20|and if so much as a beast shall touch the mount, it shall be stoned|Et si bestia tetigerit montem, lapidabitur]]. Or else inasmuch as they belonged to man; and so he commanded not only brute beasts but even inanimate things to be destroyed for men's vices, as is plain in the book of Josue concerning all that was in Jericho[[Jos 6:21||]]; and likewise concerning the horses and chariots of the Amorrhites, of which the Lord spoke to Josue: [[Jos 11:6|thou shalt hamstring their horses, and thou shalt burn their chariots with fire|Equos eorum subnervabis, et currus igne combures]]. And in the first book of Kings, where God commands Saul to kill the Amalecites, men and women, infants and little ones, and beasts[[1 Kings 15:3||]], for the sins of their fathers committed long before: all which things were done to commend divine justice, and for the instruction and terror of men.

paras.t: Ad secundum dicendum, quod Deus sæpe legitur in Scripturis, brutis esse locutus, non ut intelligerent bruta, sed ex aliis rationabilibus causis. Nam supra habetur, quod benedixit Deus piscibus et avibus, dicens: Crescite et multiplicamini; atque in libro Jonæ, Dixit Dominus pisci. Nec obstat, si quis dicat illas allocutiones non fuisse vocales, quoniam bruta non magis incapacia sunt allocutionis exterioris quam interioris. Præterea Ezechieli Dominus dixit: Fili hominis, dic omni volucri cœli: quæ allocutio fuit imaginaria, quemadmodum illa, de qua in Apocalypsi ait sanctus Joannes: Vidi angelum stantem in sole, et clamantem omnibus avibus quæ volabant per medium cœli. Insuper, nonne quotidie psallimus, Benedicite omnes bestiæ et pecora Domino: et, Laudate Dominum de terra dracones et omnes abyssi, bestiæ et universa pecora, serpentes et volucres pennatæ?
paras.en: To the second it must be said that God is often read in the Scriptures to have spoken to brute beasts, not that the brutes might understand, but for other reasonable causes. For above it is related that God blessed the fishes and birds, saying: [[Gen 1:22|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]]; and in the book of Jonas, [[Jon 2:11|the Lord spoke to the fish|Dixit Dominus pisci]]. Nor does it stand in the way if someone says those addresses were not spoken aloud, since brute beasts are no more incapable of outward address than of inward. Moreover the Lord said to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 39:17|O son of man|Fili hominis]], [[Ezech 39:17|say to every fowl|dic omni volucri]] of the air: which address was imaginary [that is, made in a vision of the imagination, not in bodily words], like that of which Saint John says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:17|I saw an angel standing in the sun|Vidi angelum stantem in sole]], and [[Apoc 19:17|he cried|clamantem]] [[Apoc 19:17|to all the birds that did fly through the midst of heaven|omnibus avibus quæ volabant per medium cœli]]. Besides, do we not sing daily in the psalms: [[Dan 3:81|O all ye beasts and cattle, bless the Lord|Benedicite omnes bestiæ et pecora Domino]]; and: [[Ps 148:7|Praise the Lord from the earth, ye dragons, and all ye deeps|Laudate Dominum de terra dracones et omnes abyssi]], [[Ps 148:10|Beasts and all cattle: serpents and feathered fowls|bestiæ et universa pecora, serpentes et volucres pennatæ]]?

paras.t: Ad tertium respondendum, quod statura perfecte erecta, competit homini ex tota specie sua. Per quod non excluditur, quin cuidam serpentum generi competebat statura aliquo modo erecta, imo et usque nunc competit, ut præcedenti articulo continetur. Nec tamen ex hoc mutatus est naturalis ordo universi aut species rerum, quoniam maledictionem primi serpentis, non oportet ad universa suæ speciei individua referre.
paras.en: To the third it must be answered that a perfectly upright stature belongs to man by reason of his whole species. By this it is not excluded that a stature in some way upright belonged to a certain kind of serpent, nay belongs to it even now, as is set out in the preceding article. Nor yet was the natural order of the universe or the species of things changed by this, since the curse of the first serpent need not be referred to all the individuals of its species.

paras.t: Ex his constat, quam insufficienter quidam reprobet expositionem præfatam, et argumenta ipsius nunc plene soluta sunt. Præinducta quoque solutio a viris authenticis approbatur. Nam et Hieronymus libro de Quæstionibus Hebraicis eam commendat, et consonat litteræ ac dictis Strabi ac Bedæ. In Scholastica item historia dicitur: Serpens, utpote diabolus per serpentem, peccavit in tribus, quia invidit, et mentitus est, ac decepit: quibus tribus peccatis, redditæ sunt tres maledictiones. Nam quia invidit hominis excellentiæ, humiliatus est, et dictum est ei: Super pectus tuum gradieris. Quia mentitus est, punitus est in ore, quum dictum est: Terram comedes; imo abstulit ei vocem, et posuit ei venenum in ore. Quia decepit, recepit vicissitudinem hanc: Inimicitiam ponam inter te et mulierem. Ubi innuitur, quod Eva pœnituit, utpote facta serpenti contraria seu inimica. Nam sicut naturale est odium inter equos et gryphos, inter lupos et canes, sic inter homines et serpentes. Quemadmodum enim venenum serpentis interficit hominem, sic sputum hominis jejuni necat serpentem. Et quoniam nudi erant primi homines quando per serpentem prolapsi sunt, serpens adhuc timet ac fugit hominem nudum, et insilit in vestitum. Hæc in Historia illa. Josephus quoque testatur, quod Deus posuit serpenti venenum sub lingua, et abstulit ei vocem.
paras.en: From these things it is evident how insufficiently a certain writer rejects the aforesaid explanation; and his arguments have now been fully answered. The solution given above is also approved by men of authority. For Jerome commends it in the book of Hebrew Questions, and it agrees with the letter and with the sayings of Strabo and Bede. Likewise in the Scholastic History it is said: The serpent, that is, the devil through the serpent, sinned in three things, for he envied, and lied, and deceived; and for these three sins three curses were rendered. For because he envied man's excellence, he was humbled, and it was said to him: [[3:14|upon thy breast shalt thou go|Super pectus tuum gradieris]]. Because he lied, he was punished in the mouth, when it was said: [[3:14|earth shalt thou eat|Terram comedes]]; nay, he took away its voice and put poison in its mouth. Because he deceived, he received this requital: [[3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman|Inimicitiam ponam inter te et mulierem]]. Where it is hinted that Eve repented, having been made contrary or hostile to the serpent. For as there is a natural hatred between horses and griffins, between wolves and dogs, so there is between men and serpents. For as the venom of the serpent kills a man, so the spittle of a fasting man kills a serpent. And because the first men were naked when they fell through the serpent, the serpent still fears and flees a naked man, and leaps upon one clothed. Thus far that History. Josephus also testifies that God put venom under the serpent's tongue and took away its voice.

paras.t: Nunc exponendus est passus iste de diabolo per serpentem locuto. Et ait Dominus ad serpentem, id est diabolum, qui fuit usus serpente ad maleficia sua: Quia fecisti hoc, id est, primos parentes sic ad vitia induxisti, maledictus eris inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ, id est, omnibus illis vilior et miserior eris propter tuam nequitiam, quibus per naturam multo sublimior es. Nam ut ait Philosophus, Impius decies millies vilior exstat brutis. Super pectus tuum gradieris, id est, per superbiam serpes seu gradieris ad homines impugnandos. Superbia quippe designatur per pectus, in quo animositatis impetus dominatur. Et terram comedes, id est, terrenis et carnalibus hominum actibus reficieris, hominesque terrenos iniquos tibi incorporabis, qui ad tuum corpus mysticum pertinebunt, omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ: ex quibus miseria tua augebitur. Quemadmodum enim accidentale præmium angelorum augetur ex eorum consortio, qui per ipsorum custodiam evadunt pericula et salvantur, ita et pœna sensus dæmonum augetur ex societate et condemnatione eorum quos vincunt, quanquam ob hoc non cessent ab hominum tentatione ex nimia sua invidentia atque malitia.
paras.en: Now this passage is to be explained of the devil, who spoke through the serpent. [[3:14|And the Lord God said to the serpent|Et ait Dominus ad serpentem]], that is, to the devil, who used the serpent for his evil deeds: [[3:14|Because thou hast done this thing|Quia fecisti hoc]], that is, hast thus led our first parents into vice, [[3:14|thou art cursed among all cattle, and beasts of the earth|maledictus eris inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ]], that is, thou shalt be viler and more wretched than all of them because of thy wickedness, though by nature thou art far higher than they. For, as the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] says, the wicked man is ten thousand times viler than the brutes. [[3:14|upon thy breast shalt thou go|Super pectus tuum gradieris]], that is, by pride thou shalt creep or go forth to assail men. For pride is signified by the breast, in which the impulse of high spirit holds sway. [[3:14|and earth shalt thou eat|Et terram comedes]], that is, thou shalt be fed with the earthly and carnal acts of men, and shalt incorporate into thyself earthly and wicked men, who will belong to thy mystical body, [[3:14|all the days of thy life|omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ]]: by which thy misery will be increased. For as the accidental reward of the angels [that is, the joy added to their essential happiness in the vision of God] is increased by the company of those who through their guardianship escape dangers and are saved, so too the pain of sense of the demons [that is, their positive torment, as distinct from the pain of loss] is increased by the company and condemnation of those whom they overcome; although for this reason they do not cease from tempting men, out of their excessive envy and malice.

paras.t: Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, et semen tuum et semen illius. Augustinus super Genesim dicit, per mulierem hic designari rationem inferiorem, seu partem sensitivam ac animalem; per semen mulieris, actum virtuosum; per semen serpentis, pravam suggestionem, ut sit sensus: Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, id est inter te et rationem inferiorem, seu partem sensitivam, quam immediate potes tentare; et inter tuam pravam suggestionem et bonam rationis illius operationem, per quam rationem inferiorem seu sensitivam partem, tentare potes rationem superiorem. Ipsa conteret caput tuum, id est, exordium tuæ suggestionis calcabit ac vincet. Et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus, hoc est, ab inferiori conaberis ei nocere ac prævalere, proponendo ei objecta carnalia et mundana. Porro ratio est idem quod intellectus. Et dicitur ratio superior, in quantum respicit spiritualia ac divina; inferior autem, in quantum respectum habet ad temporalia et caduca.
paras.en: [[3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed|Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, et semen tuum et semen illius]]. Augustine on Genesis says that by the woman here is signified the lower reason, or the sensitive and animal part; by the woman's seed, a virtuous act; by the serpent's seed, an evil suggestion; so that the sense is: [[3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman|Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem]], that is, between thee and the lower reason, or the sensitive part, which thou canst tempt directly; and between thy evil suggestion and the good working of that reason; through which lower reason, or sensitive part, thou canst tempt the higher reason. [[3:15|she shall crush thy head|Ipsa conteret caput tuum]], that is, she will tread down and overcome the beginning of thy suggestion. [[3:15|and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel|Et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus]], that is, from below thou shalt try to harm her and prevail over her, by setting carnal and worldly objects before her. Now reason is the same as intellect. And it is called the higher reason inasmuch as it looks to spiritual and divine things; the lower, inasmuch as it has regard to temporal and passing things.

paras.t: Porro multi Sanctorum per mulierem istam intelligunt Virginem gloriosam, quam dæmones specialissime timent ac odiunt, quæ et dæmonibus valde gravis et metuenda effecta est, et undique conterit caput seu potestatem diaboli ac seminis ejus, utpote dæmonum ceterorum. Estque inimicitia ista posita etiam inter semen mulieris istius, et semen præfatum diaboli, id est inter Christum et dæmones; quoniam Christus omnes illos devicit ac spoliavit, quasi dicat Deus judex justus ac sapiens: Quia tu serpens nequissime decepisti hanc feminam primam ac fragilem, creabo feminam unam, quæ tanta gratia ac virtute implebitur, quod per Filium suum et per se, te atque satellites tuos penitus supplantabit, et tibi terribilis erit quasi castrorum acies ordinata.
paras.en: Further, many of the Saints understand by this woman the glorious Virgin, whom the demons most especially fear and hate, who has also been made very grievous and fearsome to the demons, and on every side crushes the head, or power, of the devil and of his seed, that is, of the other demons. And this enmity is set also between the seed of this woman and the aforesaid seed of the devil, that is, between Christ and the demons; since Christ conquered and despoiled them all. As if God, the just and wise judge, said: Because thou, most wicked serpent, hast deceived this first and frail woman, I will create one woman who shall be filled with such grace and virtue that through her Son and through herself she shall utterly overthrow thee and thy satellites, and shall be to thee [[Cant 6:3|terrible as an army set in array|terribilis erit quasi castrorum acies ordinata]].

3.title: Elucidatio residuæ partis hujus tertii capituli: Mulieri quoque dixit Deus
3.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this third chapter: “To the woman also he said”

paras.t: Consequenter describitur punitio mulieris, quæ secundo loco narratur, quoniam per serpentem inducta est ad peccandum antequam vir peccavit. Et quoniam gravius viro peccavit, gravius ac multiplicius est punita quam vir, sicut subjungitur: Mulieri quoque dixit Deus: Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas et conceptus tuos: quemadmodum multipliciter excessisti, videlicet superbiendo et serpenti credendo, ac fructum prohibitum comedendo, atque ad idem tuum inducendo maritum, te quoque inaniter excusando; sic et ego multas calamitates tibi infligam, et diversos habebis conceptus, ut frequentius crucieris in portando pariendoque fetum. Non enim simul concipies nisi unum aut duas proles, de cursu communi. In dolore paries filios. Magnus enim est dolor in pariendo, et forsan major, quam delectatio in concipiendo. In statu autem innocentiæ fuisset conceptio sine indecentia, turpitudine, atque libidine; deportatio prolis sine gravamine, et partus sine dolore. Porro per filios, intelliguntur et filiæ, ut nomen filii notet hic prolem dumtaxat, non sexum. Itaque quoniam mulier peccavit in fructu ligni, punita est in fructu uteri sui, ut pœna correspondeat culpæ. Et illud Sapientiæ impletur: Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur.
paras.en: Next is described the punishment of the woman, which is told in the second place, because she was led into sin by the serpent before the man sinned. And because she sinned more gravely than the man, she was punished more gravely and in more ways than the man, as follows: [[3:16|To the woman also he said|Mulieri quoque dixit]] God: [[3:16|I will multiply thy sorrows, and thy conceptions|Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas et conceptus tuos]]: as thou hast transgressed in many ways, namely by pride, by believing the serpent, by eating the forbidden fruit, by leading thy husband to the same, and by excusing thyself to no purpose, so I too will inflict many calamities on thee; and thou shalt have several conceptions, so that thou mayest be tormented the more often in carrying and bearing offspring. For in the common course thou shalt not conceive more than one or two children at a time. [[3:16|in sorrow shalt thou bring forth children|In dolore paries filios]]. For great is the pain in giving birth, and perhaps greater than the pleasure in conceiving. In the state of innocence, however, conception would have been without unseemliness, shame and lust; the carrying of the child without burden, and the birth without pain. Further, by *children* [Latin *filios*, literally "sons"] daughters also are understood, so that the word *son* here denotes only offspring, not sex. And so, since the woman sinned in the fruit of the tree, she was punished in the fruit of her womb, that the punishment might answer to the fault. And that word of Wisdom is fulfilled: [[Wis 11:17|by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented|Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur]] [Denis reads *punitur*, "is punished", where the Vulgate has *torquetur*, "is tormented"].

paras.t: Insuper, quia peccavit superbiendo, punita est per subjectionem et humiliationem pœnalem sub viro, secundum quod subditur: Et sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui, id est, marito eris subjecta cum timore, correctione et pœna, quæ si non peccasses, non fuisses ei subjecta, nisi cum delectatione, amore et naturali habitudine ac directione convenientissima. Circa hæc quæri posset, an in statu innocentiæ fuissent dominatio et servitus, imperium atque subjectio, et quomodo mulier diversimode subjecta fuit viro ante peccatum et postea. Ad quod infra in introductione et solutione quæstionum patebit responsio.
paras.en: Moreover, because she sinned by pride, she was punished by a penal subjection and humbling under the man, according to what follows: [[3:16|and thou shalt be under thy husband's power, and he shall have dominion over thee|Et sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui]]: that is, thou shalt be subject to thy husband with fear, correction and punishment; whereas, hadst thou not sinned, thou wouldst not have been subject to him except with delight and love, by a natural relation and a most fitting direction. Concerning this it might be asked whether in the state of innocence there would have been lordship and servitude, command and subjection, and how the woman was subject to the man in a different way before sin and after it. The answer to this will appear below, where the questions are put and solved.

paras.t: Adæ vero dixit. Nam quia et ultimo peccavit, et minus quam mulier, idcirco ultimo sibi infligitur pœna ista exterior et etiam mitior. Subtractio autem originalis justitiæ, fuit viro ac mulieri communis, quæ etiam fuit pœna interior et ambobus simul inflicta. Inordinati quoque motus carnales, et ceteræ culpæ subtractionem illam secutæ, sunt pœnæ simul et culpæ: pœnæ quidem illius primæ prævaricationis, quoniam propter illam homines meruerunt eos incidere; culpæ vero, in quantum sunt legi Dei contrarii. Quia audisti vocem uxoris tuæ, non solum exteriori auditu, sed et interiori consensu contra jussionem divinam, et comedisti de ligno, ex quo præceperam tibi ne comederes, maledicta terra in opere tuo. Non est hoc intelligendum de terra paradisi, quæ in sua permansit integritate, fertilitate atque decore, sed de terra extra paradisum, ad quam Adam erat mox expellendus, quæ dicitur maledicta, id est naturalibus quibusdam donis Dei privata, puta solita fecunditate, ornatu ac colendi et fecundandi facilitate: quod factum est in opere Adæ, id est demerito suæ transgressionis, ut qui peccavit edendo de vetito fructu, puniretur in procuratione fructuum terræ pro sustentaculo vitæ suæ, imo et conjugis ac sobolis suæ; quoniam pertinet ad maritum, providere de necessariis vitæ tam sibi quam suis domesticis. Unde secundum Lyram in Hebræo habetur: Maledicta terra propter te, hoc est, propter tuam transgressionem. Vel, maledicta terra in opere tuo, hoc est: in cultura et operatione, quas facies circa terram fecundandam et circa fructus ipsius, subjacebit terra maledictioni præfatæ, experierisque eam, ita quod terra quæ ante peccatum tuum protulit uberes fructus atque spontaneos, scilicet sine humano labore, de cetero indigebit laboriosa cultura, et minus solito fertilis erit, imo et aliquando sterilis.
paras.en: [[3:17|And to Adam he said|Adæ vero dixit]]. For because he sinned both last and less than the woman, this outward punishment is inflicted on him last, and also more mildly. But the withdrawal of original justice was common to the man and the woman; it was also an inward punishment, inflicted on both together. The disordered motions of the flesh, too, and the other faults that followed upon that withdrawal, are at once punishments and faults: punishments of that first transgression, since because of it men deserved to fall into them; and faults inasmuch as they are contrary to the law of God. [[3:17|Because thou hast hearkened to the voice of thy wife|Quia audisti vocem uxoris tuæ]], not only with the outward hearing but also with inward consent, against the divine command, [[3:17|and hast eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee, that thou shouldst not eat|et comedisti de ligno, ex quo præceperam tibi ne comederes]], [[3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|maledicta terra in opere tuo]]. This is not to be understood of the earth of paradise, which remained in its soundness, fruitfulness and beauty, but of the earth outside paradise, into which Adam was soon to be driven. It is called *cursed*, that is, deprived of certain natural gifts of God, such as its wonted fruitfulness, its adornment, and the ease with which it could be tilled and made fruitful. And this was done *in the work* of Adam, that is, through the demerit of his transgression, so that he who sinned by eating the forbidden fruit should be punished in procuring the fruits of the earth for the sustenance of his life, and indeed of his wife's and his children's; for it belongs to the husband to provide the necessaries of life both for himself and for his household. Hence, according to Lyra, the Hebrew has: Cursed is the earth because of thee, that is, because of thy transgression. Or, [[3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|maledicta terra in opere tuo]]: that is, in the tilling and working that thou shalt do about the earth to make it fruitful, and about its fruits, the earth will lie under the aforesaid curse, and thou shalt find it so; so that the earth, which before thy sin brought forth rich fruits of its own accord, that is, without human labour, will henceforth need laborious tilling, and will be less fruitful than it was wont, and indeed sometimes barren.

paras.t: Si autem quæratur, cur maledicatur terra, quæ non peccavit, et non potius Adam qui peccavit: respondetur, quod terra maledicta est, tanquam res ad hominem pertinens, et propter eum creata, ita quod ipse homo maledicitur in re sua, puta in terra. Maledictio enim ista homini est nociva atque pœnosa, non terræ, quemadmodum pandunt verba sequentia: In laboribus comedes ex ea, id est, fructus terræ quibus vesceris, laboriose acquires. Cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi. Communiter dicunt doctores, sicut præhabitum est, quod terra ante primorum peccata parentum protulit spinas ac tribulos, maxime quum spinæ et tribuli pertineant ad ordinem universi: sed tunc non producebantur homini ad tormentum, nec ad pœnam peccati, quemadmodum postea; nec generabantur tunc tam abundanter, neque tam copiose inter ceteros comestibiles ac necessarios fructus, ut postmodum. Hinc Rabanus ait: Spinæ antea erant, sed non ut homini laborem inferrent, cui post peccatum ad laborem fuerunt et afflictionem, sicut serpentes et quæcumque noxia, erant homini ante innoxia. Hinc Scriptura non ait absolute, Spinas et tribulos germinabit, sed addit, tibi, id est ad tuæ miseriæ cumulum.
paras.en: But if it be asked why the earth, which did not sin, is cursed, and not rather Adam who sinned, the answer is that the earth was cursed as a thing belonging to man and created for his sake, so that man himself is cursed in what is his, namely in the earth. For this curse is hurtful and painful to man, not to the earth, as the words that follow make plain: [[3:17|with labour and toil shalt thou eat thereof|In laboribus comedes ex ea]], that is, thou shalt get with toil the fruits of the earth on which thou feedest. [[3:17|all the days of thy life|Cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]] [[3:18|Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee|spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi]]. The doctors commonly say, as was set out earlier, that the earth brought forth thorns and thistles before the sin of our first parents, especially since thorns and thistles belong to the order of the universe; but then they were not produced for man's torment, nor as a punishment of sin, as they were afterwards; nor were they then produced so abundantly, nor so plentifully among the other fruits that are eatable and needful, as afterwards. Hence Rabanus says: There were thorns before, but not so as to bring toil to man; after sin they were to him for toil and affliction; just as serpents and all harmful things were harmless to man before. Hence Scripture does not say simply, [[3:18|Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth|spinas et tribulos germinabit]], but adds, [[3:18|to thee|tibi]], that is, to heap up thy misery.

paras.t: Et comedes herbas terræ, id est, quia peccando brutis similis es effectus, et brutales sustines motus, in hoc assimilaberis bestiis, quod herbis terræ vesceris, non tamen eas ore carpendo de terra instar brutorum. Comedes itaque herbas terræ, qui ante comedisti fructus paradisi, ut aliqui exponendo adjiciunt: et verum est, si Adam in paradiso actualiter manducavit de aliarum arborum fructu; sin autem, sic intelligendum est, qui ante comedisti, id est, comedendi licentiam habuisti de fructibus paradisi.
paras.en: [[3:18|and thou shalt eat the herbs of the earth|Et comedes herbas terræ]] [the margin notes the reading *herbam*, "herb", in the singular, as the Vulgate has it]: that is, because by sinning thou art made like the brutes and sufferest brutish motions, thou shalt be likened to the beasts in this, that thou shalt feed on the herbs of the earth; not, however, cropping them from the ground with thy mouth as the brutes do. Thou shalt eat, then, the herbs of the earth, thou who before didst eat the fruits of paradise, as some add in expounding it: and that is true if Adam in paradise actually ate of the fruit of the other trees; but if not, it is to be understood thus: thou who before didst eat, that is, hadst leave to eat, of the fruits of paradise.

paras.t: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo, id est, cibum quotidianum cum tribulatione et angustia ac grandi conatu acquires ac præparabis tibi ac tuis, aut etiam sumes; donec revertaris in terram de qua sumptus es, id est usque ad finem vitæ tuæ, quia hæ pœnæ perdurant per universam hominis vitam in via hujus exsilii. Sumptus est autem homo de terra, quantum ad corporis sui materiam prædominantem in eo secundum quantitatem, ut plenius dictum est supra.
paras.en: [[3:19|In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread|In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo]], that is, thou shalt get and prepare thy daily food for thyself and thine, or also take it, with tribulation and distress and great effort; [[3:19|till thou return to the earth out of which thou wast taken|donec revertaris in terram de qua sumptus es]], that is, to the end of thy life, for these punishments last through the whole life of man on the way of this exile. Now man was taken from the earth as regards the matter of his body, which predominates in him in quantity, as was said more fully above.

paras.t: Quia pulvis es, id est pulveri similis, quantum ad tuam fragilitatem, inconstantiam et levitatem. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Quid superbit terra et cinis? Et sanctus Job profitetur: Assimilatus sum favillæ et cineri. Vel, pulvis es, id est de pulveribus humore conglutinatis, puta de limo formatus, quantum ad corpus, quemadmodum scriptum est: Formavit Dominus Deus hominem de limo terræ, ubi (ut fertur) in Hebræo habetur, De pulvere terræ. Et in pulverem reverteris, id est, corpus tuum in pulverem resolvetur. Unumquodque enim in illa resolvitur, ex quibus componitur. Per hæc verba designatur fragilitas naturæ et conditionis humanæ, et primus homo aptissime humiliatus est, quasi Dominus dicat: Tu qui voluisti inordinate deificari, et tibi ex te ipso sufficere, juxta sensum inductum, tot subjacebis miseriis, quod pulvis rite vocaris, atque in pulverem resolveris.
paras.en: [[3:19|for dust thou art|Quia pulvis es]], that is, like dust as to thy frailty, inconstancy and lightness. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:9|Why is earth, and ashes proud|Quid superbit terra et cinis?]]? And holy Job confesses: I [[Job 30:19|am likened to embers and ashes|Assimilatus sum favillæ et cineri]]. Or, [[3:19|dust thou art|pulvis es]], that is, made of dust held together by moisture, namely formed of slime, as to the body, as it is written: [[Gen 2:7|the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit Dominus Deus hominem de limo terræ]]; where (so it is said) the Hebrew has, Of the dust of the earth. [[3:19|and into dust thou shalt return|Et in pulverem reverteris]], that is, thy body will be resolved into dust; for each thing is resolved into the things of which it is composed. By these words is signified the frailty of human nature and condition, and the first man is most fittingly humbled, as if the Lord said: Thou who didst wish inordinately to be made a god and to be sufficient to thyself of thyself, according to the suggestion put into thee, shalt lie under so many miseries that thou art rightly called dust, and shalt be resolved into dust.

paras.t: Circa præhabita ait Alcuinus: Deus maledixit terræ, non aquis: quoniam homo contra præceptum comedit de fructu terræ, nec sic bibit de aquis. In aquis quoque peccatum fuerat abluendum, per fructum terræ contractum. Animalia item terrestria plus habent maledictionis quam aquatica, quia plus vivunt de terra maledicta. Inde est quod Christus post resurrectionem suam manducavit de pisce, non de animali terrestri. His consonat illud Scholasticæ historiæ: Terræ maledixit, quia de fructu terræ transgressio facta est, et non aquis. Hinc Christus comedit piscem, sed non legitur comedisse carnem animalium viventium de terra maledicta, nisi forte de agno paschali pro observando legis præcepto. Verumtamen est probabile quod Christus qui cœpit facere et docere, qui suis dixit discipulis, Edentes et bibentes quæ apud illos sunt, fecit hoc ipsum.
paras.en: On what has gone before, Alcuin says: God cursed the earth, not the waters, because man ate of the fruit of the earth against the command, but did not so drink of the waters. In the waters, too, the sin contracted through the fruit of the earth was to be washed away. Likewise land animals have more of the curse than those of the water, because they live more from the cursed earth. Hence it is that Christ after his resurrection ate of a fish, not of a land animal. With this agrees the saying of the Scholastic History [the *Historia scholastica* of Peter Comestor]: He cursed the earth, because the transgression was done through the fruit of the earth, and not the waters. Hence Christ ate fish, but we do not read that he ate the flesh of animals living on the cursed earth, unless perhaps of the paschal lamb, to observe the precept of the law. Yet it is probable that Christ, who began to do and to teach, and who said to his disciples, [[Luke 10:7|eating and drinking such things as they have|Edentes et bibentes quæ apud illos sunt]], did this very thing.

paras.t: Amplius, circa præscriptas maledictiones seu pœnas pensandum quod Rabanus ait: Adæ imponitur pœna extrinseca, quum dicitur: Maledicta terra in opere tuo; mulieri autem pœna intrinseca, quum Dominus loquitur: Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas, etc., quia seducta, seduxit virum. Sed serpens, id est diabolus, qui summe peccavit, maledicitur in se ipso, quum fertur: Maledictus eris inter omnia animantia, etc.
paras.en: Further, concerning the curses or punishments set down above, we should weigh what Rabanus says: On Adam an outward punishment is laid, when it is said: [[3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|Maledicta terra in opere tuo]]; but on the woman an inward punishment, when the Lord says: [[3:16|I will multiply thy sorrows|Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas]], etc., because, having been seduced, she seduced the man. But the serpent, that is, the devil, who sinned most of all, is cursed in himself, when it is said: [[3:14|thou art cursed among all cattle|Maledictus eris inter omnia animantia]], etc.

paras.t: Et vocavit Adam nomen uxoris suæ Eva, cujus appellationis subjungitur ratio, eo quod mater esset omnium viventium, id est, universorum hominum nasciturorum genitrix immediata aut mediata esset futura. Eva quippe in Hebræo sonat vitam, tamen pœnalitatibus subditam, ut ait hic Lyra. Unde in Scholastica historia legitur: Tunc Adam deplorans posteritatis suæ miseriam, vocavit uxorem suam Evam, quasi alludens ejulatui parvulorum. Masculus enim recens natus dicit A, quasi filius Adæ, et similis ei in sexu: femina vero, E, quasi filia Evæ, et ei sexu consimilis. Isidorus quoque testatur: Post peccatum, judicisque sententiam, vocavit Adam uxorem suam Evam, quia sit mater vivorum, quum jam meruit parere mortem et fetus mortales.
paras.en: [[3:20|And Adam called the name of his wife Eve|Et vocavit Adam nomen uxoris suæ Eva]], and the reason for this name is added: [[3:20|because she was the mother of all the living|eo quod mater esset omnium viventium]], that is, she was to be the mother, immediate or mediate, of all the men who would be born. For *Eva* [Eve] in Hebrew means *life*, yet a life subject to penalties, as Lyra says here. Hence we read in the Scholastic History: Then Adam, lamenting the misery of his posterity, called his wife Eve, as if alluding to the wailing of little children. For a male child newly born says *A*, as being a son of Adam and like him in sex; but a female says *E*, as being a daughter of Eve and like her in sex. Isidore too bears witness: After the sin and the judge's sentence, Adam called his wife Eve, because she is the mother of the living, when she had already deserved to bring forth death and mortal offspring.

paras.t: Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus contradicit verbo Lyræ, dicentis quod Eva in Hebræo sonat vitam pœnalitatibus subditam. Et asserit Paulus iste, quod Eva in Hebræo sonat vitam simpliciter, non connotando quod sit pœnalitati subjecta. Deinde adjungit: Licet Adam scivit naturas omnium animalium, et omnem scientiam habuit, de quibus homo natus est instrui, non tamen habuit notitiam contingentium futurorum, nisi in quantum ex revelatione divina accepit, aut experimentaliter acquirere potuit: idcirco mulier ei adducta, statim quando formata est, vocata est ab eo virago, ad denotandum quod erat sibi data in consortium domesticæ conversationis, non declarans, an esset sibi data etiam ad prolis propagationem; ita quod tunc nescivit, an Deus disponeret eos sic remanere, et alios homines de novo procreare, an ex muliere illa esset proles per propagationem procreanda. Postea vero ex divina sententia contra ipsum et uxorem prolata, cognovit duo: Unum, quod essent morituri; secundum, quod essent generaturi: idcirco vocavit conjugem suam Evam, quod nomen interpretatus est ipse Adam, dicendo, eo quod esset mater cunctorum viventium.
paras.en: Yet Rabbi Paul [probably Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, whose *Additions* to Lyra's Postil often dispute him] contradicts the word of Lyra, who says that *Eva* in Hebrew means life subject to penalties. This Paul asserts that *Eva* in Hebrew means life simply, without connoting that it is subject to penalty. Then he adds: Although Adam knew the natures of all animals, and had all the knowledge in which man is by nature fitted to be instructed, yet he had no knowledge of future contingents, except so far as he received it by divine revelation or could acquire it by experience. Therefore the woman, brought to him as soon as she was formed, was called by him *virago* [the Vulgate's word at Gen 2:23, rendered "woman", formed from *vir*, "man"], to denote that she was given him as a partner in household life; not declaring whether she was given him also for the propagation of offspring; so that he did not then know whether God would arrange that they should remain thus and would create other men anew, or whether offspring was to be procreated from that woman by propagation. But afterwards, from the divine sentence pronounced against him and his wife, he learned two things: first, that they would die; second, that they would beget. Therefore he called his wife Eve, a name which Adam himself interpreted, saying, [[3:20|because she was the mother of all the living|eo quod esset mater cunctorum viventium]].

paras.t: Sed quidquid sit de significatione hujus nominis Eva juxta Hebræum, ista additio Pauli istius videtur nimium imperita et Scripturæ contraria. Scriptum est enim supra: Masculum et feminam creavit eos, benedixitque illis Deus, et ait: Crescite et multiplicamini et replete terram; quod dictum est Adæ evidenter, et ipse intellexit hoc de multiplicatione hominum ex se per generationem. Unde secundum expositores, per illa verba dedit ei præceptum de multiplicatione speciei, sicut præhabitum est. Et illud præceptum per Adam devenit ad Evam. Rursus habetur supra, quemadmodum Eva ex costa Adæ formata, locutus est Adam: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea: quamobrem relinquet homo patrem suum et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ, et erunt duo in carne una: per quæ utique verba insinuavit se scire, quod mulier illa esset sibi data in conjugem, ad prolificandum ex ea per carnalem commixtionem. Denique Adam in statu innocentiæ non indiguit muliere, nec adjutorio ejus ad domesticam conversationem, quoniam sine omni cura et conatu habuit necessaria vitæ: ideo Adam scivit ante suam transgressionem, quod femina esset ei collata in adjutorium generandi.
paras.en: But whatever may be said of the meaning of this name Eve in Hebrew, this addition of that Paul seems very unlearned and contrary to Scripture. For it is written above: [[Gen 1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum et feminam creavit eos]]; [[Gen 1:28|And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth|benedixitque illis Deus, et ait: Crescite et multiplicamini et replete terram]]: which was plainly said to Adam, and he understood it of the multiplying of men from himself by generation. Hence, according to the expositors, by those words He gave him the precept of multiplying the species, as was set out earlier; and that precept came to Eve through Adam. Again, it is told above how, when Eve had been formed from Adam's rib, Adam said: [[Gen 2:23|This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh|Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea]]: [[Gen 2:24|Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they shall be two in one flesh|quamobrem relinquet homo patrem suum et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ, et erunt duo in carne una]]: by which words he certainly gave to understand that he knew that woman had been given him as wife, to have offspring by her through carnal union. Finally, Adam in the state of innocence had no need of the woman, nor of her help in household life, since he had the necessaries of life without any care or effort: therefore Adam knew before his transgression that the woman had been given him as a help in begetting.

paras.t: Fecit quoque Dominus Deus Adæ et uxori ejus tunicas pelliceas. Circa hoc Strabus ait: Ipsi fecerunt sibi perizomata, ut peccatum suum absconderent. Deus autem fecit eis pelliceas tunicas, quibus induit totum corpus amborum, quia in corpore et anima juste eos punivit. Stulta quoque est quæstio, si quæratur, qualiter aut in quo operante pelles ab animalibus sunt deductæ: qui enim de nihilo omnia condidit, fecit hoc quoque et qualiter voluit. Hæc Strabus. Porro in Scholastica historia legitur, quod de pellibus mortuorum animalium factæ sunt tunicæ illæ. Estque credendum quod totum hoc fecit Deus angelico famulatu. Et induit eos, ut signum suæ mortalitatis secum efferent, seque morituros semper attenderent, et item ut contra intemperiem loci ac temporis essent operti, quia de paradiso erant protinus expellendi.
paras.en: [[3:21|And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skins|Fecit quoque Dominus Deus Adæ et uxori ejus tunicas pelliceas]]. On this Strabus [Walafrid Strabo] says: They themselves made aprons for themselves, to hide their sin; but God made them garments of skins, with which He clothed the whole body of both, because He justly punished them in body and soul. It is also a foolish question, if one asks how, or by whose working, the skins were taken from the animals; for He who made all things from nothing did this too, and in the way He willed. So far Strabus. Further, we read in the Scholastic History that those garments were made from the skins of dead animals. And it is to be believed that God did all this by the service of angels. [[3:21|and clothed them|Et induit eos]], that they might carry with them a sign of their mortality and ever bear in mind that they were to die, and also that they might be covered against the harshness of place and season, since they were forthwith to be driven out of paradise.

paras.t: Specialiter quoque induit eos vestes has ex pellibus mortuorum animalium factas, ad justam derisionem ipsorum, qui ad immoderatam Dei assimilationem adspiraverunt. Unde subjungitur, et ait: Ecce Adam quasi unus ex nobis factus est, id est, per immortalitatem, sapientiam, et sui in se sufficientiam, assimilatus est nobis. Et est justa ironia, implicitaque negatio. Quasi dicat: Jam apparet ad oculum, quam vane se habuit in peccando, et quantum deceptus sit, dejectus, et depauperatus; estque vox summæ Trinitatis ad se, vel Dei ad angelos: imo Dominus dixit hæc potius quasi compatiendo, et humanam superbiam corrigendo, quam insultando. Sciens bonum et malum, id est, sufficienter edoctus ad sui ipsius et inferiorum gubernationem, prout serpens promisit.
paras.en: In particular, too, He clothed them with these garments made from the skins of dead animals, in just mockery of them who had aspired to an immoderate likeness to God. Hence it follows: [[3:22|And he said: Behold Adam is become as one of us|et ait: Ecce Adam quasi unus ex nobis factus est]], that is, by immortality, wisdom, and sufficiency of himself in himself he has become like us. And it is a just irony, and an implied denial; as if He said: It is now plain to the eye how vainly he behaved in sinning, and how far he has been deceived, cast down and impoverished. And it is the voice of the most high Trinity to itself, or of God to the angels; or rather the Lord said these things more as in compassion, and to correct human pride, than in mockery. [[3:22|knowing good and evil|Sciens bonum et malum]], that is, sufficiently taught for the governing of himself and of the things below him, as the serpent promised.

paras.t: Nunc ergo. Aliqui autem textus habent, Videte, quod tamen non est in Hebræo. Si autem non habeatur in textu, subintelligendum est. Itaque Dominus ait ad angelos, quibus paradisi custodiam et primorum parentum inde expulsionem commiserat: Nunc ergo videte, id est, præcavete ne forte mittat manum suam, hoc est, ne extendat, et sumat de ligno vitæ, et comedat, et vivat in æternum.
paras.en: [[3:22|now therefore|Nunc ergo]]. Some texts have *Videte* [that is, "see ye"], which, however, is not in the Hebrew; but if it is not in the text, it is to be understood. So the Lord says to the angels, to whom He had committed the keeping of paradise and the driving of our first parents out of it: [[3:22|now therefore|Nunc ergo]] see ye, that is, beware [[3:22|lest perhaps he put forth his hand|ne forte mittat manum suam]], that is, lest he stretch it out, [[3:22|and take also of the tree of life|et sumat de ligno vitæ]], [[3:22|and eat, and live for ever|et comedat, et vivat in æternum]].

paras.t: Totum hoc dupliciter accipi potest. Primo, quasi ironice dictum, quemadmodum præcedentia verba, quasi Dominus dicat: Ex quo Adam ita dejectus est, et tot miseriis, necessitatique mortis et redactioni in pulverem adjudicatus a me, non est periculum neque possibile, quod de cetero comesturus sit de ligno vitæ ad vivendum in sempiternum, ideo non oportet hoc præcavere. Secundo, intelligi potest, quasi seriose et præceptive prolatum, quasi Dominus dicat: Ex quo Adam ita peccavit et lapsus est, prohibete ne præsumat manum extendere ad sumendum de fructu arboris vitæ, quo se fecit indignum. Sed huic expositioni videtur obstare, quod quamvis post peccatum fuisset permissus edere de ligno vitæ, non tamen ex hoc fuisset immortalitatem seu vitam æternam sortitus. Respondetur quod nihilo minus vita sua potuisset multum prolongari ex esu hujusmodi, et talis diuturnitas designatur per verbum hoc, in æternum. Sic namque, in æternum, in Scripturis frequenter accipitur, sicut et Achis primo libro Regum dixit ad David: Erit mihi servus in sempiternum. Hinc in Scholastica historia continetur: Non est mirum si etiam post peccatum, per esum ligni illius vixissent diutius, quum adhuc sint quædam viventium insulæ, in quibus nemo moritur, id est vix aliquis, utpote quia diu valde vivunt ibidem. Sicut fit etiam lanugo in foliis arborum apud Seres, cujus usu protelatur vita. Alexander quoque Aristoteli scripsit de sacerdotibus solis et lunæ, quod ex esu quorumdam pomorum longissimam vitam ducant, utpote quadringentis annis vivendo, ut legitur.
paras.en: All this can be taken in two ways. First, as said ironically, like the preceding words, as if the Lord said: Since Adam is so cast down, and has been sentenced by me to so many miseries, to the necessity of death and to being brought back to dust, there is no danger, nor is it possible, that he should henceforth eat of the tree of life so as to live for ever; so there is no need to guard against this. Secondly, it can be understood as said seriously and by way of command, as if the Lord said: Since Adam has so sinned and fallen, forbid him to presume to stretch out his hand to take of the fruit of the tree of life, of which he has made himself unworthy. But against this exposition there seems to stand this: even had he been allowed after sin to eat of the tree of life, he would not thereby have obtained immortality or everlasting life. The answer is that his life could nonetheless have been much prolonged by such eating, and such long duration is signified by these words, *for ever*. For so is *for ever* often taken in the Scriptures, as when Achis, in the first book of Kings, said to David: [[1 Kings 27:12|he shall be my servant for ever|Erit mihi servus in sempiternum]] [in the text Achis says this of David to himself, not to him]. Hence the Scholastic History has: It is no wonder if even after sin they would have lived longer by eating of that tree, since there are still certain islands of the living in which no one dies, that is, hardly anyone, since they live there a very long time. So too there grows a down on the leaves of trees among the Seres [a people of the far East, from whom silk came], by the use of which life is prolonged. Alexander also wrote to Aristotle of the priests of the sun and moon that from eating certain apples they lead a very long life, living four hundred years, as we read.

paras.t: Et emisit eum Dominus Deus, id est, exire præcepit ipsum de paradiso voluptatis, ut operaretur, id est, coleret, fecundaret, exerceretque terram de qua sumptus est, id est, formatus secundum corpus, juxta expositionem præhabitam. Porro ex hoc verbo accipiunt multi, quod Adam in illum locum reductus est, in quo fuit formatus: qui ubi fuerit, superius dictum est quantum poterat dici.
paras.en: [[3:23|And the Lord God sent him out|Et emisit eum Dominus Deus]], that is, commanded him to go out [[3:23|of the paradise of pleasure|de paradiso voluptatis]], [[3:23|to till|ut operaretur]], that is, to cultivate, make fruitful and work, [[3:23|the earth from which he was taken|terram de qua sumptus est]], that is, formed as to the body, according to the exposition given before. Further, from this word many gather that Adam was brought back to the place in which he was formed; where that was has been said above, as far as it could be said.

paras.t: Ejecitque Adam ministerio angelorum: qui ejectus, cœpit cum muliere paulatim progredi cum mœrore. Nec fit hic mentio de Eva, sed tantum de Adam tanquam de principali. Sed quare Deus non dixit de utrisque, Ecce Adam et Eva quasi duo ex nobis facti sunt, scientes bonum et malum, etc.? Responderi potest, quod Deus condoluit et pepercit in hoc mulieri, quæ adhuc virgo fuit, propter teneritudinem verecundiæ suæ et fragilem sexum, ne abundantiori absorberetur tristitia. Verumtamen ambos simul ejecit, nec privavit eos in toto mutuæ societatis solatio, neque custodia angelorum, a quibus prius dirigebantur, deinceps graviter ac intime pœnitentes.
paras.en: [[3:24|And he cast out Adam|Ejecitque Adam]], by the ministry of angels; and he, being cast out, began to go forward little by little with the woman, in sorrow. No mention is made here of Eve, but only of Adam, as the principal. But why did God not say of both, Behold Adam and Eve are become as two of us, knowing good and evil, etc.? It may be answered that in this God felt for the woman and spared her, who was still a virgin, because of the tenderness of her modesty and her frail sex, lest she be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Yet He cast out both together, and did not wholly deprive them of the comfort of each other's company, nor of the keeping of the angels by whom they had been guided before, they being thenceforth grievously and inwardly penitent.

paras.t: Et collocavit ante paradisum voluptatis Cherubim, et flammeum gladium atque versatilem, ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ. Per Cherubim intelligitur angelicus spiritus seu angelus sanctus: per flammeum atque versatilem gladium, efficacissima ac pavenda potestas ipsius, quæ instar ignis gladiique ancipitis est activa ac superativa universæ contrariæ potestatis: quem angelum, talem gladium semper in promptu habentem, posuit Deus ante fores paradisi, ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ, id est, ad hoc, ut iter ad paradisum faceret omni homini inaccessibile. Porro in Scholastica historia dicitur: Ministerio angelorum posuit ignem, qui intercluderet paradisi ingressum. Qui ignis dicitur gladius non qualiscumque, sed versatilis, utpote utrobique secans et puniens, quia per eum punitus est homo in corpore et anima, per hoc quod irrevertibiliter de paradiso est expulsus. Vel dictus est versatilis, id est, aptus versari ac tolli quum Deo placeret, sicut ablatus est, dum primo Enoch, deinde Elias, illuc translati sunt.
paras.en: [[3:24|and placed before the paradise of pleasure Cherubims|Et collocavit ante paradisum voluptatis Cherubim]], [[3:24|and a flaming sword, turning every way, to keep the way of the tree of life|et flammeum gladium atque versatilem, ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ]]. By the Cherubim is understood an angelic spirit or holy angel; by the flaming and turning sword, his most effective and dreadful power, which, like fire and a two-edged sword, acts upon and overcomes every opposing power. This angel, having such a sword always at hand, God placed before the gates of paradise, [[3:24|to keep the way of the tree of life|ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ]], that is, to make the road to paradise inaccessible to every man. Further, the Scholastic History says: By the ministry of angels He set a fire to shut off the entry of paradise. This fire is called a sword, not of any kind, but turning, as cutting and punishing on both sides, because by it man was punished in body and soul, in that he was driven out of paradise beyond return. Or it is called turning, that is, apt to be turned aside and taken away when it should please God; as it was taken away when first Enoch and then Elias were carried there.

paras.t: Præterea quidam dicentes paradisum situm sub circulo æquinoctiali, per flammeum gladium intelligunt torridam zonam, quæ est inter paradisum et habitabilem terram: quæ zona vocatur versatilis gladius, quoniam sol causans impertransibilem illum calorem, accedit ad nos in æstate, et elongatur in hieme. Alii opinantes paradisum esse circa tropicum Cancri, per gladium istum intelligunt ignem aliquem materialem, divina virtute ibi factum et constitutum, ac exsurgentem de terra, quemadmodum de quibusdam montibus ignis erumpere legitur, præsertim de monte Ætnæ, qui jugiter ardet: qui ignis dicitur gladius, quoniam ascendendo instar gladii, paulatim in superiori sui parte acuitur. Per Cherubim autem angelica designatur custodia, quia secundum Augustinum, tota corporalis creatura per Sanctos administratur ac regitur: quod factum est, ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ, id est totius paradisi, a parte totum intelligendo, præsertim a parte tam principali, ut fuit hoc lignum; ad custodiendum, inquam, ne primi parentes, nec alii, possent naturali virtute illuc reverti aut aggredi, ita quod ignis ille est ante paradisi introitum, impediens accessum ad ipsum.
paras.en: Moreover, some who say that paradise is situated under the equinoctial circle understand by the flaming sword the torrid zone, which lies between paradise and the habitable earth; and this zone is called a turning sword because the sun, which causes that impassable heat, comes near to us in summer and draws away in winter. Others, thinking that paradise is near the tropic of Cancer, understand by this sword some material fire, made and set there by divine power and rising out of the earth, as fire is read to break forth from certain mountains, especially from Mount Etna, which burns continually; and this fire is called a sword because, as it rises, it grows gradually sharper in its upper part, like a sword. By the Cherubim, again, is signified the keeping of the angels, because according to Augustine the whole bodily creation is administered and ruled through the Saints [that is, the holy angels]; and this was done [[3:24|to keep the way of the tree of life|ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ]], that is, of the whole of paradise, the whole being understood from the part, especially from so principal a part as this tree was: to keep it, I say, so that neither our first parents nor others could return or make their way there by natural power; so that that fire is before the entrance of paradise, barring access to it.

3.title: Explanatio spiritualis ejusdem capituli tertii
3.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same third chapter

paras.t: Adam, ut ait Apostolus, erat forma futuri, id est figura Christi, nec solum Christi, sed et cujuslibet Christiani. Quemadmodum ergo diabolus invidit primis parentibus in paradiso constitutis, atque ex invidia eos tentavit, ita invidet universis fidelibus, qui in spirituali paradiso, videlicet in Ecclesia militante, sunt positi; vel in spirituali paradiso, hoc est in affluentia spiritualium consolationum ac divinorum charismatum.
paras.en: Adam, as the Apostle says, was [[Rom 5:14|a figure of him who was to come|forma futuri]], that is, a type of Christ; and not of Christ only, but of every Christian. As, then, the devil envied our first parents when they were set in paradise, and out of envy tempted them, so he envies all the faithful who are placed in the spiritual paradise, namely in the Church militant; or in the spiritual paradise, that is, in an abundance of spiritual consolations and divine gifts.

paras.t: Itaque ait Scriptura: Sed et serpens erat callidior cunctis animantibus terræ. Per serpentem designatur diabolus, veneno nequitiæ atque malitiæ plenus, qui callidior est cunctis animantibus terræ, id est hominibus, quos naturali acumine, experientia ac scientia, et præsertim in omni versutia ac fraudulentia antecedit. Qui dixit ad mulierem. Per mulierem, ut habitum est, intelligitur ratio inferior seu sensitiva pars animæ, quæ instar feminarum, mollis, fragilis atque inconstans est. Cur præcepit vobis Deus, ut non comederetis ex omni ligno paradisi? Per ligna paradisi, possunt intelligi ecclesiastici viri, virtutibus ac sapientia decorati. Porro, per lignum scientiæ boni et mali, Christus, in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi, qui inter bonum et malum perfectissime discrevit, et discernere docuit ac præcepit. Præcipit igitur nobis Deus comedere ex omni ligno paradisi, uno, utpote Christo, dempto, hoc est, omnium reliquorum sanctorum ac devotorum, qui sunt in Ecclesia militante, verbis et actibus refici, ædificari et informari, ita ut perfectionem eorum attingere studeamus. Nec desperemus nos posse eis parificari in perfectione gratiæ ac virtutum; imo unusquisque conari debet, ut alium præveniat ac vincat in omni humilitate, patientia, mansuetudine, custodia, diligentia, puritate ac caritate. Unde hortatur Apostolus: Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum. Sic autem non licet nobis refici verbis et actibus Christi, ut scilicet arbitremur nos posse ei coæquari in sapientia et virtute. Nec debemus præsumere, posse nos ejus perfectionem attingere, sed imitari pro viribus, quemadmodum dixit: Qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur.
paras.en: So the Scripture says: [[3:1|Now the serpent was more subtle than any of the beasts of the earth|Sed et serpens erat callidior cunctis animantibus terræ]]. By the serpent is signified the devil, full of the venom of wickedness and malice, who is more subtle than all the beasts of the earth, that is, than men, whom he surpasses in natural keenness, in experience and knowledge, and above all in every craft and deceit. [[3:1|he said to the woman|Qui dixit ad mulierem]]. By the woman, as has been said, is understood the lower reason [that is, the reason as it is turned toward temporal things, as distinct from the higher reason, which looks to the eternal], or the sensitive part of the soul, which, like women, is soft, frail and inconstant. [[3:1|Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?|Cur præcepit vobis Deus, ut non comederetis ex omni ligno paradisi]] By the trees of paradise may be understood men of the Church, adorned with virtues and wisdom; and by the tree of knowledge of good and evil, Christ, [[Col 2:3|In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge|in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi]], who discerned most perfectly between good and evil, and taught and commanded us to discern. God therefore commands us to eat of every tree of paradise save one, namely Christ: that is, to be fed, built up and formed by the words and deeds of all the other saints and devout souls who are in the Church militant, so that we strive to attain to their perfection. Nor should we despair of being able to equal them in the perfection of grace and virtues; rather, each one ought to strive to outstrip and surpass another in all humility, patience, meekness, watchfulness, diligence, purity and charity. Hence the Apostle exhorts us: [[Heb 10:24|let us consider one another, to provoke unto charity and to good works|Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum]]. But we may not be fed by the words and deeds of Christ in such a way as to think that we could be made equal to him in wisdom and virtue. Nor ought we to presume that we can attain to his perfection, but imitate it as far as our strength allows, as he said: [[John 12:26|If any man minister to me, let him follow me|Qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur]].

paras.t: Itaque diabolus tentat nos dicens, cur Deus istud præcepit nobis? Conatur enim ad hoc, ut transgrediamur terminos nobis præfixos, et plus sentiamus de nobis ipsis quam veritas habet, aut propriis viribus innitamur, et confidamus nos ex nobis ipsis posse proficere ac salvari, sicque parificemus nos quodammodo Christo: quod faciendo, comedimus de fructu scientiæ boni et mali; atque perimus, dum vir, id est ratio superior, consentit hujusmodi suggestioni serpentis antiqui, quæ suggestio venit ad rationem superiorem per inferiorem. Denique, dum ratio inferior recolit sibi a Deo esse prohibitum tale, imo et omne peccatum, ne moriatur nunc morte culpæ, deinde morte æternæ miseriæ, diabolus intus respondet: Nequaquam morte moriemini, quoniam persuadet licitum esse, quod exstat illicitum, et sub specie boni mala proponit: quod si persuadere nequiverit, tale quid licitum esse, suggerit Deum esse benignum, et hominem postea pœnitentiam esse acturum, vel saltem in fine vitæ sola contritione faciliter posse veniam impetrare. Insuper sæpe suadet quibusdam plus sapere quam oportet, et majestatem scrutari, atque incomprehensibilia fidei velle nimium profundare, discutere, ac rimari: qua suggestione decepit hæresiarchas, et per illos innumerabiles alios simplices et carnales, quibus occulte promisit interiorum oculorum aperitionem seu illustrationem, ita quod essent quasi dii inter ceteros futuri præfulgendo in sapientia, vita et fama: sicque recesserunt ab ecclesiastica unitate, opinantes se non indigere doctrina Ecclesiæ, eo quod ipsimet sufficienter cognoscerent bonum et malum.
paras.en: So the devil tempts us, saying: Why has God commanded us this? For he strives to make us pass beyond the bounds set for us, and think more of ourselves than the truth allows, or lean on our own strength and trust that we can of ourselves make progress and be saved, and so in a manner make ourselves equal to Christ. In doing this we eat of the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil; and we perish when the man, that is, the higher reason, consents to such a suggestion of the old serpent, a suggestion that comes to the higher reason through the lower. Then, when the lower reason calls to mind that such a thing, indeed every sin, has been forbidden it by God, lest it die, now by the death of guilt and afterwards by the death of eternal misery, the devil answers within: [[3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam morte moriemini]]; for he persuades it that what is unlawful is lawful, and sets evil before it under the appearance of good. And if he cannot persuade it that such a thing is lawful, he suggests that God is kind, and that the man will do penance afterwards, or at least can easily obtain pardon at the end of his life by contrition alone. Moreover, he often persuades some to be more wise than they ought, and to search into the majesty, and to want to sound, sift and probe too deeply the incomprehensible things of the faith. By this suggestion he deceived the heresiarchs, and through them countless other simple and carnal men, to whom he secretly promised an opening or enlightening of the inward eyes, so that they would be as gods among the rest, outshining them in wisdom, life and fame. And so they left the unity of the Church, thinking that they had no need of the Church's teaching, since they themselves knew good and evil well enough.

paras.t: Denique generalius loquendo, quandocumque sensualitas aut ratio inferior ex diabolica suggestione afficitur cum delectatione alicujus rei sensibili seu carnali, eo quod habeat aliquid dulcedinis aut decoris seu appetibilitatis vel utilitatis, tunc impletur quod dicitur: Vidit mulier quod bonum esset lignum, id est terrenum objectum instar ligni terræ infixum, bonum, inquam, ad vescendum, hoc est, ad oblectandum se in eo, adspectuque delectabile; et tulit de fructu ejus, et comedit, deditque viro suo qui comedit, hoc est, superiorem rationem ad consensum pertraxit. Et aperti sunt oculi amborum. Multi dum ex vehementia passionum inclinantur ad mala agenda, ita propriis passionibus obfuscantur, quod non advertunt suum errorem et magnitudinem sui periculi. Quum autem satisfecerunt motibus passionum suarum, motibus ipsis sedatis, aperiuntur oculi cordis eorum, et vident quam turpiter sint dejecti ac victi. Quumque cognovissent se esse nudos, consuerunt folia ficus, et fecerunt sibi perizomata. Sic multi quotidie, dum se peccasse cognoscunt, et gratia Dei nudatos, ac erubescibiliter supplantatos, faciunt perizomata sibi, excusando se ipsos, et velando turpitudines passionum et prævaricationum suarum. In quibus impletur quod scriptum est: Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum.
paras.en: Then, to speak more generally, whenever the sensuality or the lower reason, at the devil's suggestion, is moved with delight in some sensible or carnal thing, because it has some sweetness or beauty, or desirability or usefulness, then is fulfilled what is said: [[3:6|the woman saw that the tree was good|Vidit mulier quod bonum esset lignum]], that is, an earthly object, fixed in the earth like a tree; good, I say, [[3:6|to eat|ad vescendum]], that is, for taking delight in it, [[3:6|delightful to behold|adspectuque delectabile]]; [[3:6|and she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave to her husband, who did eat|et tulit de fructu ejus, et comedit, deditque viro suo qui comedit]]: that is, she drew the higher reason into consent. [[3:7|And the eyes of them both were opened|Et aperti sunt oculi amborum]]. Many, while they are inclined to do evil by the violence of their passions, are so blinded by their own passions that they do not notice their error and the greatness of their danger. But when they have satisfied the stirrings of their passions, and those stirrings have died down, the eyes of their heart are opened, and they see how shamefully they have been cast down and overcome. [[3:7|when they perceived themselves to be naked, they sewed together fig leaves, and made themselves aprons|Quumque cognovissent se esse nudos, consuerunt folia ficus, et fecerunt sibi perizomata]]. So many every day, when they know that they have sinned, and that they have been stripped of the grace of God and shamefully tripped up, make aprons for themselves by excusing themselves and veiling the foulness of their passions and transgressions. In them is fulfilled what is written: [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum]].

paras.t: Et quum audissent vocem Domini Dei deambulantis in paradiso ad auram post meridiem, abscondit se Adam et uxor ejus a facie Domini. Ambulat Dominus incessanter in paradiso, id est in militante Ecclesia, spatiando in cordibus electorum ac devotorum suorum, cum quibus esse sunt suæ deliciæ, quia per fidem et caritatem eos inhabitat: et ipsi portant eum in cordibus suis, quod modo fit post meridiem, id est, post ardentissimum illum Spiritus Sancti fervorem, qui fuit in primitiva Ecclesia, et postea diu ac sæpius interim: quod dum fit, quidam imitantes transgressionem primorum parentum, abscondunt se, quantum in ipsis est, a facie Domini, a quo impie se avertunt, et fugiunt lucem, sicut ait Salvator: Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem; et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus. Denique qui retrahunt se a superiorum suorum præsentia, nec volunt verba correptionis ac salutis audire, ne increpentur, et juste confundantur, abscondunt se a facie Domini, quales sunt qui in pravitatibus suis latere nituntur. Abscondunt se quoque in medio ligni paradisi, qui auctoritatibus et allegationibus Scripturarum se excusare ac justificare conantur. Nam et ipsa Scriptura per paradisum significatur, secundum Damascenum.
paras.en: [[3:8|And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the afternoon air, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord|Et quum audissent vocem Domini Dei deambulantis in paradiso ad auram post meridiem, abscondit se Adam et uxor ejus a facie Domini]]. The Lord walks unceasingly in paradise, that is, in the Church militant, going about in the hearts of his elect and devout, with whom to be is his delight[[Prov 8:31||]], because he dwells in them by faith and charity[[Eph 3:17||]]; and they bear him in their hearts. And this now happens in the afternoon, that is, after that most ardent fervour of the Holy Ghost which was in the primitive Church, and afterwards for long and often in the meantime. While this happens, some, imitating the transgression of our first parents, hide themselves, as far as in them lies, from the face of the Lord, from whom they wickedly turn away, and they flee the light, as the Saviour says: [[John 3:20|every one that doth evil hateth the light and cometh not to the light, that his works may not be reproved|Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem; et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus]]. Again, those who withdraw from the presence of their superiors and will not hear words of correction and salvation, lest they be rebuked and justly put to shame, hide themselves from the face of the Lord: such are those who strive to hide in their wickedness. They also hide [[3:8|amidst the trees of paradise|in medio ligni paradisi]] who try to excuse and justify themselves by the authorities and texts of the Scriptures. For Scripture itself is signified by paradise, according to Damascene.

paras.t: Vocavitque Dominus Deus Adam, et dixit ei: Ubi es? Sic benignissimus Deus quotidie vocat aversos a se, ut attendant in quantis miseriis, periculis, vitiisque prostrati sint: vocat, inquam, per inspirationem internam, per angelicam custodiam, per prælatos et prædicatores Ecclesiæ, per proximorum exhortationes, per correptiones, per miracula, per beneficia, per adversa. Qui ait: Vocem tuam Domine, audivi in paradiso, et timui. Sic quidam in suis iniquitatibus deprehensi, quando se vident non posse latere, neque evadere, se peccasse fatentur, ac metuunt saltem servili timore. Cui dixit Dominus Deus: Quis enim indicavit tibi, quod nudus esses, nisi quod ex ligno, de quo præceperam tibi ne comederes, comedisti? Quasi Dominus dicat unicuique peccatori hujusmodi: Unde jam per experientiam scis te esse nudatum donis ac gratiis Spiritus Sancti, nisi quia conscius tibi es, te egisse contra meum præceptum, et præsumpsisti de viribus propriis ac extulisti inaniter temetipsum?
paras.en: [[3:9|And the Lord God called Adam, and said to him: Where art thou?|Vocavitque Dominus Deus Adam, et dixit ei: Ubi es?]] So the most kind God daily calls those who have turned away from him, that they may consider in what great miseries, dangers and vices they lie prostrate. He calls, I say, by inward inspiration, by the guardianship of the angels, by the prelates and preachers of the Church, by the exhortations of their neighbours, by corrections, by miracles, by benefits, by adversities. [[3:10|And he said|Qui ait]]: [[3:10|I heard thy voice|Vocem tuam]], O Lord, [[3:10|in paradise; and I was afraid|audivi in paradiso, et timui]]. So some, caught in their iniquities, when they see that they cannot hide or escape, confess that they have sinned, and are afraid, at least with servile fear [that is, fear of punishment, as distinct from the filial fear that springs from love]. Then the Lord God said to him: [[3:11|who hath told thee that thou wast naked, but that thou hast eaten of the tree whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat?|Quis enim indicavit tibi, quod nudus esses, nisi quod ex ligno, de quo præceperam tibi ne comederes, comedisti?]] As if the Lord were saying to every such sinner: How do you now know by experience that you have been stripped of the gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost, except that you are conscious of having acted against my commandment, and have presumed on your own strength and vainly exalted yourself?

paras.t: Dixitque Adam: Mulier quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi. Sic multi quotidie se ipsos excusant per alios, a quibus se ad mala attractos causantur, quasi non sponte peccassent, et quasi non magis debuissent Deum, quam homines attendisse, aut quasi nil melius cognovissent. Præterea quidam excusant se per mulierem, id est per propriam sensualitatem, seu carnis fragilitatem, quam suo spiritui sociatam commemorant, dicentes: Homo non est angelus, humanum est peccare, quis perfectus nisi Deus? Et ita palpant ac fallunt miseri semetipsos, imo peccata sua occulte atque implicite retorquent in Creatorem, qui tam fragilem eis contulit carnem, et sensualitatem ad mala tam pronam. Nec attendunt, quam multa et magna remedia et auxilia præstiterit eis Deus contra peccata ac hostes suæ salutis.
paras.en: [[3:12|And Adam said: The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion, gave me of the tree, and I did eat|Dixitque Adam: Mulier quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi]]. So many every day excuse themselves by others, by whom they plead that they were drawn into evil, as though they had not sinned willingly, and as though they ought not to have heeded God rather than men, or as though they had known nothing better. Some, again, excuse themselves by the woman, that is, by their own sensuality or the frailty of the flesh, which they recall was joined as a companion to their spirit, saying: Man is not an angel; to sin is human; who is perfect but God? And so the wretches flatter and deceive themselves; nay, they secretly and implicitly turn their sins back upon the Creator, who gave them flesh so frail and a sensuality so prone to evil. Nor do they consider how many and how great are the remedies and helps God has given them against sins and the enemies of their salvation.

paras.t: Et dixit Dominus Deus ad mulierem: Quare hoc fecisti? Quæ respondit: Serpens decepit me. Sic et ratio inferior, seu homo ex parte suæ sensualitatis, solet se excusare, eo quod diabolica fraude, aut tentationis fervore deceptus sit. Hæc est culpa gravissima et insipientia miseranda, excusare se ipsum, et alium potius accusare. Propter quod oravit Psalmista: Ne declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis. Unde et Salomon loquitur: Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit, et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur.
paras.en: [[3:13|And the Lord God said to the woman: Why hast thou done this? And she answered: The serpent deceived me|Et dixit Dominus Deus ad mulierem: Quare hoc fecisti? Quæ respondit: Serpens decepit me]]. So too the lower reason, or man on the side of his sensuality, is wont to excuse himself on the ground that he was deceived by the devil's fraud or by the heat of temptation. This is a most grievous fault and a pitiable folly, to excuse oneself and rather to accuse another. For this reason the Psalmist prayed: [[Ps 140:4|Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins|Ne declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis]]. And so Solomon says: [[Prov 28:13|He that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy|Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit, et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur]].

paras.t: Et ait Dominus ad serpentem: Quia hoc fecisti, maledictus eris. Diabolus enim homines decipiendo, meretur suæ maledictionis augmentum, præsertim quantum ad accidentalis sui supplicii cumulum, sicut et angelorum sanctorum accidentale præmium augmentatur ex eorum, quos custodiunt, salvatione. Quæ autem sequuntur, videlicet, Super pectus tuum gradieris, usque ad illud, Mulieri quoque dixit Deus, in præcedenti articulo satis spiritualiter sunt tractata.
paras.en: And the Lord [[3:14|said to the serpent|ait Dominus ad serpentem]]: [[3:14|Because thou hast done this thing|Quia hoc fecisti]], [[3:14|thou art cursed|maledictus eris]] [Denis reads *maledictus eris*, "thou shalt be cursed", for the Vulgate's *maledictus es*]. For the devil, by deceiving men, earns an increase of his curse, above all as regards the heaping up of his accidental punishment [that is, the pains added to the essential punishment of the damned], just as the accidental reward of the holy angels is increased by the salvation of those whom they guard. What follows, namely [[3:14|upon thy breast shalt thou go|Super pectus tuum gradieris]], as far as [[3:16|To the woman also he said|Mulieri quoque dixit Deus]], has been treated spiritually enough in the preceding article.

paras.t: Mulieri quoque dixit Deus: Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas et conceptus tuos. Hoc spiritualiter factum est, quoniam homo male agendo, incurrit calamitatem multiplicem, et sensitiva pars ratioque inferior difficultatem incurrit ad bene agendum, ad resistendum peccato, ad fructificandum justitiæ, et in dolore parit opera bona. Et sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui, hoc est, propter peccata tua subjacebis actibus tuis, atque laboribus pœnitentiæ ac flagellis, juxta superioris rationis imperium, quæ si non peccasses, sine hujusmodi castigatione posses rationi superiori parere.
paras.en: [[3:16|To the woman also he said: I will multiply thy sorrows, and thy conceptions|Mulieri quoque dixit Deus: Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas et conceptus tuos]]. This has come about spiritually, since man by doing evil incurs manifold calamity, and the sensitive part and the lower reason incur difficulty in doing good, in resisting sin, in bearing the fruit of justice, and bring forth good works in sorrow. [[3:16|and thou shalt be under thy husband's power, and he shall have dominion over thee|Et sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui]]: that is, because of your sins you shall be subject to your own acts, and to the labours and scourges of penance, at the command of the higher reason; whereas had you not sinned, you could have obeyed the higher reason without chastisement of this kind.

paras.t: Adæ vero dixit: Quia audisti vocem uxoris tuæ, maledicta terra in opere tuo, id est, unicuique peccatori loquitur Deus in Scripturis: Quoniam sensitivæ parti, et inferiori rationi impie consensisti, caro tua multis subjacebit miseriis, et motus rebelles tanquam spinas ac tribulos pariet tibi, multisque modis impediet te a bonis, et terrenis reficieris operibus. Nec sine gemitu et sudore exerces assidue opera bona. Istud est grave jugum super omnes posteros Adæ inductum, de quo in Ecclesiastico legitur: Occupatio magna creata est omnibus hominibus, et jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium, cogitationes eorum et timores cordis, etc. In Zacharia quoque habetur: Homo agricola ego sum, et Adam exemplum meum ab adolescentia mea.
paras.en: [[3:17|And to Adam he said: Because thou hast hearkened to the voice of thy wife|Adæ vero dixit: Quia audisti vocem uxoris tuæ]], [[3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|maledicta terra in opere tuo]]: that is, God says to every sinner in the Scriptures: Because you have wickedly consented to the sensitive part and the lower reason, your flesh shall be subject to many miseries, and shall bring forth for you rebellious stirrings like thorns and thistles, and shall hinder you from good things in many ways, and you shall be fed with earthly works. Nor do you constantly do good works without groaning and sweat.
