This is the heavy yoke laid upon all the descendants of Adam, of which we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 40:1|Great labour is created for all men, and a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming out of their mother's womb, until the day of their burial into the mother of all|Occupatio magna creata est omnibus hominibus, et jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium]], [[Ecclus 40:2|Their thoughts, and fears of the heart|cogitationes eorum et timores cordis]], etc. And in Zacharias we have: [[Zach 13:5|I am a husbandman: for Adam is my example from my youth|Homo agricola ego sum, et Adam exemplum meum ab adolescentia mea]].

paras.t: Et vocavit Adam nomen uxoris suæ, Eva, eo quod mater esset omnium viventium. Sic peccator postquam vere conversus est, carnem suam nominat Evam, id est vitam, quia per eam efficit de cetero opera bona, quæ sunt spiritualiter viva ac meritoria. Fecit quoque Deus Adæ et uxori ejus tunicas pelliceas, et induit eos. Per tunicas pelliceas designantur pœnalitates et defectuositates vitæ mortalis, quibus homines peccatores in sæculo isto implentur et operiuntur ita, ut juste ac pie derelinquantur a Deo de suis præsumptionibus, elationibus vanitatibusque diversis.
paras.en: [[3:20|And Adam called the name of his wife Eve: because she was the mother of all the living|Et vocavit Adam nomen uxoris suæ, Eva, eo quod mater esset omnium viventium]]. So the sinner, once he is truly converted, names his flesh Eve, that is, life, because through it he henceforth does good works, which are spiritually living and meritorious. [[3:21|And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skins, and clothed them|Fecit quoque Deus Adæ et uxori ejus tunicas pelliceas, et induit eos]]. By the garments of skins are signified the penalties and defects of mortal life, with which sinful men are filled and covered in this world, so that, justly and mercifully, they are forsaken by God on account of their presumptions, their pride and their various vanities [the sense of *derelinquantur a Deo de suis præsumptionibus* is uncertain; it may mean that God mercifully leaves them stripped of these].

paras.t: Nunc ergo ne forte mittat manum suam, et sumat de ligno vitæ, etc. Sic Deus per angelos sanctos repulit, et misericorditer impedit homines a multis præsumptionibus et peccatis. Et emisit eum Dominus Deus de paradiso voluptatis, ut operaretur terram. Quamdiu homo manet in caritate et gratia ac gaudio spirituali, manet in Ecclesia, et item in interiori suæ animæ paradiso. Quum autem mortaliter peccat, utroque hoc paradiso privatur, et de mystico corpore Christi ejicitur, atque diabolo incorporatur. Verumtamen fit hoc ut se emendet, et terram, utpote propriam carnem, per opera pœnitentiæ exercere et castigare festinet. Et collocavit Deus ante paradisum Cherubim et flammeum gladium, id est, Ecclesiam suam munivit angelorum custodia, ac plenitudine sapientiæ salutaris, rigore quoque justitiæ, ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ, id est ingressum et aditum ad ecclesiasticam unitatem et Christi communionem, ad quas iniqui redire non valent, nisi per pœnitentiam veram.
paras.en: [[3:22|now therefore lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life|Nunc ergo ne forte mittat manum suam, et sumat de ligno vitæ]], etc. So God through the holy angels has driven back, and mercifully hinders, men from many presumptions and sins. [[3:23|And the Lord God sent him out of the paradise of pleasure, to till the earth|Et emisit eum Dominus Deus de paradiso voluptatis, ut operaretur terram]]. As long as a man remains in charity and grace and spiritual joy, he remains in the Church, and also in the inner paradise of his soul. But when he sins mortally, he is deprived of both these paradises, and is cast out of the mystical body of Christ and incorporated into the devil. Yet this is done so that he may amend himself, and make haste to work and chastise the earth, that is, his own flesh, by works of penance. And God [[3:24|placed before the paradise of pleasure Cherubims, and a flaming sword|collocavit Deus ante paradisum Cherubim et flammeum gladium]]: that is, he has fortified his Church with the guardianship of the angels, with the fullness of saving wisdom, and also with the rigour of justice, [[3:24|to keep the way of the tree of life|ad custodiendam viam ligni vitæ]], that is, the entrance and approach to the unity of the Church and the communion of Christ, to which the wicked cannot return except by true penance.

paras.t: Denique ejectio Adæ de paradiso, fuit quasi excommunicatio ejus, quæ in solenni pœnitentia specialiter designatur. Fiat autem pœnitentia solennis hoc modo: In capite jejunii tales pœnitentes præsentant se cum presbyteris suis episcopo ante fores ecclesiæ, sacco induti, nudis pedibus, vultibus inclinatis, et coma deposita. Quum autem in ecclesiam fuerint introducti, episcopus cum omni clero dicit septem psalmos pœnitentiales, deinde manum eis imponit, aquam benedictam adspergit, cineremque imponit eorum capitibus, cilicio quoque operit colla eorum, et lacrimabiliter eis denuntiat, quod sicut Adam ejectus est de paradiso, sic ipsi de ecclesia ejiciuntur, et jubet ministris, ut eos ab ecclesia pellant, clero eos persequente cum responsorio isto: In sudore vultus tui. In Cœna autem Domini quolibet anno a suis presbyteris in ecclesiam reducuntur, et erunt in ea usque ad octavas Paschæ, ita tamen quod non communicabunt nec pacem accipient. Sicque fiet omni anno quamdiu aditus ecclesiæ ipsis est interdictus, quorum ultima reconciliatio reservatur episcopo, ad quem solum spectat impositio pœnitentiæ hujus solennis. Quæ etiam potest imponi viris ac mulieribus, sed non clericis, propter scandalum evitandum, et ne Ordo veniat in contemptum. Nec debet imponi pœnitentia talis, nisi pro peccato quod totam commoverit urbem. Hæc Thomas super quartum, distinctione 14.
paras.en: Lastly, the casting of Adam out of paradise was as it were his excommunication, which is especially represented in solemn penance [that is, the public penance enjoined by the bishop for grave and notorious sins]. Solemn penance is done in this way. At the beginning of the fast [that is, on Ash Wednesday] such penitents present themselves with their priests to the bishop before the doors of the church, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, with faces bowed and hair shorn. When they have been brought into the church, the bishop with all the clergy says the seven penitential psalms; then he lays his hand on them, sprinkles holy water, puts ashes on their heads, covers their necks with haircloth, and with tears declares to them that as Adam was cast out of paradise, so they are cast out of the church; and he bids the ministers drive them out of the church, the clergy following them with this responsory: [[3:19|In the sweat of thy face|In sudore vultus tui]]. On the day of the Lord's Supper [that is, Maundy Thursday] each year they are brought back into the church by their priests, and remain in it until the octave of Easter, yet in such a way that they do not communicate or receive the peace. And so it shall be done every year as long as entry into the church is forbidden them; their final reconciliation is reserved to the bishop, to whom alone belongs the imposing of this solemn penance. It may be imposed on men and women, but not on clerics, to avoid scandal and lest Holy Orders come into contempt. Nor ought such penance to be imposed except for a sin that has stirred the whole city. Thus Thomas on the fourth book of the Sentences, distinction 14.

paras.t: Porro in Scholastica historia dicitur: Ejectionem primorum parentum repræsentat Ecclesia in capite jejunii, quum ejicit extra pœnitentes, quibus cilicium dat in signum tunicarum pellicearum, cinerem quoque sub his verbis: Cinis es, et in cinerem reverteris. In memoriam maledictionis, ejecti candelas ferunt ardentes: quia pro opere, quo porrexerunt manus ad pomum vetitum, apposita est ignea romphæa paradiso. Transeunt item ad aliam ecclesiam, cujus fores coram eis clauduntur, in signum aditus paradisi quondam occlusi. Non ad mensam, sed super terram comedunt, quasi dicatur eis: Maledicta terra in opere tuo. Nemo dicit eis, ave, quia nondum mutatum erat nomen Evæ.
paras.en: Further, it is said in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]: The Church represents the casting out of our first parents at the beginning of the fast, when she casts the penitents out, giving them haircloth as a sign of the garments of skins, and ashes also, with these words: Ashes thou art, and unto ashes thou shalt return [the rite says "ashes" where Genesis has "dust"]. In memory of the curse, those cast out carry burning candles, because, for the deed by which they stretched out their hands to the forbidden apple, a fiery sword [*romphæa*] was set before paradise. They also pass on to another church, whose doors are shut in their faces, as a sign of the entrance to paradise once closed. They eat not at table but on the ground, as if it were said to them: [[3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|Maledicta terra in opere tuo]]. No one says *Ave* ["hail"] to them, because the name of Eve had not yet been changed [*Ave* reverses *Eva*: the name of Eve was "changed" when the Angel greeted Mary with *Ave*].

paras.t: Præterea in modo tentationis primorum parentum, præfiguratus est ordo tentationum nostrarum quotidianarum. Quemadmodum enim serpens tentavit primo mulierem, et per eam virum, sic dæmon per sensitivam partem et inferiorem rationem, tentat in nobis rationem superiorem.
paras.en: Moreover, in the manner of the temptation of our first parents is prefigured the order of our daily temptations. For as the serpent tempted first the woman, and through her the man, so the demon tempts the higher reason in us through the sensitive part and the lower reason.

paras.t: De hac materia ait Magister Sententiarum libro secundo: Duæ sunt species tentationis, interior atque exterior. Exterior tentatio est, quando nobis extrinsecus visibiliter suggeritur verbo aut signo, ut ad peccati consensum trahamur, et talis tentatio non fit nisi ab adversario, scilicet diabolo, vel ab homine malo. Interior vero tentatio est, quando invisibiliter suggeritur nobis malum intrinsecus, quæ tentatio aliquando fit ab hoste, quandoque a carne. Nam et diabolus invisibiliter suggerit mala, et ex carnis corruptione suboritur motus illicitus et titillatio prava: idcirco tentatio quæ fit ex carne, non est sine peccato; quæ autem ab hoste fit, nisi ei consentiatur, non habet peccatum, sed est materia exercendæ virtutis.
paras.en: On this matter the Master of the Sentences [Peter Lombard] says in the second book: There are two kinds of temptation, inward and outward. Outward temptation is when something is suggested to us visibly from without, by word or sign, so that we may be drawn to consent to sin; and such temptation comes only from the adversary, that is, the devil, or from a wicked man. Inward temptation is when evil is suggested to us invisibly from within; and this temptation comes sometimes from the enemy, sometimes from the flesh. For the devil too suggests evil invisibly, and from the corruption of the flesh there springs up an unlawful stirring and a wicked tickling. Therefore the temptation that comes from the flesh is not without sin; but that which comes from the enemy, unless it be consented to, has no sin, but is matter for the exercise of virtue.

paras.t: Circa hæc verba Magistri scribit Thomas super secundum, distinctione 21: Peccatum unius non consistit in actu alterius, sed in proprio actu. In tentatione autem carnis, ipse appetitus illicitus secundum quem aliquis tentari dicitur, est actus ejus qui tentatur. Non enim sola caro concupiscit, sed totus homo: ideo talis tentatio est peccatum in eo qui tentatur. Tentatio autem quæ est a mundo, vel ab hoste, est a principio extrinseco: unde actus non pertinet ad tentatum, sed passio tantum; et propter hoc non est peccatum in tali tentatione, nisi per delectationem et consensum tentati, quoniam tunc tentatus incipit cooperari tentanti. Porro motus concupiscibilis dupliciter potest consurgere. Primo, ex qualitate organi, sicut corpore calefacto, insurgit motus libidinis sine omni imaginatione, et iste motus est pure naturalis, nec habet rationem peccati: ad hunc quoque motum excitandum in nobis potest virtus dæmonis ex potestate suæ naturæ, qua potest corpora transmutare, nisi cohibeatur virtute divina. Alius motus concupiscibilis est, qui insurgit ex apprehensione rei delectabilis. Et ex hac parte appetitus concupiscibilis aliquam habet libertatem in homine, secundum quod potest obedire imperio rationis. Sed hunc motum diabolus extorquere non valet. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: On these words of the Master, Thomas writes on the second book, distinction 21: The sin of one man does not consist in the act of another, but in his own act. Now in the temptation of the flesh, the unlawful desire itself, in respect of which someone is said to be tempted, is an act of the one who is tempted. For it is not the flesh alone that lusts, but the whole man; and so such temptation is sin in the one who is tempted. But the temptation that comes from the world or from the enemy comes from an outward principle; hence the act does not belong to the one tempted, but only the undergoing of it; and for this reason there is no sin in such temptation except through the delight and consent of the one tempted, since then the one tempted begins to work together with the tempter. Further, a stirring of the concupiscible appetite [that is, the appetite that desires what is pleasant to the senses] can arise in two ways. First, from the condition of the bodily organ, as when, the body being heated, a stirring of lust arises without any imagining; and this stirring is purely natural and has not the nature of sin. The power of the demon too can excite this stirring in us, by the power of his nature, by which he can change bodies, unless he is restrained by divine power. The other stirring of the concupiscible appetite is that which arises from the apprehension of something delightful. And on this side the concupiscible appetite has some freedom in man, in so far as it can obey the command of reason. But this stirring the devil cannot force from us. Thus Thomas.

paras.t: At vero Bonaventura in scripto secundi circa hæc scribit: Tentare multa significat, sed proprie idem est quod probare; idcirco tentatio dici potest quidam tactus, quo probatur res illa quæ tangitur, quemadmodum dicitur cæcus tentare, quando tactu suo certitudinem aliquam vult habere de eo quod tangit. Juxta hunc modum in spiritualibus tentatio dicitur quidam tactus ad probandum ordinatus, quod quadrupliciter fieri potest: Aut enim ille qui pulsat seu tentat, intendit probare et approbare, seu probatum ostendere; et hoc modo tentare convenit Deo, secundum quod dicitur a Sapiente: Deus tentavit illos, et invenit eos dignos se. Aut quia ille qui pulsat, intendit probare et reprobare seu reprobum facere; sicque tentat diabolus, secundum quod scribitur in Actis: Cur tentavit Satanas cor tuum? Aut intendit solum probare, et experimentum sumere de eo quod est in homine; et ita tentare dicitur homo cautus. Aut quia etsi pulsans nihil intendit, ad ejus tamen pulsationem sequitur approbatio aut reprobatio hominis; sicque tentare dicitur caro et concupiscentia ejus, ut Jacobus ait: Unusquisque tentatur a concupiscentia sua, etc. A carne enim seu carnis concupiscentia homo pulsatur, et quasi tangitur: cui pulsationi si consenserit, probatur et reprobatur; si dissenserit, probatur et approbatur.
paras.en: But Bonaventure, in his writing on the second book, says on these things: To tempt has many meanings, but properly it is the same as to test; therefore temptation can be called a kind of touching by which the thing touched is tested, as a blind man is said to try [*tentare*, the same word as "tempt"] when by his touch he wishes to have some certainty about what he touches. In this way, in spiritual things, temptation is called a kind of touching ordered to testing, which can happen in four ways. Either he who knocks or tempts intends to test and approve, or to show a thing tested and proved; and in this way tempting befits God, as the Wise Man says: [[Wis 3:5|God hath tried them, and found them worthy of himself|Deus tentavit illos, et invenit eos dignos se]]. Or he who knocks intends to test and reject, or to make reprobate; and so the devil tempts, as is written in the Acts: [[Acts 5:3|why hath Satan tempted thy heart|Cur tentavit Satanas cor tuum]]? Or he intends only to test and to find out by trial what is in a man; and so a cautious man is said to try. Or, though the one knocking intends nothing, yet upon his knocking there follows the approval or rejection of the man; and so the flesh and its concupiscence are said to tempt, as James says: [[Jas 1:14|every man is tempted by his own concupiscence|Unusquisque tentatur a concupiscentia sua]], etc. For a man is knocked at, and as it were touched, by the flesh or the concupiscence of the flesh: if he consents to that knocking, he is tested and rejected; if he refuses consent, he is tested and approved.

3.title: Introductio et solutio quæstionum concernentium præsens tertium capitulum
3.title_en: Introduction and solution of questions concerning the present third chapter

paras.t: MULTA occurrunt quærenda circa capitulum istud: Primum est, cur Deus permisit primos parentes tentari, quos præscivit mox esse vincendos; et, an decuit Deus hoc ipsum permittere, præsertim quum viderit tot mala ex originali illo peccato esse protinus secutura. Quamvis autem Magister Sententiarum libro secundo hanc moveat quæstionem et solvat similiter doctores ibidem, videtur tamen hæc quæstio posse reprimi per multas quæstiones consimiles. Nam simili modo quæri posset, cur Deus creavit Luciferum, quem vidit confestim casurum; et, cur permisit eum peccare, ex cujus casu noverat secutura statim tot mala: imo, cur condidit eum, per quem noverat tot millia angelorum esse confestim casura. Iterum quæri posset, cur Deus promovit Jeroboam filium Nabat in regem decem tribuum Israel, quem noverat statim tot horribilia mala acturum, et aversurum subditos suos a cultu Dei, atque ad idololatriam inducturum. Item, cur creavit sceleratissimum Mahometum, per quem noverat pene tertiam aut quartam mundi partem esse decipiendam. Cur item nequissimos hæresiarchas, Manichæum, Arium, Nestorium, etc., a quibus scivit tot millia hominum esse fallenda. In his atque similibus debemus incomprehensibilia Dei judicia potius formidare ac venerari, quam discutere ac scrutari. Nihilo minus rationabiles causæ horum assignantur. Deus enim cuncta propter bonum finem creavit, nec debuit omittere quod est suum, propter abusiones rerum factarum: quas tamen non permisisset, nisi scivisset, potuisset, ac voluisset multa bona ex malis aliorum elicere. Porro solutio quæstionis de parentibus primis propositæ, patet ex solutione quæstionis superius motæ, videlicet, cur Deus condidit hominem, quem noverat mox casurum.
paras.en: Many things present themselves to be inquired into concerning this chapter. The first is why God permitted our first parents to be tempted, whom He foreknew would soon be overcome; and whether it was fitting for God to permit this, especially since He saw that so many evils would at once follow from that original sin. Now although the Master of the Sentences [Peter Lombard] raises this question in his second book and solves it, as do the doctors likewise in the same place, yet this question can, it seems, be put to rest by many like questions. For in like manner it might be asked why God created Lucifer, whom He saw would fall at once; and why He permitted him to sin, from whose fall He knew that so many evils would straightway follow; nay, why He made him through whom He knew that so many thousands of angels would at once fall. Again, it might be asked why God raised Jeroboam the son of Nabat to be king of the ten tribes of Israel[[3 Kings 11:31||]], whom He knew would at once do so many horrible evils, turn his subjects away from the worship of God and lead them into idolatry. Likewise, why He created the most wicked Mahomet, by whom He knew that almost a third or a fourth part of the world would be deceived. Why, likewise, the most wicked heresiarchs, Manichæus, Arius, Nestorius, etc., by whom He knew that so many thousands of men would be led astray. In these and the like we ought rather to fear and revere the incomprehensible judgments of God than to discuss and scrutinize them. Nonetheless reasonable causes are assigned for them. For God created all things for a good end, and He ought not to leave off what is His own because of the abuses of the things He made: abuses which, however, He would not have permitted, had He not known how, and been able, and willed to draw many goods out of the evils of others. Furthermore, the solution of the question put about our first parents is plain from the solution of the question raised above, namely why God made man, whom He knew would soon fall.

paras.t: Secundo quæritur, an primi parentes fuerint creati in gratia gratum faciente, et virtutibus ei annexis. Et respondendum est, quod circa hoc est triplex opinio: Prima dicentium, quod non fuerunt creati in gratia tali, nec eam promeruerunt post creationem et ante lapsum, sic quod nunquam habuerunt gratiam gratum facientem in paradiso. Hanc autem opinionem reprobat Magister libro secundo per multas auctoritates Sanctorum, quæ infra tangentur. Secunda ergo est opinio ipsius Magistri, qui libro secundo dicit primum hominem non fuisse creatum in gratia gratificante, sed meruisse eamdem ante suam ruinam: ad quod adduxit quasdam auctoritates, præcipue Augustini. Hanc opinionem sequuntur Bonaventura et alii multi. Tertia opinio tenet, quod primus homo fuit in gratia gratum faciente creatus, sicut et angeli: quam opinionem sequuntur Albertus et Thomas, multique alii.
paras.en: Secondly, it is asked whether our first parents were created in sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a person pleasing to God] and the virtues joined to it. And the answer must be that there are three opinions about this. The first is of those who say that they were not created in such grace, nor did they merit it after their creation and before the fall, so that they never had sanctifying grace in paradise. This opinion the Master rejects in his second book by many authorities of the Saints, which will be touched on below. The second, then, is the opinion of the Master himself, who says in his second book that the first man was not created in sanctifying grace, but merited it before his ruin; for which he brought forward certain authorities, chiefly of Augustine. This opinion Bonaventure and many others follow. The third opinion holds that the first man was created in sanctifying grace, as were the angels too; and this opinion Albert and Thomas follow, and many others.

paras.t: Et sanctus Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 95, probat hoc sic: Deus creavit primos parentes in originali justitia, quemadmodum ait Scriptura: Deus fecit hominem ab initio rectum. Hæc autem justitia seu rectitudo consistit in subjectione rationis ac voluntatis sub Deo, inferiorumque virium sub ratione, corporis quoque sub anima. Porro subjectio inferiorum virium sub ratione, dependebat ex subjectione rationis et voluntatis sub Deo; subjectio autem carnis sub anima, ex utraque pendebat, sed talis rectitudo sine gratificante gratia esse non potuit, alioqui mansisset in illis post culpam. Hinc insuper scribit Thomas, quod primus homo habuit ante suum lapsum quodammodo omnes virtutes, quia præfata rectitudo hoc exigit. Sunt tamen quædam virtutes, quæ in sua ratione nullam imperfectionem includunt, sicut justitia, caritas, prudentia: et hæ erant in eo secundum actum et habitum. Aliæ autem imperfectionem includunt, vel ex parte actus, aut ex parte objecti: et istæ etiam in eo fuerunt actu et habitu, si imperfectio illa perfectioni primi status, utpote innocentiæ, non derogavit, ut fides et spes; si autem derogavit, erant in ipso secundum habitum, non secundum actum, ut pœnitentia quæ est dolor de peccato, et misericordia quæ est compassio miseriæ alienæ.
paras.en: And St Thomas, in the First Part, question 95, proves it thus. God created our first parents in original justice, as Scripture says: [[Eccles 7:30|God made man right|Deus fecit hominem ab initio rectum]] [Denis's wording adds *ab initio*, "from the beginning"]. Now this justice or rectitude consists in the subjection of reason and will to God, of the lower powers to reason, and also of the body to the soul. Furthermore, the subjection of the lower powers to reason depended on the subjection of reason and will to God; and the subjection of the flesh to the soul depended on both. But such rectitude could not be without sanctifying grace; otherwise it would have remained in them after the fault. Hence Thomas writes moreover that the first man before his fall had in a manner all the virtues, since the aforesaid rectitude requires this. There are, however, certain virtues which in their nature include no imperfection, such as justice, charity, prudence; and these were in him both in act and in habit. Others include an imperfection, either on the side of the act or on the side of the object; and these too were in him in act and habit if that imperfection did not take away from the perfection of the first state, that is, of innocence, as faith and hope; but if it did, they were in him in habit, not in act, as penance, which is sorrow for sin, and mercy, which is compassion for another's misery.

paras.t: Hæc autem opinio verior rationabiliorque videtur. Primo, quoniam ratio et voluntas non potuerunt Deo esse subjectæ sine fide et caritate. Inferiores quoque vires, sine virtutibus moralibus subjectæ nequeunt esse rationi et voluntati. Secundo, quoniam Augustinus in quadam loquitur homilia: Adam perdita caritate, malus inventus est. Denique: Princeps vitiorum diabolus, dum vicit Adam, de limo terræ ad imaginem Dei factum, pudicitia armatum, temperantia compositum, caritate splendidum, primos parentes illis bonis expoliavit, pariterque peremit. Ambrosius quoque ad Sabinum disserit: Quando Adam solus fuit, prævaricatus non est, quia mens ejus Deo adhæsit. Et rursus Augustinus fatetur, quod spirituali mente præditus fuit. Superius etiam dictum est super illud, Misit Dominus soporem in Adam, quod tunc in altissimam contemplationem huic vitæ possibilem, est perductus. Iterum S. Bernardus: Quum omnium, inquit, hominum æmulus videret patrem nostrum Adam caritate circumdatum, et omni virtute vestitum, invidit ei. Insuper Damascenus libro secundo fatetur: Deus fecit hominem rectum, innocentem, virtuosum, omni virtute decoratum, omnibus bonis comatum, velut quemdam mundum secundum. Postremo in Ecclesiastico legitur: Deus de terra creavit hominem, et secundum se vestivit illum virtute.
paras.en: And this opinion seems the truer and the more reasonable. First, because reason and will could not be subject to God without faith and charity; and the lower powers cannot be subject to reason and will without the moral virtues. Secondly, because Augustine says in a certain homily: Adam, having lost charity, was found evil. And again: The devil, the prince of vices, when he overcame Adam, who was made of the slime of the earth to the image of God, armed with chastity, ordered with temperance, resplendent with charity, stripped our first parents of those goods and likewise slew them. Ambrose too discourses to Sabinus: So long as Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind cleaved to God. And again Augustine confesses that he was endowed with a spiritual mind. It was said above too, on the words [[Gen 2:21|the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam|Misit Dominus soporem in Adam]], that he was then brought into the highest contemplation possible in this life. Again St Bernard: When the enemy of all men, he says, saw our father Adam surrounded with charity and clothed with every virtue, he envied him. Moreover Damascene confesses in his second book: God made man upright, innocent, virtuous, adorned with every virtue, decked with all goods, as a kind of second world. Lastly, in Ecclesiasticus we read: [[Ecclus 17:1|God created man of the earth|Deus de terra creavit hominem]], and [[Ecclus 17:2|clothed him with strength according to himself|secundum se vestivit illum virtute]] [*virtus* means both "strength" and "virtue"; Denis takes it as virtue].

paras.t: Tertio quæritur, utrum justitia originalis fuit donum gratiæ gratis datæ, an potius gratiæ gratum facientis? Et respondendum, quod circa hoc est duplex opinio: Una, quod sit donum gratiæ gratificantis: et hoc dici oportet secundum prætactam Thomæ opinionem, ita quod sine caritate haberi non possit. Sed contra hoc est duplex objectio. Prima, quia Magister Sententiarum et alii multi, dicentes primum hominem esse creatum in originali justitia, negant eum esse creatum in gratia gratificante. Secundo, quoniam si originalis justitia pertinebat ad dona gratiæ gratificantis, stare non potuit cum mortali. Ergo Eva quum consensisset comedere de fructu prohibito, et præsertim quum inde manducasset, mox fuisset privata originali justitia; similiter Adam quum consensisset in illum esum: quod tamen factum non fuit. Alioqui erubuissent propriam nuditatem ante fructus perceptionem, vel saltem Eva post illius comestionem.
paras.en: Thirdly, it is asked whether original justice was a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*, a grace given for the good of others, such as prophecy, which does not of itself make its bearer holy] or rather of sanctifying grace. And the answer is that there are two opinions on this. One, that it is a gift of sanctifying grace; and this must be said according to the opinion of Thomas touched on above, so that it could not be had without charity. But against this there are two objections. First, that the Master of the Sentences and many others, who say that the first man was created in original justice, deny that he was created in sanctifying grace. Secondly, because if original justice belonged to the gifts of sanctifying grace, it could not stand with mortal sin. Therefore Eve, when she had consented to eat of the forbidden fruit, and above all when she had eaten of it, would at once have been deprived of original justice; and likewise Adam when he had consented to that eating: which, however, did not happen. Otherwise they would have blushed at their own nakedness before taking the fruit, or at least Eve after eating it.

paras.t: Hinc alii dicunt, quod originalis justitia fuit gratia gratis data, et stare potuit cum mortali culpa: quod etiam dicit Lyra in expositione tertii capituli Geneseos. Contra quod Rabbi Paulus sic arguit: In statu innocentiæ, in quo homo institutus fuit in originali justitia, nulla erat rebellio carnis ad spiritum, nec spiritus contra Deum: ergo impossibile erat, stante illo statu, inesse peccatum mortale, quum mortale peccatum (secundum Ambrosium) sit transgressio legis divinæ, et cœlestium inobedientia mandatorum. Et istud argumentum videtur satis concludere. Non enim simul stare potuit aversio mentis a Deo per mortale peccatum, et rectitudo præfata originalis justitiæ, per quam mens erat Deo subjecta, et recte ac ordinate se habens. Sed juxta hanc viam videtur difficile, qualiter originalis justitia mansit in Eva post consensum et esum, atque in Adam post consensum iniquum usque ad manducationem prædictam. Ad hoc Rabbi Paulus respondet, quod quamvis transgressio divini præcepti fuisset incepta per manducationem mulieris, non tamen fuit consummata nisi per viri comestionem. Verumtamen istud non videtur evadere vim argumenti, et Paulus iste proprio argumento confodit se. Dicit namque, quod in statu innocentiæ mortale peccatum incurri non poterat, statu hujusmodi stante, ita quod simul esse non poterant originalis justitia, mortalisque culpa. Sed constat Adam et Evam peccasse mortaliter actu interiori ante realem fructus comestionem, ergo per actum illum interiorem amisissent originalem justitiam. Rursus, quamvis transgressio præcepti ambobus dati de non comedendo fructum prohibitum, non fuerit consummata, quantum ad ambos ante Adæ comestionem; tamen quantum ad mulierem, exstitit consummata protinus ut comedit.
paras.en: Hence others say that original justice was a grace freely given, and could stand with mortal fault; which Lyra too says in his exposition of the third chapter of Genesis. Against this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, the converted rabbi, in his Additions to Lyra] argues thus: In the state of innocence, in which man was established in original justice, there was no rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, nor of the spirit against God; therefore it was impossible, while that state stood, for mortal sin to be present, since mortal sin (according to Ambrose) is a transgression of the divine law and a disobedience to the heavenly commandments. And this argument seems conclusive enough. For the turning of the mind away from God by mortal sin could not stand together with the aforesaid rectitude of original justice, by which the mind was subject to God and disposed rightly and in order. But on this view it seems hard to see how original justice remained in Eve after her consent and eating, and in Adam after his wicked consent until the said eating. To this Rabbi Paul answers that, although the transgression of the divine precept was begun by the woman's eating, it was not consummated except by the man's eating. Yet this does not seem to escape the force of the argument, and this Paul runs himself through with his own argument. For he says that in the state of innocence mortal sin could not be incurred while that state stood, so that original justice and mortal fault could not be together. But it is certain that Adam and Eve sinned mortally by an interior act before actually eating the fruit; therefore by that interior act they would have lost original justice. Again, although the transgression of the precept given to both, not to eat the forbidden fruit, was not consummated as regards both before Adam ate, yet as regards the woman it was consummated as soon as she ate.

paras.t: Insuper Rabbi Paulus dicit: Sola comestio illa fuit prohibita Adæ, non autem deliberatio seu consensus præcedens. Unde sicut de quibusdam præceptis veteris Testamenti a doctoribus dicitur, quod lex prohibuit manum, non animum, sic in proposito dici posset. Istud non videtur posse salvari. Primo, quia si deliberatio et consensus illius vitiosæ comestionis non erant a Deo prohibiti, ergo Adam et Eva non peccaverunt, saltem mortaliter, proponendo et consentiendo in opus illud. Secundo, quoniam consensus in rem illicitam exstat illicitus. Tertio, quia voluntas deliberativa reputatur a Deo pro opere. Quarto, quoniam actus exterior inordinationem et culpam suam ab interiori deordinatione sortitur. Quinto, nam quamvis doctores dicant, quod lex veteris Testamenti prohibuit manum, non animum, non tamen intelligunt hoc sic, quod absolute loquendo, non prohibuit animum, sed quod non prohibuit animum ita explicite sicut manum. Vel ideo, quia non infligebat pœnam temporalem in lege taxatam pro animo solo.
paras.en: Moreover Rabbi Paul says: That eating alone was forbidden to Adam, not the deliberation or consent going before it. Hence, just as the doctors say of certain precepts of the Old Testament that the law forbade the hand, not the mind, so it might be said in the case before us. This does not seem able to be upheld. First, because if the deliberation and consent to that sinful eating were not forbidden by God, then Adam and Eve did not sin, at least not mortally, in purposing and consenting to that deed. Secondly, because consent to an unlawful thing is itself unlawful. Thirdly, because a deliberate will is reckoned by God as the deed. Fourthly, because the outward act takes its disorder and its fault from the inward disorder. Fifthly, because although the doctors say that the law of the Old Testament forbade the hand, not the mind, they do not understand it to mean that, speaking absolutely, it did not forbid the mind, but that it did not forbid the mind as explicitly as the hand; or else that it laid down no temporal penalty, fixed in the law, for the mind alone.

paras.t: Hinc opinor quod mox privati fuerunt originali justitia, quando interius mortaliter peccaverunt. Quod autem de sua nuditate non erubuerunt ante comestionem ipsius Adæ, arbitror accidisse vel ex vehementi atque intensa valde occupatione circa alia, vel ex dispensatione divina. Poterat enim esse, quod mulier præceptum transgressa, fuit ita attonita et occupata qualiter ad idem perduceret virum, quod nuditatem suam non advertit, nec carnaliter stimulata fuit ex nudi viri intuitu. Similiter Adam post elationem et assensum, usque ad comestionem, satis erat occupatus circa factum illud, et opus mulieris commissum, et suam deliberationem seu alia considerando quæ pertinebant ad illud, quod propriam nuditatem non advertit, neque erubuit, nec stimulum sensit; sed statim post comestionem, cessantibus occupationibus illis. Et si ita non contigit, dici potest quod dispensatione divina, repressa et dilata fuit erubescentia Evæ, quatenus vir tentaretur per feminam: quæ si jam erubuisset suam nuditatem, non fuisset ausa virum nuda accedere. Et si accessisset cum tali rubore, vir videns eam sic erubescentem, non consensisset eidem; sicque potius ex consideratione pœnæ, quam amore virtutis, dissensisset. Deus autem voluit virum probari ac tentari, quamvis non ut vinceretur et peccaret, sed ut vincens coronaretur. Istud opinative sit dictum.
paras.en: Hence I am of opinion that they were deprived of original justice as soon as they sinned mortally within. And that they did not blush at their nakedness before Adam himself ate, I think came about either from a vehement and very intense occupation with other things, or from a divine dispensation. For it could be that the woman, having transgressed the precept, was so astonished and so taken up with how she might lead her husband to the same, that she did not notice her nakedness, nor was she carnally stirred by the sight of her naked husband. Likewise Adam, after his pride and assent until the eating, was so taken up with that deed and with what the woman had done, and with his own deliberation, or with considering other things that belonged to it, that he did not notice his own nakedness, nor blush, nor feel the goad; but [he did] at once after the eating, when those occupations ceased. And if it did not happen so, it can be said that by divine dispensation Eve's shame was held back and delayed, so that the man might be tempted by the woman: for had she already blushed at her nakedness, she would not have dared to approach her husband naked. And if she had approached him with such a blush, the man, seeing her blushing so, would not have consented to her; and so he would have refused rather from consideration of the punishment than from love of virtue. But God willed the man to be proved and tempted, not indeed that he should be overcome and sin, but that, overcoming, he should be crowned. Let this be said as an opinion.

paras.t: Quarto quæritur, quis gravius peccavit, Adam, an Eva. Et videtur quod Adam, quia sapientior et virtuosior fuit quam Eva. Oppositum vero apparet, quoniam Eva gravius est punita. Adam quoque, secundum Apostolum, non est seductus, sed Eva. Respondent doctores concorditer, quod Eva magis peccavit. Primo, quia ex majori elatione transgressa est Dei præceptum, quam vir. Credidit enim absolute verum esse quod serpens dixit, atque possibile esse quod promisit, et ita absolute appetiit inordinatam Dei assimilationem. Secundo, quia seducta est credendo serpenti, quam tamen seductionem elatio ejus præcessit. Tertio, quoniam virum ad transgressionem induxit. Adam autem peccavit ex aliquali elatione et quadam benevolentia amicabili, quasi feminæ morem gerens, ut dictum est plenius.
paras.en: Fourthly, it is asked who sinned more grievously, Adam or Eve. And it seems that Adam did, because he was wiser and more virtuous than Eve. But the opposite appears, since Eve was more grievously punished. Adam also, according to the Apostle, [[1 Tim 2:14|was not seduced|non est seductus]], but Eve was. The doctors answer with one accord that Eve sinned more. First, because she transgressed God's precept out of greater pride than the man. For she believed absolutely that what the serpent said was true, and that what he promised was possible, and so she absolutely desired an inordinate likeness to God. Secondly, because she was seduced by believing the serpent, a seduction which her pride nevertheless went before. Thirdly, because she led the man to transgress. But Adam sinned out of some measure of pride and a certain friendly goodwill, as it were humouring the woman, as was said more fully above.

paras.t: Quinto quæritur, quod fuit principale et primum peccatum amborum. Respondetur quod elatio, scilicet amor propriæ excellentiæ, prout supra satis expositum est. Nec obstat illud Apostoli, quod per inobedientiam unius hominis mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Ibi enim inobedientia sumitur, prout est vitium generale, secundum quod omnis transgressio præcepti, est inobedientia quædam, sicque elatio inobedientia est. Verumtamen in peccato primorum parentum multæ deformitates fuerunt, sed elatio erat principalior atque formalior; et ceteræ ordinabantur ad finem elationis, utpote ad excellentiam propriam.
paras.en: Fifthly, it is asked what was the chief and first sin of both. The answer is: pride, that is, love of one's own excellence, as was set out sufficiently above. Nor does that saying of the Apostle stand in the way, that [[Rom 5:19|by the disobedience of one man|per inobedientiam unius hominis]] death [[Rom 5:12|entered into this world|introivit in orbem terrarum]] [the margin gives Rom. v, 12, 19; Denis joins words of the two verses]. For there disobedience is taken as a general vice, in the sense that every transgression of a precept is a kind of disobedience, and so pride is disobedience. Yet in the sin of our first parents there were many deformities, but pride was the more principal and more formal, and the rest were ordered to the end of pride, that is, to their own excellence.

paras.t: Hinc in fine libri secundi asserit Damascenus: Invidia diaboli victus est homo. Non enim ferebat invidiosus diabolus per propriam elationem dejectus, nos superius fortunari: unde et deitatis specie mendax decepit miserum hominem, atque ad propriam altitudinem per elationem illum reducens, ad simile intulit barathrum casus. Augustinus quoque libro de Virginitate: Diabolus, inquit, in cœlo voluit esse sicut Deus; cadensque persuasit homini similitudinem suæ voluntatis: sicque diabolus in se ipso expertus quantum Deo displiceret superbia, maxime illa qua rationabilis creatura vult sibi per se sufficere, conatus est primos parentes sui imitatores efficere, et prævaluit in hoc ipso.
paras.en: Hence at the end of his second book Damascene asserts: Man was overcome by the envy of the devil. For the envious devil, cast down by his own pride, could not bear that we should prosper on high; and so, a liar, he deceived wretched man with the semblance of godhead, and, leading him by pride up toward his own height, brought him into a like abyss of falling. Augustine too, in the book on Virginity: The devil, he says, willed in heaven to be as God; and falling, persuaded man to the likeness of his own will: and so the devil, having found out in himself how much pride displeases God, above all that by which a rational creature wishes to be sufficient to itself by itself, strove to make our first parents his imitators, and prevailed in this very thing.

paras.t: Sexto quæritur, an in statu innocentiæ fuisset generatio, et qualiter; et, an commixtio illa fuisset ita delectabilis, ut est modo. Et respondendum secundum quod refert sanctus Doctor in Summa contra gentiles, atque in prima parte Summæ suæ, quæstione 98: Quidam antiqui doctores attendentes concupiscentiæ fœditatem in coitu, posuerunt quod non fuisset multiplicatio hominum in statu innocentiæ per generationem et coitum, sed per divinam virtutem eo modo, quo multiplicati sunt angeli. Et ista fuit opinio Gregorii Nysseni in libro suo de Homine, quam Damascenus videtur secutus, qui ait: Poterat Deus genus humanum absque generatione multiplicare, si homo mandatum suum servasset usque in finem. Sed istud non est rationabiliter dictum, nec Scripturæ consonum, quum ante prævaricationem Deus locutus sit: Crescite et multiplicamini, et replete terram. Masculum quoque et feminam creavit eos, et muliere nondum formata, Dominus dixit: Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi. Originale item peccatum non abstulit naturæ humanæ naturalem propagationem, quæ est per sexuum commixtionem.
paras.en: Sixthly, it is asked whether in the state of innocence there would have been generation, and how; and whether that union would have been as pleasurable as it is now. And the answer must be given according to what the holy Doctor relates in the Summa contra Gentiles and in the First Part of his Summa, question 98. Certain ancient doctors, considering the foulness of concupiscence in intercourse, held that in the state of innocence the multiplication of men would not have been by generation and intercourse, but by the divine power, in the way in which the angels were multiplied. And this was the opinion of Gregory of Nyssa in his book On Man, which Damascene seems to have followed, who says: God could have multiplied the human race without generation, if man had kept His commandment to the end. But this is not reasonably said, nor in accord with Scripture, since before the transgression God said: [[Gen 1:28|Increase and multiply, and fill the earth|Crescite et multiplicamini, et replete terram]]. Also, [[Gen 1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum quoque et feminam creavit eos]]; and when the woman was not yet formed, the Lord said: [[Gen 2:18|let us make him a help like unto himself|Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi]]. Again, original sin did not take away from human nature its natural propagation, which is by the union of the sexes.

paras.t: Denique commixtio illa fuisset delectabilis, sicut et nunc; imo et plus, quanto natura tunc fuisset integrior, et sensus vivacior, et naturalis virtus perfectior. Delectatio enim coitus non est in se vitiosa, sed naturalis et instituta a Deo; nec impedisset in aliquo actum rationis et contemplationis in primo statu, quoniam sensitiva pars animæ fuit rationi perfecte subjecta: ideo in coitu illo non fuisset aliqua indecentia, turpitudo aut fervor libidinis, sed ratio delectationi dominans, retulisset eam in debitum. Hanc opinionem sequitur Thomas. Alia autem est opinio dicentium, quod delectatio fuisset in coitu illo, sed non tanta ut modo: quoniam ratio ad libitum suum temperasset eamdem, ita quod sensitiva pars non tendisset toto impetu in suum objectum. Et istud approbat Bonaventura. Tertia quoque fuit opinio, quod in coitu illo non fuisset major delectatio, quam in applicatione manus ad barbam, aut manus ad manum. Ad quod approbandum allegaverunt quædam verba Augustini. Unde et Magister ait libro secundo: Si primi homines non peccassent, sine omni peccato et macula in paradiso carnali copula convenissent. Et esset tunc torus immaculatus, et commixtio sine concupiscentia; atque genitalibus membris, sicut ceteris, imperarent, ut ibi nullum motum sentirent illicitum: sicut alia corporis membra aliis admovemus, ut manum ori sine ardore libidinis, ita genitalibus membris uterentur sine omni pruritu carnis. Harum opinionum prima rationabilior esse videtur, nec est contraria verbis Augustini et Magistri jam tactis. Delectatio quippe oritur ex conjunctione convenientis cum convenienti, seu potentiæ cum congruenti objecto et sensu, seu perceptione ejusdem: ideo dicunt naturales, delectationem esse in coitu ex transitu humorum per locum nervosum, in quo maxime viget sensus.
paras.en: Further, that union would have been pleasurable, as it is now too; nay, even more so, inasmuch as nature would then have been more whole, sense more lively and the natural power more perfect. For the pleasure of intercourse is not vicious in itself, but natural and instituted by God; nor would it in any way have hindered the act of reason and contemplation in the first state, since the sensitive part of the soul was perfectly subject to reason. Therefore in that intercourse there would have been no unseemliness, foulness or heat of lust, but reason, ruling over the pleasure, would have directed it to its due end. This opinion Thomas follows. Another is the opinion of those who say that there would have been pleasure in that intercourse, but not so great as now, since reason would have tempered it at will, so that the sensitive part would not have tended with its whole force to its object. And this Bonaventure approves. There was also a third opinion, that in that intercourse there would have been no greater pleasure than in putting the hand to the beard, or hand to hand. In support of which they alleged certain words of Augustine. Hence the Master too says in his second book: If the first men had not sinned, they would have come together in paradise in carnal union without any sin or stain. And then the bed would have been undefiled, and the union without concupiscence; and they would command the members of generation as they do the others, so that they would feel no unlawful movement there: as we move some members of the body to others, as the hand to the mouth, without the heat of lust, so would they have used the members of generation without any itch of the flesh. Of these opinions the first seems the more reasonable, nor is it contrary to the words of Augustine and the Master just touched on. For pleasure arises from the joining of what is fitting with what is fitting, or of a power with its suitable object, and from the sense or perception of it; so the natural philosophers say that the pleasure in intercourse comes from the passage of the humours through a place full of nerves, in which sense is most vigorous.

paras.t: Denique communiter dicitur, quod in statu illo omnes genuissent, et ex quolibet coitu proles fuisset secuta. Viri quoque et feminæ æquali numero fuissent multiplicatæ. Verumtamen in paradiso non coierunt primi parentes, cujus rationem assignat Magister libro secundo, dicens: Quia muliere formata, mox transgressio facta […] et ejecti sunt de paradiso, vel quia Deus nonnullis præcepit hoc, quia prævidit casum eorum.
paras.en: Further, it is commonly said that in that state all would have begotten children, and that from every union offspring would have followed. Men and women too would have been multiplied in equal number. Yet our first parents did not come together in paradise, the reason for which the Master gives in his second book, saying: Because, as soon as the woman was formed, the transgression was committed […] and they were cast out of paradise; or because God did not command this to them [the text reads *nonnullis*, "to some", which gives no sense here; probably *non illis*, "not to them"], since He foresaw their fall.

paras.t: Septimo quæritur: si primi parentes non peccassent, an pueri ex eis nati mox habuissent perfectum robur et usum membrorum ita quod protinus potuissent ambulare, operari et loqui, an per temporum intervalla profecissent et pertigissent ad ista, ut modo. Ad istud respondet Magister libro secundo multum rationabiliter, quod de hoc certitudinem non habemus, quamvis certum sit quod parvuli nascerentur, propter materni uteri et membri genitalis, quo egrederentur, parvitatem. Augustinus quoque circa hoc dicit: Quamvis exigua corporis pars sit costa, non tamen propter hoc Deus fecit viro parvulam conjugem. Unde et omnipotentia Creatoris poterat parvulos natos mox facere grandes, et poterat eis præstare per gratiam, quod multis animalibus præstitit per naturam, quorum pulli quamvis sint parvuli, tamen mox ut nascuntur, currunt, et matrem sequuntur. Porro Thomas dicit super secundum: Probabilius tenetur, quod naturalis cursus habet, ubi Scripturæ auctoritas non repugnat. Ideo Thomas potius tenet, quod pueri paulatim crevissent et confortati fuissent, ac loqui addiscerent. Idem dicit Bonaventura. Teneritudo enim complexionis puerorum hoc magis exigeret. Verumtamen reor, quod citius et expeditius pervenissent ad perfectionem staturæ ac roboris et loquelæ, quam modo, quia et cibi eorum fuissent vigorosiores, vires vegetativæ ac sensitivæ et rationales efficaciores, fuissetque ibi convenientior aer et locus.
paras.en: Seventhly, it is asked: if our first parents had not sinned, would the children born of them have had at once full strength and use of their limbs, so that they could straightway walk, work and speak, or would they have advanced and reached these things over intervals of time, as now? To this the Master answers very reasonably in his second book that we have no certainty about this, though it is certain that they would have been born little, because of the smallness of the mother's womb and of the member of generation by which they would come forth. Augustine too says about this: Although a rib is a small part of the body, God did not for that reason make the man a little wife. Hence the Creator's omnipotence could have made little ones grown as soon as they were born, and could have granted them by grace what He has granted to many animals by nature, whose young, little though they are, yet run and follow their mother as soon as they are born. But Thomas says on the second book [of the Sentences]: That is the more probable opinion which follows the course of nature, where the authority of Scripture is not against it. Therefore Thomas rather holds that children would have grown and been strengthened little by little, and would have learned to speak. Bonaventure says the same. For the tenderness of children's constitution would rather require this. Yet I think they would have reached the fullness of stature, strength and speech more quickly and readily than now, since their foods too would have been more vigorous, their vegetative, sensitive and rational powers more effective, and the air and the place there more suitable.

paras.t: Octavo quæritur, an pueri nati, statim habuissent perfectum usum rationis. Respondetur proportionabiliter ad prædicta. Qui enim dicunt quod mox fuissent perfecti a Deo effecti, quantum ad corporis robur, staturam, operationem et loquelam, etiam dicunt quod confestim fuissent perfecti in scientia et cognitione. Qui autem alterius opinionis sunt, dicere habent, quod non habuissent mox usum rationis propter cerebri humiditatem, et organorum indispositionem ad hoc. Quidam etiam dicunt, quod scientiæ fuissent eis concreatæ, quantum ad habitum. Alii dicunt, quod in scientia atque notitia profecissent paulatim inveniendo ac addiscendo, quamvis multo citius faciliusque quam modo.
paras.en: Eighthly, it is asked whether children, once born, would at once have had the full use of reason. The answer is in proportion to what has been said. For those who say that they would at once have been made perfect by God as regards bodily strength, stature, working and speech, say also that they would at once have been perfect in knowledge and understanding. But those of the other opinion must say that they would not at once have had the use of reason, because of the moistness of the brain and the unfitness of the organs for it. Some say too that knowledge would have been created in them as to the habit. Others say that they would have advanced in knowledge and understanding little by little, by finding out and learning, though much more quickly and easily than now.

paras.t: Nono quæritur, an pueri fuissent nati in originali justitia. Respondetur communiter quod […]. Et quia juxta præhabita, originalis justitia non habetur sine gratia gratum faciente, consequenter dicendum, quod etiam concreata eis fuisset gratia illa, et charismata inseparabiliter ei annexa in via, videlicet virtutes theologicæ et infusæ, ac dona Spiritus Sancti, sicut de pueris dicimus baptizatis. Sed huic obviare videtur, quod ait Hugo de S. Victore: Primus homo ante peccatum generaret filios absque peccato, non tamen hæredes paternæ justitiæ. Hoc tamen Thomas solvit, dicendo, intelligendum hoc esse quantum ad actus exsecutionem, non quantum ad habitum.
paras.en: Ninthly, it is asked whether children would have been born in original justice. The common answer is that […]. And since, by what was said before, original justice is not had without sanctifying grace, it must consequently be said that that grace too would have been created in them, and the gifts inseparably joined to it in the way [*in via*, that is, in the state of wayfarers on the way to heaven], namely the theological and infused virtues and the gifts of the Holy Ghost, as we say of baptized children. But against this there seems to be what Hugh of St Victor says: The first man before sin would have begotten sons without sin, yet not heirs of their father's justice. This, however, Thomas solves by saying that this is to be understood as regards the exercise of the act, not as regards the habit.

paras.t: Præterea dicit Thomas: Rationalis creatura non confirmatur in bono, nisi per immediatam unionem cum Deo, quæ unio est beatitudo æterna. Ideo primus homo quamdiu generasset, nec Deum per speciem conspexisset, potuisset peccare, nec confirmatus fuisset in bono. Unde nec pueri tunc nati, fuissent confirmati in originali justitia, sed tempore procedente potuissent peccare. Verumtamen hujus contrarium multi dicunt, præsertim quum dicat Anselmus in libro, Cur Deus homo: Si primi parentes non fuissent victi in ipsa eorum tentatione, ita confirmarentur cum omni sua propagine, quod ultra peccare non possent. Denique beatissimus Joannes Baptista in utero, gloriosi quoque Apostoli in die Pentecostes fuerunt confirmati in gratia, ita quod ultra peccare mortaliter non valebant. Sanctissima autem Virgo sic fuit confirmata in gratia etiam in utero matris, quod nunquam poterat venialem incurrere culpam. Multa præterea possent objici et moveri circa opinionem illam Thomæ prætactam. Qui autem de his et multis consimilibus quæstionibus cupit plenius informari, legat secundum Sententiarum et scripta doctorum circa eumdem.
paras.en: Moreover Thomas says: A rational creature is not confirmed in good except by immediate union with God, which union is eternal beatitude. Therefore the first man, so long as he begot children and had not beheld God by sight [*per speciem*, that is, face to face], could have sinned, and would not have been confirmed in good. Hence neither would the children then born have been confirmed in original justice, but as time went on they could have sinned. Yet many say the contrary of this, especially since Anselm says in the book Why God Became Man: If our first parents had not been overcome in their temptation, they would have been so confirmed, with all their offspring, that they could sin no more. Further, the most blessed John the Baptist in the womb, and the glorious Apostles too on the day of Pentecost, were confirmed in grace, so that they could no longer sin mortally. And the most holy Virgin was so confirmed in grace, even in her mother's womb, that she could never incur a venial fault. Many things besides could be objected and raised concerning that opinion of Thomas touched on above. But whoever wishes to be more fully informed on these and many like questions, let him read the second book of the Sentences and the writings of the doctors on it.

paras.t: Decimo quæritur, an in statu innocentiæ homines fuissent successive translati ad paradisum cœlestem, an potius pariter omnes. Ad hoc videtur Magister libro secundo sentire, quod omnes pariter fuissent translati, dicens: De hoc statu transferendus erat homo cum universa sua posteritate, ad meliorem dignioremque statum, ubi æterno et cœlesti bono, sibi in cœlis parato, perfrueretur. Alii dicunt, quod parentes ante filios fuissent paulatim translati, et glorificati in carne et anima absque intermedia morte, quia dispendium magnum fuisset parentibus, retardari a gloria quousque electorum numerus impleretur, præsertim quoniam spes quæ differtur, affligit: nec videtur quod omnes potuissent contineri decenter in paradiso. Denique, Deus unumquemque prædestinatum elegit ad certum gradum atque mensuram felicitatis æternæ, quem quum sufficienter meruerit, satis cito hinc tollitur: qui autem in paradiso mansissent, fuissent viatores quamdiu mansissent in eo. Ideo non videtur quod mansissent ibi diutius, quam quousque meruissent gradum beatitudinis, ad quem præordinati fuissent, nec fuisset ratio tantæ dilationis. Ideo ista opinio probabilior esse censetur.
paras.en: Tenthly, it is asked whether in the state of innocence men would have been taken up to the heavenly paradise one after another, or rather all together. On this the Master in his second book seems to think that all would have been taken up together, saying: From this state man was to be taken up, with all his posterity, to a better and worthier state, where he would enjoy an eternal and heavenly good prepared for him in heaven. Others say that the parents would have been taken up little by little before the children, and glorified in flesh and soul without death coming between, since it would have been a great loss to the parents to be held back from glory until the number of the elect was filled up, especially since [[Prov 13:12|Hope that is deferred afflicteth|spes quæ differtur, affligit]]; nor does it seem that all could have been fittingly held in paradise. Further, God chose each of the predestined for a fixed degree and measure of eternal happiness, and when he has sufficiently merited it, he is taken hence soon enough; but those who would have remained in paradise would have been wayfarers so long as they remained in it. Therefore it does not seem that they would have stayed there longer than until they had merited the degree of beatitude to which they had been foreordained, nor would there have been any reason for so great a delay. Therefore this opinion is judged the more probable.

paras.t: Undecimo quæritur, an in statu innocentiæ fuisset dominium. Videtur quod non, quia omnes fuissent æquales, servitus quoque in pœnam peccati inflicta est, secundum Gregorium. Respondet Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 96: Dominium accipitur uno modo, prout opponitur seu repugnat libertati ejus, cui quis dominatur: sicque dominus appellatur qui servum habet, servus autem opponitur libero: liberum quippe vocatur, quod est causa sui: servile vero, quod ordinatur ad aliud. Dominium ergo sic sumptum, est prout aliquis principatur subjectis, non ad illorum utilitatem, sed ad proprium commodum, et tale dominium non est sine pœna inferiorum. Quemadmodum enim unumquodque naturale est et jucundum propriam perfectionem acquirere, ita pœnale est ei, ut bonum quod habet vel est, non sibi, sed alteri cedat in commodum: hinc tale dominium in statu innocentiæ non fuisset. Secundo, dominium nuncupatur quæcumque prælatio, superioritas aut præsidentia; sicque etiam is dominari asseritur, qui alios dirigit ad utilitatem ipsorum, vel ad bonum commune, et tale dominium in statu innocentiæ exstitisset.
paras.en: Eleventhly, it is asked whether in the state of innocence there would have been dominion. It seems not, because all would have been equal; servitude too was inflicted as a punishment of sin, according to Gregory. Thomas answers in the First Part, question 96: Dominion is taken in one way as it is opposed to, or conflicts with, the freedom of him over whom one rules; and so he is called a lord who has a slave, and a slave is opposed to a free man: for that is called free which is its own cause, and servile, that which is ordered to another. Dominion taken in this way, then, is when one rules over subjects not for their benefit but for his own advantage; and such dominion is not without pain to those beneath. For as it is natural and pleasant to each thing to gain its own perfection, so it is painful to it that the good which it has or is should go to the advantage not of itself but of another; hence such dominion would not have existed in the state of innocence. In the second way, any headship, superiority or presidency is called dominion; and so he too is said to rule who directs others to their own benefit or to the common good; and such dominion would have existed in the state of innocence.

paras.t: Primo, quoniam homo naturaliter est animal sociale, secundum Philosophum. Vitam ergo socialem homines in statu innocentiæ habuissent: talis autem vita convenienter duci non potest, nisi sit aliquis præsidens, qui ad omnium commune bonum respiciat. Præterea, in statu innocentiæ fuisset optima ordinatio, quæ sine prælatione et subjectione esse non valuisset. Iterum, in statu innocentiæ unus fuisset sapientior, perfectior et sanctior alio. Quemadmodum enim de singulis sanctorum angelorum ordinibus aliqui corruisse creduntur, sic homines singuli ad singulos angelicorum spirituum choros assumendi fuissent. Sapientiores ergo et perfectiores sic dominati fuissent minus sapientibus et perfectis, viri uxoribus, parentesque filiis. Unde constat, quod omnes non fuissent æquales in accidentalibus atque gratuitis. Primo nempe fuisset ibi disparitas sexuum et ætatum, prout generatio exigit corporalis. Fuisset quoque disparitas circa animam in scientia et virtute, quoniam homo per liberum operabatur arbitrium. Ideo unus potuisset se intensius applicare ad appetendum et cognoscendum, ad contemplandum et operandum, quam alter: sicque unus plus profecisset, quam alter. Insuper, ex parte corporis potuisset esse disparitas. Non enim exemptum erat corpus humanum ab influentia corporum superiorum. Idcirco secundum diversum respectum stellarum et dispositionem materiæ aut influentiam exteriorum causarum, quidam fuissent aliis pulchriores, robustiores, ac melius complexionati. Hæc Thomas.
paras.en: First, because man is by nature a social animal, according to the Philosopher. Men in the state of innocence, then, would have led a social life; but such a life cannot be fittingly led unless there is someone presiding who looks to the common good of all. Moreover, in the state of innocence there would have been the best ordering, which could not have been without headship and subjection. Again, in the state of innocence one would have been wiser, more perfect and holier than another. For as some are believed to have fallen from each of the orders of the holy angels, so particular men were to be taken up into the particular choirs of the angelic spirits. So the wiser and more perfect would have ruled in this way over the less wise and perfect, husbands over wives, and parents over children. Hence it is plain that all would not have been equal in things accidental and gratuitous. For first there would have been a disparity there of sexes and of ages, as bodily generation requires. There would have been a disparity too as regards the soul, in knowledge and virtue, since man acted by free will: therefore one could have applied himself more intensely than another to desiring and knowing, to contemplating and acting, and so one would have advanced more than another. Moreover, there could have been disparity on the side of the body. For the human body was not exempt from the influence of the higher bodies. Therefore, according to the differing aspect of the stars and the disposition of the matter or the influence of outward causes, some would have been fairer than others, sturdier and of better constitution. Thus far Thomas.

paras.t: Duodecimo quæritur, an irrationabilia animalia habitassent cum hominibus in paradiso. Ad hoc Damascenus libro secundo respondet: Paradisus fuit divina regio et digna habitatio ejus, qui secundum imaginem Dei erat creatus, in quo nullum irrationabilium habitabat, sed solus homo. Et istud Thomas allegat. Sed videtur contrariari, quod quartodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: Cum duobus illis hominibus masculo et femina, scilicet Adam et Eva, animalia etiam terrestria cetera, subdita et innoxia versabantur in paradiso. Damascenus quoque libro secundo fatetur: Ante transgressionem omnia homini erant subjecta, sed et serpens homini erat assuetus, magis aliis ei adhærens, et delectabilibus motibus ei adjunctus. Unde et per eum pessimam suppositionem inseruit diabolus primis parentibus. Ad has auctoritates arbitror posse responderi, quod intelligi possint pro tempore illo, quo animalia erant coram Adam in paradiso adducta.
paras.en: Twelfthly, it is asked whether the irrational animals would have dwelt with men in paradise. To this Damascene answers in his second book: Paradise was a divine region and a worthy dwelling for him who had been created after the image of God, in which none of the irrational creatures dwelt, but man alone. And this Thomas alleges. But what Augustine says in the fourteenth book of the City of God seems contrary: With those two human beings, male and female, that is, Adam and Eve, the other land animals too lived in paradise, subject and harmless. Damascene also confesses in his second book: Before the transgression all things were subject to man; and the serpent, too, was familiar with man, keeping closer to him than the others, and joined to him with pleasing motions. Hence too the devil, through it, put the most evil suggestion into our first parents. To these authorities I think it can be answered that they may be understood of that time when the animals had been brought before Adam in paradise.

paras.t: Tertiodecimo quæritur, quamdiu fuerat Adam extra paradisum ante translationem suam in paradisum, et item, quamdiu ipse et Eva in paradiso fuerunt. Ad hujus quæstionis primam partem communiter respondetur, quod Adam statim post suam productionem, in paradisum translatus est, per modum superius tactum. Verumtamen Henricus de Hassia super Genesim tangit, quod aliqui imaginantur Adam transisse pedestrem a loco suæ formationis usque in paradisum, ut rerum naturas et animalium proprietates, dispositionemque terræ eundo consideraret: secundum quam imaginationem diu fuisset in via. Ad quod posset quis retorquere verba Damasceni ultimo jam inducta; sed imaginatio ista apparentiam parvam habet, quum et præfatarum rerum scientia fuerit Adæ in principio concreata. Ad aliam quæstionis partem aliqui dicunt, quod Adam fuit hora tertia factus, et in paradisum perductus, animalibus quoque imposuit nomina: hora autem sexta dicunt Evam formatam, et statim prævaricatam; horaque nona dicunt ambos ejectos. Verumtamen in textu habetur, quod audierunt vocem Domini in paradiso post meridiem ambulantis ad auram, et post hoc leguntur ejecti. Communiter quoque tenetur, quod eodem die Adam est factus et lapsus, et Christi conceptio Virgini nuntiata, ipseque Christus cruci affixus. Verum quamdiu fuerint Adam et Eva in paradiso, non scitur pro certo.
paras.en: Thirteenthly, it is asked how long Adam was outside paradise before he was taken into paradise, and likewise how long he and Eve were in paradise. To the first part of this question it is commonly answered that Adam, straight after his production, was taken into paradise in the manner touched on above. Yet Henry of Hesse, on Genesis, mentions that some imagine Adam went on foot from the place of his formation to paradise, so as to consider on the way the natures of things, the properties of the animals and the lie of the land; on which imagining he would have been long on the road. Against this one could turn the words of Damascene last brought forward; but this imagining has little likelihood, since the knowledge of the aforesaid things was created in Adam from the beginning. To the other part of the question some say that Adam was made at the third hour and brought into paradise, and gave names to the animals too; and they say that at the sixth hour Eve was formed and at once transgressed, and that at the ninth hour both were cast out. Yet in the text we have that [[3:8|they heard the voice of the Lord|audierunt vocem Domini]] [[3:8|walking in paradise at the afternoon air|in paradiso post meridiem ambulantis ad auram]], and after this we read that they were cast out. It is also commonly held that on the same day Adam was made and fell, and Christ's conception was announced to the Virgin, and Christ Himself was fastened to the cross. But how long Adam and Eve were in paradise is not known for certain.

paras.t: Postremo quæritur, an ultra paradisum sit habitatio hominum. Ad quod sancti et docti viri responderunt, quod non. Verumtamen quidam in itinerario suo dicit oppositum, asserens illic, scilicet ultra paradisum, terram inhabitari in maxima multitudine civitatum ac regionum, quarum institores (ut dicit) Indiam visitant per Mare oceanum. Principes quoque et gentes ex utraque parte manentes, visi sunt invicem nuntia destinare. Istud nec rationi nec fidei christianæ consentaneum esse censetur. Omnes namque historiographi et qui usque fines terræ habitabilis devenerunt, testati sunt ultra loca illa ad quæ devenerunt, aut de quibus scripserunt, non esse hominum mansionem: ad quod multa possent adduci ex gestis Alexandri et Herculis, diversisque chronicis; sed et in visionibus et revelationibus quarumdam sanctarum personarum fidelium idem asseritur.
paras.en: Lastly, it is asked whether beyond paradise there is any dwelling of men. To which holy and learned men have answered that there is not. Yet a certain man in his Itinerary says the opposite, asserting that there, namely beyond paradise, the land is inhabited by a very great multitude of cities and regions, whose merchants (as he says) visit India by the Ocean Sea; and that the princes and peoples dwelling on either side have been seen to send embassies to each other. This is judged agreeable neither to reason nor to the Christian faith. For all the historians, and those who have come to the ends of the habitable earth, have testified that beyond the places they reached, or of which they wrote, there is no dwelling of men; for which many things could be brought from the deeds of Alexander and Hercules and from various chronicles; and the same is asserted also in the visions and revelations of certain holy and faithful persons.

paras.t: Denique secundum fidem catholicam, sicut Christus est totius generis humani salvator, sic fides christiana per totum orbem est prædicata, quamvis aliquæ parvæ provinciæ esse dicantur, in quibus nondum prædicatum est evangelium Christi. Verumtamen nequaquam convenit veritati novi et veteris Testamenti, asserere, quod sint multæ et maximæ regiones ac urbes, in quibus prædicata non est evangelica lex. Non autem legitur ultra superiorem Indiam prædicata. Amplius, aliqui Indi interdum venerunt et sæpe scripserunt ad loca ista, et tamen tale nil insinuaverunt. Credimus item, quod post Antichristi occisionem totus mundus, paucissimis Antichristi indurandis satellitibus demptis, convertetur ad Christum, et ipse Antichristus per totum orbem suos mittet ministros: quæ stare non possent, si ultra paradisum esset hujuscemodi hominum multitudo. Verumtamen esse potest, quod aliqui per Mare oceanum ad Indiam veniant ex aliquibus terris, a paradisi latere sitis.
paras.en: Further, according to the Catholic faith, as Christ is the Saviour of the whole human race, so the Christian faith has been preached throughout the whole world, although some small provinces are said to exist in which the gospel of Christ has not yet been preached. But it in no way agrees with the truth of the New and Old Testament to assert that there are many very great regions and cities in which the law of the gospel has not been preached. And we do not read that it was preached beyond Upper India. Again, some Indians have at times come to these parts and have often written to them, and yet have hinted nothing of the kind. We believe likewise that after the slaying of Antichrist the whole world, except for very few of Antichrist's followers who are to be hardened, will be converted to Christ, and that Antichrist himself will send his ministers through the whole world: which could not stand if beyond paradise there were such a multitude of men. Yet it may be that some come to India by the Ocean Sea from certain lands lying at the side of paradise.

paras.t: Præterea communiter dicitur, quod Jerusalem vel Judæa aut Syria, saltem sit in medio terræ habitabilis: quod secundum illam assertionem stare non posset. Legimus, insuper in Prophetis, quemadmodum Deus quatuor principalibus regnis, præsertim Romano imperio, contulit monarchiam: quod verum non esset, si tot regiones essent ultra paradisum. Amplius, vir ille in itinerario suo ait, quod ex quo de fonte paradisi exeunt quatuor flumina ab hac parte paradisi, merito videatur credendum, alia quatuor flumina ab eodem procedere fonte versus paradisi aliam partem directe oppositam. Istud consequentiam nullam, imo nec apparentiam, habere censetur. Videmus enim in terra fontes multos et magnos, ex quibus diversi fluvii oriuntur versus unam terræ habitabilis partem, non tamen versus partem oppositam.
paras.en: Moreover, it is commonly said that Jerusalem, or Judæa, or at least Syria, is in the middle of the habitable earth; which could not stand according to that assertion. We read besides in the Prophets how God gave the monarchy to four principal kingdoms, especially to the Roman empire: which would not be true if there were so many regions beyond paradise. Further, that man says in his Itinerary that, since four rivers go out from the fountain of paradise on this side of paradise, it seems rightly to be believed that four other rivers proceed from the same fountain toward the other side of paradise, directly opposite. This is judged to have no force as a consequence, nay, not even any likelihood. For we see on earth many great fountains from which divers rivers arise toward one part of the habitable earth, yet not toward the opposite part.

4.title: Expositio capituli quarti: Adam vero cognovit uxorem suam, etc.
4.title_en: Exposition of the fourth chapter: “And Adam knew Eve his wife,” etc.

paras.t: DESCRIPTIS primorum parentum productione, transgressione et ejectione a paradiso, consequenter describitur generatio eorumdem, et multiplicatio generis humani. Adam vero cognovit uxorem suam Evam, quæ concepit et peperit Cain. Ex hoc loco duplex Judæorum error reprobatur. Unus est, quo dicunt Adam habuisse duas uxores: unam et primam, de qua illud Genesis primo scriptum, Masculum et feminam creavit eos, intelligunt: aliam, quæ in paradiso legitur facta de costa Adæ. Aliam enim dicunt factam de limo terræ cum Adam. Unde et Josephus dicit mulierem extra paradisum formatam, simul cum viro in paradisum translatam. In hunc, inquiens, hortum, utpote paradisum, introduxit Deus Adam et Evam, præcipiens eis sollicitudinem habere plantationis. Atque ex his duabus Adæ uxoribus, interminabiles confingunt genealogias: imo (ut fertur) dicunt simias ex una illarum uxorum natas. Sed ex textu eorum error ostenditur, quia in processu textus non fit mentio, nisi de una Adæ uxore, et de hominum generatione ex ea, solaque una uxor legitur a serpente tentata, victa, et cum Adam expulsa. Certumque est et facillime potest probari, quod simiæ ab hominibus distinguantur specifice. Secundus error est Judæorum, quo dicunt quod Adam et Eva genuerunt Cain et Abel in paradiso.
