paras.en: Moreover, everyone who goes out from the face of God by mortal sin, turning his mind away from the Creator, dwells as a fugitive from the mystical unity of the Church, a vagabond too and unsteady upon the earth, as belonging to the body of the devil; and the wicked are unsteady of heart, and subject to the passions, and wander away from God on every side. For [[Ps 11:9|The wicked walk round about|In circuitu etenim impii ambulant]], who are [[Is 57:20|like the raging sea, which cannot rest|tanquam mare fervens, quod non potest quiescere]], and [[Ps 1:4|like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth|tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]].

paras.t: Cognovit autem Cain uxorem suam, quæ concepit et peperit Enoch. Per quod designatur, quod ex pravæ cogitationis radice et interiori animæ passione procedit opus perversum. Rursus quasi spiritualis uxor incredulæ plebis Judææ est Scriptura veteris Testamenti, secundum occidentem litteram intellecta, quam plebs ista sic cognoscit, seque in ea exercet, et gignit ex ea Enoch, id est posteritatem sibi in infidelitate et carnali intellectu Scripturæ consimilem.
paras.en: [[4:17|And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived, and brought forth Henoch|Cognovit autem Cain uxorem suam, quæ concepit et peperit Enoch]]. By this is signified that a perverse work proceeds from the root of an evil thought and from an inward passion of the soul. Again, the spiritual wife, as it were, of the unbelieving Jewish people is the Scripture of the Old Testament understood according to the letter that kills; this people so knows her and exercises itself in her, and of her begets Henoch, that is, a posterity like itself in unbelief and in a carnal understanding of Scripture.

paras.t: Et ædificavit Cain civitatem. In exordio mundi urbem construxit: per quod significatum est, quod amatores mundi et omnes iniqui in hoc sæculo remanere, prosperari, ac locupletari desiderant, et via utuntur pro patria. Quocontra de sanctis Patriarchis ait Apostolus, quod in casulis habitabant tanquam hospites et peregrini. Et rursus: Non habemus hic, inquit, manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus. Et vocavit nomen ejus ex nomine filii sui Enoch, quod interpretatur dedicatio, secundum Hieronymum. Tales namque se ipsos et pertinentes ad se, ac sua, dedicant et mancipant prosperitati terrenæ ac vitæ præsenti.
paras.en: [[4:17|and he built a city|Et ædificavit Cain civitatem]]. He built a city at the beginning of the world: by which is signified that lovers of the world and all the wicked desire to remain, to prosper and to grow rich in this world, and take the road for the homeland. Against which the Apostle says of the holy Patriarchs that they dwelt in cottages[[Heb 11:9||]] as guests and pilgrims[[Heb 11:13||]] [the margin gives Heb. xi, 13; the cottages are from Heb 11:9]. And again: [[Heb 13:14|we have not here|Non habemus hic]], he says, [[Heb 13:14|a lasting city: but we seek one that is to come|manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus]]. [[4:17|and called the name thereof by the name of his son Henoch|Et vocavit nomen ejus ex nomine filii sui Enoch]], which is interpreted *dedication*, according to Jerome. For such men dedicate and make over themselves, and those who belong to them, and what is theirs, to earthly prosperity and the present life.

paras.t: Lamech accepit uxores duas. Per Lamech intelliguntur lascivi, præsertim adulteri et concubinarii; similiter illi qui cum sapientia evangelicæ legis, quam sibi desponsarunt, amplectuntur sæcularem prudentiam, atque in sæculo hoc cupiunt videri ac reputari prudentes.
paras.en: Lamech [[4:19|took two wives|accepit uxores duas]]. By Lamech are understood the lewd, especially adulterers and those who keep concubines; likewise those who, along with the wisdom of the law of the Gospel, to which they have espoused themselves, embrace worldly prudence, and desire to seem and to be reputed prudent in this world.

paras.t: Genuit quoque Lamech tres filios, quorum primus, scilicet Jabel, pater habitantium in tentoriis ac pastorum, designat cupidos et avaros, qui hinc inde moventur, ut colligant sibi terrena et pascant pecora, id est desideria sua brutalia. Secundus, videlicet Jubal, pater canentium cithara et organo, eos designat, qui exteriorum sensuum quærunt et amplectuntur oblectamenta. Tertius, puta Tubalcain, malleator et faber, significat bellicosos, contentiosos, iracundos, et aliorum tribulatores, qui proximos suos cædunt verbis duris aut ictibus seu scandalosis operibus, aut etiam omissionibus et negligentiis vitiosis. Soror demum fratrum istorum Noema, sensualitatem designat.
paras.en: Lamech also begot three sons. The first of them, namely Jabel, [[4:20|the father of such as dwell in tents, and of herdsmen|pater habitantium in tentoriis ac pastorum]], signifies the covetous and the greedy, who are moved hither and thither to gather earthly things for themselves and to feed their cattle, that is, their brutish desires. The second, namely Jubal, [[4:21|the father of them that play upon the harp and the organs|pater canentium cithara et organo]], signifies those who seek and embrace the delights of the outward senses. The third, namely Tubalcain, [[4:22|a hammerer and artificer|malleator et faber]], signifies the warlike, the quarrelsome, the wrathful and the troublers of others, who strike their neighbours with harsh words or blows, or with works that give scandal, or even with sinful omissions and neglects. Lastly the sister of these brothers, Noema, signifies sensuality [that is, the lower, sensitive appetite].

paras.t: Dixitque Lamech uxoribus suis, Adæ et Sellæ: Quoniam occidi virum in vulnus meum, et adolescentulum in livorem meum. Libidinosi namque, omnium ætatum homines scandalizant ad sui ipsius perniciem, imo sæpe violenter aut fraudulenter interimunt viros et filios mulierum quas appetunt, ut eis fruantur securius. Verumtamen non vult Deus ut quis scandalizet tales libidinosos, aut inordinate perimat eos, sed potius ad pœnitentiam reserventur et retrahantur a vitiis.
paras.en: [[4:23|And Lamech said to his wives Ada and Sella|Dixitque Lamech uxoribus suis, Adæ et Sellæ]]: [[4:23|for I have slain a man to the wounding of myself, and a stripling to my own bruising|Quoniam occidi virum in vulnus meum, et adolescentulum in livorem meum]]. For the lustful give scandal to men of every age to their own ruin; indeed they often kill, by violence or by fraud, the husbands and sons of the women they desire, so as to enjoy them more securely. Yet God does not will that anyone should scandalize such lustful men or kill them wrongfully; rather they are to be kept for penance and drawn back from their vices.

paras.t: Cognovit quoque adhuc Adam uxorem suam; et peperit filium, vocavitque nomen ejus Seth: id est, Christus ex Ecclesia post sanctos martyres genuit confessores, ita quod Ecclesia dixit: Posuit mihi Deus semen aliud pro Abel, quem interfecit Cain. Confessores etenim sancti post martyres in eorum locum surrexerunt ac positi sunt.
paras.en: [[4:25|Adam also knew his wife again: and she brought forth a son, and called his name Seth|Cognovit quoque adhuc Adam uxorem suam; et peperit filium, vocavitque nomen ejus Seth]]: that is, after the holy martyrs Christ begot confessors of the Church, so that the Church said: [[4:25|God hath given me another seed for Abel, whom Cain slew|Posuit mihi Deus semen aliud pro Abel, quem interfecit Cain]]. For after the martyrs the holy confessors rose up and were put in their place [Denis plays on posuit, “hath given”, literally “hath put”].

paras.t: Sed et Seth natus est filius, quem vocavit Enos. Iste cœpit invocare nomen Domini. Per hunc Enos intelliguntur devotissimi religiosi, præsertim primi illi anachoretæ ac eremitæ sanctissimi, Paulus, Antonius, Macarius, Hilarion, Pacomius, atque innumerabiles, qui cœperunt Deum cum inaudita devotione, instantia, puritate die ac nocte exorare, laudare et colere, abstinentissima et rigorosissima conversatione.
paras.en: [[4:26|But to Seth also was born a son, whom he called Enos: this man began to call upon the name of the Lord|Sed et Seth natus est filius, quem vocavit Enos. Iste cœpit invocare nomen Domini]]. By this Enos are understood the most devout religious, especially those first most holy anchorites and hermits, Paul, Antony, Macarius, Hilarion, Pachomius, and countless others, who began to pray to God, to praise and worship Him day and night, with unheard-of devotion, earnestness and purity, in a most abstinent and rigorous way of life.

paras.t: Præterea, per Adam potest intelligi Deus omnium pater, qui ex Eva, id est Synagoga, sibi olim per fidem desponsata, genuit Cain, id est populum Judæorum, qui fuit tempore Christi, et Abel, id est Dominum Jesum, quem Judæi illi crucifixerunt, quemadmodum Cain occidit innoxium Abel, qui in multis Christum præfiguravit, videlicet innocentia, justitia, immolatione, martyrio. Inflammavit quoque Deus super Dominum Jesum, qui obtulit semetipsum oblationem et hostiam Patri in odorem suavitatis, ex ardentissima caritate desuper animæ suæ infusa: quæ immolatio Patri superacceptissima fuit. Similiter per Seth, qui interpretatur positio et resurrectio, designatus est Christus primitiæ resurgentium, et primus resurgens ex mortuis, propria potestate, primusque dignitate. Et sicut ex Seth nati sunt electi et virtuosi, ita ex Christo omnes re et nomine Christiani.
paras.en: Moreover, by Adam may be understood God the Father of all, who of Eve, that is, the Synagogue, once espoused to Him by faith, begot Cain, that is, the people of the Jews who lived in the time of Christ, and Abel, that is, the Lord Jesus, whom those Jews crucified, as Cain slew the innocent Abel, who prefigured Christ in many things: in innocence, justice, sacrifice and martyrdom. God also kindled fire upon the Lord Jesus [an allusion to v. 4, where for *had respect* Theodotion read “kindled fire upon”, as Jerome reports], who offered Himself [[Eph 5:2|an oblation and a sacrifice|oblationem et hostiam]] to the Father [[Eph 5:2|for an odour of sweetness|in odorem suavitatis]], out of the most ardent charity poured into His soul from above; which sacrifice was most supremely acceptable to the Father. Likewise by Seth, which is interpreted *placing* and *resurrection*, is signified Christ, the firstfruits of them that rise again[[1 Cor 15:20||]], and the first to rise from the dead by His own power, and first in dignity. And as from Seth were born the elect and the virtuous, so from Christ all who are Christians in deed and in name.

5.title: Expositio litteralis capituli quinti: Hic est liber generationis Adam
5.title_en: Literal exposition of the fifth chapter: “This is the book of the generation of Adam”

paras.t: REPETIT et recapitulat Moyses in exordio hujus capituli generationem Adæ, ut eam plenius prosequatur. Hic est liber, id est scriptura seu littera, generationis Adam, hoc est, generationem activam ipsius Adæ describens, quam generationem Adam exercuit seu incepit ; in die qua creavit, id est, tempore quo formavit Deus hominem, scilicet ipsum Adam et ejus uxorem. Ex quo nunc dictum est, In die qua creavit Deus hominem, Hebræi (ut fertur) dicunt ipsum Adam genuisse in paradiso, sicut et ante narratum est. Sed argumentum eorum nil valet, quia dies nunc capitur pro tempore, prout sæpissime in Scripturis contingit, sicut in Isaia : In illa die erit germen Domini in magnificentia et gloria. In Joel : In die illa stillabunt montes dulcedinem. Potest etiam dici, quod dies nunc capitur pro diebus, quemadmodum frequenter singulare ponitur pro plurali ; et ita supponit simpliciter seu confuse, ut supra secundo capitulo : Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ, in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram et omne virgultum agri.
paras.en: Moses repeats and recapitulates at the opening of this chapter the generation of Adam, so as to follow it out more fully. [[5:1|This is the book|Hic est liber]], that is, the writing or letter, [[5:1|of the generation of Adam|generationis Adam]], that is, describing the active generation of Adam himself, the generation which Adam carried out or began; [[5:1|In the day that God created|in die qua creavit]], that is, at the time when [[5:1|God|Deus]] formed [[5:1|man|hominem]], namely Adam himself and his wife. From what has just been said, [[5:1|In the day that God created man|In die qua creavit Deus hominem]], the Hebrews (so it is reported) say that Adam begot children in paradise, as was also related before. But their argument is worth nothing, since *day* is here taken for time, as very often happens in the Scriptures; as in Isaias: [[Is 4:2|In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory|In illa die erit germen Domini in magnificentia et gloria]]. In Joel: [[Joel 3:18|in that day|In die illa]] [[Joel 3:18|the mountains shall drop down sweetness|stillabunt montes dulcedinem]]. It can also be said that *day* is here taken for *days*, just as the singular is often put for the plural; and so it stands simply or confusedly [terms of the logic of supposition: the word stands for many days at once, without singling out any one], as above in the second chapter: [[Gen 2:4|These are the generations of the heaven and the earth|Istæ sunt generationes cœli et terræ]], [[Gen 2:4|in the day that the Lord God made the heaven and the earth|in die quo fecit Deus cœlum et terram]] [[Gen 2:5|and every plant of the field|et omne virgultum agri]].

paras.t: Ad similitudinem Dei fecit illum, masculum et feminam creavit eos, et benedixit illis. Omnia verba hæc habentur circa finem primi capituli, et ibi diffuse exposita sunt, ideo procedendum est modo. Et vocavit nomen eorum, Adam, id est, utrumque, scilicet tam virum quam Evam, vocavit hoc nomine Adam. Adam etenim in Hebræo est nomen commune, significans tantum sicut hæc dictio, homo : ideo sicut in Latino tam vir quam mulier dicitur homo, ita in Hebræo uterque dicitur Adam. Attamen Adam etiam in Hebræo frequenter singulariter sumitur pro homine illo primo. Sic ergo vocavit eos Deus, id est, vocandos instituit aut per subjectam creaturam expresse vocavit : ea die qua creati sunt, id est formati. Ambo enim secundum corpus ex præjacenti materia sunt plasmati, Adam ex limo, Eva ex viri costa.
paras.en: [[5:1|he made him to the likeness of God|Ad similitudinem Dei fecit illum]], [[5:2|He created them male and female|masculum et feminam creavit eos]]; [[5:2|and blessed them|et benedixit illis]]. All these words occur near the end of the first chapter, and were expounded at length there; so we must move on now. [[5:2|and called their name Adam|Et vocavit nomen eorum, Adam]], that is, he called both of them, namely the man as well as Eve, by this name Adam. For Adam in Hebrew is a common noun, meaning just what the word *homo* [man, human being] means: so just as in Latin both a man and a woman are called *homo*, so in Hebrew each is called Adam. Yet in Hebrew too Adam is often taken singly for that first man. So God called them thus, that is, appointed that they should be so called, or called them so expressly through a creature subject to him: [[5:2|in the day when they were created|ea die qua creati sunt]], that is, formed. For both, as to the body, were fashioned from pre-existing matter: Adam from the slime, Eve from the man's rib.

paras.t: Vixit autem Adam centum triginta annis, et genuit filium ad imaginem et similitudinem suam, id est similem sibi in specie imo et similem sibi in proprietate, hoc est in defectuositate, utpote destitutum originali justitia, mortalem, passibilem, et natura filium iræ. Unde ait Apostolus : Qualis terrenus, tales et terreni. Vocavitque nomen ejus Seth. Præcedenti capitulo scriptum est, quod Eva vocavit eum Seth. Itaque ambo sic eum appellabant, seu nomen ab Eva impositum, Adam confirmavit. Sicque Eva nomen primo expressit, deinde Adam. Verumtamen Adam antequam esset tantæ ætatis, genuit Cain et Abel.
paras.en: [[5:3|And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years|Vixit autem Adam centum triginta annis]], [[5:3|and begot a son to his own image and likeness|et genuit filium ad imaginem et similitudinem suam]], that is, like himself in species, and indeed like himself in his condition, that is, in his defects: namely deprived of original justice, mortal, passible, and by nature a child of wrath[[Eph 2:3||]]. Whence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:48|Such as is the earthly, such also are the earthly|Qualis terrenus, tales et terreni]] [the margin gives I Cor. xv, 45; these words are 1 Cor 15:48]. [[5:3|and called his name Seth|Vocavitque nomen ejus Seth]]. In the preceding chapter it is written that Eve called him Seth. So both called him so; or Adam confirmed the name Eve had given. And thus Eve uttered the name first, then Adam. But before Adam was of so great an age, he had begotten Cain and Abel.

paras.t: Circa hæc oritur quæstio duplex : Prima est, quomodo verum sit quod Adam genuit Seth, quum esset centum triginta annorum, quum Septuaginta et Josephus, itemque Methodius dicant eum fuisse ducentorum et triginta annorum dum genuit ipsum Seth. Respondetur secundum quosdam, quod Moyses omittit hic centum annos quibus Adam et Eva luxerunt Abel. Sed istud non videtur sufficiens ratio, quia non solum in Adam, sed etiam in posteris ejus omittuntur centum anni in Hebræo et translatione Hieronymi, quoad translationem Septuaginta. Unde ait Hieronymus, et habetur in Glossa : Usque ad diluvium, ubi in nostris codicibus legitur aliquis genuisse ducentorum annorum et quod excurrit, in Hebræo habet centum annos et reliquos qui sequuntur. Porro per codices nostros intelligit Hieronymus textus Septuaginta interpretum, quorum translatio fuit Hieronymi tempore in usu communi.
paras.en: Concerning these things a twofold question arises. The first is how it can be true that Adam begot Seth when he was a hundred and thirty years old, since the Septuagint and Josephus, and likewise Methodius, say that he was two hundred and thirty years old when he begot Seth. The answer, according to some, is that Moses here leaves out the hundred years during which Adam and Eve mourned Abel. But this does not seem a sufficient reason, since not only in Adam's case but in that of his descendants too a hundred years are left out in the Hebrew and in Jerome's translation, compared with the translation of the Seventy. Hence Jerome says, and it is in the Gloss: Up to the flood, wherever in our copies someone is read to have begotten at two hundred years and more, the Hebrew has a hundred years and the rest that follow. Now by *our copies* Jerome means the text of the Seventy translators, whose translation was in common use in Jerome's time.

paras.t: Secundo quæritur circa id quod in Glossa tangitur, et in Scholastica historia clarius fertur, Adam ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei factus est, reliqui ad similitudinem et imaginem Adæ, qualiter hoc sit verum. Respondetur, quod loquendo de his in quibus imago et similitudo Dei in homine principaliter consideratur, omnes homines ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei producti sunt, in quantum memoriam, intellectum, voluntatemque habent. Sed quantum ad accidentalia aliqua, in quibus imago et similitudo secundario consistit, ceteri ad Adæ imaginem, similitudinemque plasmati sunt, juxta sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: Secondly, a question is raised about what the Gloss touches on and the Scholastic History states more clearly, that Adam was made to the image and likeness of God, and the rest to the likeness and image of Adam: how is this true? The answer is that, speaking of those things in which the image and likeness of God in man is principally considered, all men are produced to the image and likeness of God, inasmuch as they have memory, understanding and will. But as to certain accidental things, in which the image and likeness consist secondarily, the others were fashioned to Adam's image and likeness, in the sense given above.

paras.t: Et facti sunt dies Adam postquam genuit Seth, octingenti anni, id est, usque ad tot annos creverunt et multiplicati sunt successive. Genuitque filios et filias, imo ut dictum est, Eva in omni partu peperit simul filium ac filiam, secundum Methodium et Hebræos. Horum autem filiorum et filiarum nomina non exprimuntur, quoniam Moyses brevitati studens, ad tempora Abrahæ ac Judæorum festinavit : ideo eorum nomina exprimit, ex quibus Patriarchæ et Prophetæ ac populus Judæorum, imo et Christus, exorti sunt. Aliorum quoque filiorum ac filiarum Adæ progenies diluvio perit.
paras.en: [[5:4|And the days of Adam, after he begot Seth, were eight hundred years|Et facti sunt dies Adam postquam genuit Seth, octingenti anni]], that is, they grew and were multiplied in succession up to so many years. [[5:4|and he begot sons and daughters|Genuitque filios et filias]]: indeed, as has been said, Eve at every birth bore a son and a daughter together, according to Methodius and the Hebrews. The names of these sons and daughters are not given, because Moses, intent on brevity, hastened on to the times of Abraham and of the Jews: therefore he gives the names of those from whom the Patriarchs and Prophets and the people of the Jews, and indeed Christ, sprang. The offspring of Adam's other sons and daughters, moreover, perished in the flood.

paras.t: Deinde in textu describitur, quemadmodum Seth genuit Enos, et Enos Cainan, et Cainan Malaleel, et Malaleel Jared, et Jared Enoch. Et item quo anno vitæ suæ genuerunt hi viri, atque quamdiu vixerunt : in quibus computationibus Scriptura non attendit nec curat minutias temporis, an scilicet modicum magis aut minus fuit, sed integros exprimit annos. Quæ autem facillima sunt, nec aliquid circa se dici requirunt, transilire intendo, quia in textu satis habentur. Quemadmodum autem in Scholastica historia dicitur, quidam incipiunt primam ætatem ab Adam, quidam a Seth, quia de Abel nullus est natus, tota generatio Cain diluvio est deleta, sicque Seth fuit primus gradus generationis humanæ.
paras.en: Then the text describes how Seth begot Enos, and Enos Cainan, and Cainan Malaleel, and Malaleel Jared, and Jared Enoch; and likewise in what year of their life these men begot, and how long they lived. In these reckonings Scripture does not attend to or care about small fractions of time, whether it was a little more or less, but gives whole years. What is quite easy and calls for no comment I mean to pass over, since it is plain enough in the text. Now, as is said in the Scholastic History, some begin the first age from Adam, some from Seth, because no one was born of Abel, and the whole generation of Cain was wiped out by the flood; and so Seth was the first degree of human generation.

paras.t: Porro Enoch vixit sexaginta quinque annis, et genuit Mathusalem. Iste Enoch fuit septimus ab Adam in generatione Seth, quemadmodum Lamech in generatione Cain. Et sicut septimus ille Lamech fuit pravissimus, ita septimus iste Enoch exstitit optimus.
paras.en: [[5:21|And Henoch lived sixty-five years, and begot Mathusala|Porro Enoch vixit sexaginta quinque annis, et genuit Mathusalem]]. This Enoch was the seventh from Adam in the line of Seth, as Lamech was in the line of Cain. And as that seventh, Lamech, was most wicked, so this seventh, Enoch, was most good.

paras.t: Et ambulavit Enoch cum Deo, id est juxta beneplacitum Dei, adhærendo eidem, et sequendo voluntatem ipsius per vitam justam. Et non apparuit, id est, a conversatione, societate, atque præsentia hominum repente sublatus est, quia tulit eum Deus, id est, transtulit de medio hominum ad alium locum, videlicet paradisum terrestrem, quemadmodum postea diu Eliam. Qualiter autem translatus est Enoch, Scriptura non exprimit ; et an aliquis translationi ejus interfuit, ignoratur. Creditur tamen quod angelico ministerio sit translatus.
paras.en: [[5:22|And Henoch walked with God|Et ambulavit Enoch cum Deo]], that is, according to God's good pleasure, cleaving to him and following his will by a just life. [[5:24|and was seen no more|Et non apparuit]], that is, he was suddenly taken away from the converse, company and presence of men, [[5:24|because God took him|quia tulit eum Deus]], that is, removed him from the midst of men to another place, namely the earthly paradise, as long afterwards he did Elias[[4 Kings 2:11||]]. How Enoch was translated, Scripture does not say; and whether anyone was present at his translation is not known. Yet it is believed that he was translated by the ministry of angels.

paras.t: De hoc in Scholastica historia dicitur : Transtulit illum Deus in paradisum, ut in fine temporum cum Elia veniens, convertat corda patrum in filios. Judæi tamen causam translationis Enoch magis attribuunt mysterio numeri septenarii, quam sanctitati ipsius Enoch, quum plures fuerint eo sanctiores, quorum nullus translatus est. In tantum enim aiunt Deum omnia sub septenario disposuisse, quod dicunt eum septem cœlos creasse et septem terras, quas (ut dicunt) David appellat montium fundamenta. Hæc ibi.
paras.en: Of this the Scholastic History says: God translated him into paradise, so that at the end of time, coming with Elias[[Mal 4:5||]], he may [[Mal 4:6|turn the heart of the fathers to the children|convertat corda patrum in filios]]. The Jews, however, attribute the cause of Enoch's translation more to the mystery of the number seven than to the holiness of Enoch himself, since there were many holier than he, none of whom was translated. For they say that God disposed all things under the number seven to such a degree that they say he created seven heavens and seven earths, which (so they say) David calls [[Ps 17:8|the foundations of the mountains|montium fundamenta]] [no reference in the margin; the words stand at Ps 17:8, and again at 2 Kings 22:8]. Thus far the History.

paras.t: Lyra quoque refert : Dicunt Judæi, quod licet Enoch esset justus, magnas tamen pronitates habuit ad malum, quibus cum difficultate resistebat. Ideo mortuus est ante finem vitæ suæ naturalis, ne vinceretur malitia. Hæc ille. Et potest esse quod aliqui Judæi hoc dicant, quorum assertio falsa est, quantum ad hoc quod dicunt eum mortuum esse. Non enim Scriptura ista refert de eo sicut de ceteris cunctis quod mortuus sit, sed quod non apparuit, quoniam Dominus tulit eum. Porro quod dicunt de pronitate ejus ad malum, apparentiam habet ex eo, quod scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ : Placens Deo factus dilectus, et vivens inter peccatores translatus est. Raptus est, ne malitia mutaret intellectum ejus, aut ne fictio deciperet animam illius. Consummatus in brevi, explevit tempora multa. Placita enim erat Deo anima illius : propter hoc properavit educere eum de medio iniquitatum. Quod totum de Enoch uno modo exponitur.
paras.en: Lyra also reports: The Jews say that although Enoch was just, he had strong inclinations to evil, which he resisted with difficulty; therefore he died before the end of his natural life, lest he be overcome by wickedness. Thus far Lyra. And it may be that some Jews say this; but their assertion is false in so far as they say that he died. For this Scripture does not say of him, as of all the others, that he died, but that he was seen no more, because the Lord took him. As for what they say of his inclination to evil, it has some appearance of truth from what is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 4:10|He pleased God, and was beloved, and living among sinners, he was translated|Placens Deo factus dilectus, et vivens inter peccatores translatus est]]. [[Wis 4:11|He was taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul|Raptus est, ne malitia mutaret intellectum ejus, aut ne fictio deciperet animam illius]]. [[Wis 4:13|Being made perfect in a short space, he fulfilled a long time|Consummatus in brevi, explevit tempora multa]]. [[Wis 4:14|For his soul pleased God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities|Placita enim erat Deo anima illius : propter hoc properavit educere eum de medio iniquitatum]] [the margin gives Wis. iv, 10, 11; the quotation runs on to v. 14, leaving out v. 12]. All of this is expounded, in one way, of Enoch.

paras.t: De quo etiam in Ecclesiastico asseritur : Enoch placuit Deo, et translatus est in paradisum, ut det gentibus sapientiam. Hinc sancti doctores testantur, quod circa finem mundi cum Elia venturus sit ad prædicandum contra Antichristum, sicut de hoc in Apocalypsi multa leguntur, Deo dicente : Dabo duobus testibus meis, etc. Tunc quoque ab Antichristo interficientur, et debitum mortis solvent. Denique Glossa et Alcuinus affirmant : Enoch tanto tempore præservatur a morte, in signum quia homo jugiter viveret, si non peccasset. De hoc Enoch in Scholastica fertur historia : Enoch litteras quasdam invenit, et aliquos libros scripsit, sub quo Adam creditur mortuus. Huic dicto consonat, quod Judas apostolus in sua allegat Canonica : Prophetavit autem de his septimus ab Adam, Enoch, dicens : Ecce venit Dominus in sanctis millibus suis. Dicitur autem Enoch septimus post Adam, ipsum Adam includendo, ut patet ex textu, intermedios numerando, qui fuerunt, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared.
paras.en: Of him it is also asserted in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 44:16|Henoch pleased God, and was translated into paradise|Enoch placuit Deo, et translatus est in paradisum]], that he may give wisdom to the nations [the margin's reference cannot be read; the words are Ecclus 44:16, where the Vulgate has *pœnitentiam*, "repentance", for Denis's *sapientiam*, "wisdom"]. Hence the holy doctors testify that near the end of the world he will come with Elias to preach against Antichrist, as much is read of this in the Apocalypse, where God says: [[Apoc 11:3|I will give unto my two witnesses|Dabo duobus testibus meis]], etc. Then too they will be slain by Antichrist, and will pay the debt of death. Lastly the Gloss and Alcuin affirm: Enoch is preserved from death for so long a time as a sign that man would have lived for ever, had he not sinned. Of this Enoch the Scholastic History relates: Enoch invented certain letters and wrote some books, and in his time Adam is believed to have died. With this saying agrees what the apostle Jude alleges in his canonical Epistle: [[Jude 1:14|Now of these Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying: Behold, the Lord cometh with thousands of his saints|Prophetavit autem de his septimus ab Adam, Enoch, dicens : Ecce venit Dominus in sanctis millibus suis]]. Now Enoch is called the seventh after Adam counting Adam himself, as is clear from the text, and numbering those in between, who were Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared.

paras.t: Vixit quoque Mathusalem centum octoginta septem annis, et genuit Lamech. Mathusalem qui tam diu in virginitate permansit, videtur fuisse vir magnæ devotionis.
paras.en: [[5:25|And Mathusala lived a hundred and eighty-seven years, and begot Lamech|Vixit quoque Mathusalem centum octoginta septem annis, et genuit Lamech]]. Mathusalem, who remained so long in virginity, seems to have been a man of great devotion.

paras.t: Et facti sunt omnes dies Mathusalem nongenti sexaginta novem anni ; et mortuus est. Ad quantam ætatem nullus alius legitur pervenisse. Unde antiquissimus hominum creditur exstitisse, quantum ex Scripturis habetur, fuitque annis triginta novem senior quam Adam. Verumtamen de ætate Mathusalem fuerunt diversæ opiniones : nempe secundum computationem et textum Septuaginta, vixisset quatuordecim annis post diluvium : quod stare non potest, quia non fuit in arca, legiturque obiisse. Alii quidam dixerunt eum obiisse ante diluvium septem annis, quod minus absurdum est. Sed beatus Hieronymus vere et sapienter testatur, quod eodem anno quo diluvium inundavit defunctus est modicum ante diluvium, et hoc probat ex textu secundum Hebraïcam veritatem. Mathusalem namque vixit centum octoginta septem annis antequam genuit Lamech, quibus si addantur centum octoginta duo anni, quibus vixit Lamech antequam genuit Noe, ut statim dicetur, atque sexcenti anni quibus vixit Noe ante inundationem diluvii, ut infra habetur, inveniuntur anni nongenti sexaginta novem, quibus vixit Mathusalem. Translatio autem Septuaginta, quantum ad taxationem numeri annorum Mathusalem, fuit corrupta hoc loco, sicut in aliis multis secundum Hieronymum, ut habetur in Glossa. De hoc loquitur Augustinus, ponens diversas opiniones de ætate et vita Mathusalem, et qualiter aliqui volentes salvare computationem Septuaginta, dixerunt ipsum Mathusalem, durante diluvio, fuisse cum patre suo Enoch in paradiso, deinde reductum ad terram mortalium. Quod reprobat Augustinus, et dicit eum obiisse eodem anno quo venit diluvium, secundum Hebraicam veritatem, atque ex vitio et errore scriptorum potuisse accidere errorem, qui in computatione Septuaginta invenitur.
paras.en: [[5:27|And all the days of Mathusala were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died|Et facti sunt omnes dies Mathusalem nongenti sexaginta novem anni ; et mortuus est]]. No one else is read to have reached such an age. Hence he is believed to have been the oldest of men, as far as can be had from the Scriptures, and he was thirty-nine years older than Adam. Yet there were different opinions about the age of Mathusalem: for according to the reckoning and text of the Seventy he would have lived fourteen years after the flood, which cannot stand, because he was not in the ark, and he is read to have died. Some others said that he died seven years before the flood, which is less absurd. But blessed Jerome truly and wisely testifies that he died in the same year in which the flood came, a little before the flood, and he proves this from the text according to the Hebrew truth [that is, the original Hebrew text]. For Mathusalem lived a hundred and eighty-seven years before he begot Lamech; if to these are added the hundred and eighty-two years which Lamech lived before he begot Noe, as will be said presently, and the six hundred years which Noe lived before the flood broke, as is found below, we arrive at the nine hundred and sixty-nine years which Mathusalem lived. The translation of the Seventy, as to the reckoning of the number of Mathusalem's years, was corrupt in this place, as in many others, according to Jerome, as is found in the Gloss. Augustine speaks of this, setting out different opinions on the age and life of Mathusalem, and how some, wishing to save the reckoning of the Seventy, said that Mathusalem was with his father Enoch in paradise while the flood lasted, and was afterwards brought back to the land of mortals. Augustine rejects this, and says that he died in the same year in which the flood came, according to the Hebrew truth, and that the error found in the reckoning of the Seventy could have arisen from the fault and mistake of copyists.

paras.t: Vixit autem Lamech centum octoginta duobus annis, et genuit filium, vocavitque nomen ejus Noe, dicens: Iste consolabitur nos ab operibus et laboribus manuum nostrarum in terra cui maledixit Dominus. Videtur Lamech iste fuisse vir castus et bonus, quia tamdiu continuit antequam generavit. Videtur item prophetali gratia splenduisse, quia de filio suo Noe talia pronuntiavit.
paras.en: [[5:28|And Lamech lived a hundred and eighty-two years, and begot a son|Vixit autem Lamech centum octoginta duobus annis, et genuit filium]], [[5:29|and he called his name Noe, saying|vocavitque nomen ejus Noe, dicens]]: [[5:29|This same shall comfort us from the works and labours of our hands on the earth, which the Lord hath cursed|Iste consolabitur nos ab operibus et laboribus manuum nostrarum in terra cui maledixit Dominus]]. This Lamech seems to have been a chaste and good man, since he restrained himself so long before he begot. He seems also to have shone with the grace of prophecy, since he foretold such things of his son Noe.

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem in Actis Apostolorum leguntur gloriosi et sancti Apostoli Joseph Cyprium appellasse Barnabam, id est filium consolationis, quia de ejus conversione, sanctitate et fructuositate primitiva Ecclesia magnam consolationem accepit: sic Lamech Deo revelante cognoscens, quam virtuose, fructuose ac dulciter filius suus Noe esset inter homines conversaturus, prædixit: Iste consolabitur nos ab operibus et laboribus manuum nostrarum, hoc est, suis virtutibus et fructuositatibus dabit nobis relevamen atque solatium inter ipsos labores et opera, quibus occupamur et fatigamur in terra hac a Domino maledicta propter primorum parentum peccata, juxta sensum in expositione capituli tertii introductum. Et aliqui dicunt, quod Lamech prædixit hæc verba de Noe, quia prævidit quod erat reparaturus terram et animalia ac genus humanum post diluvium, et juxta hoc Lamech iste cognovisset quod diluvium erat venturum sub filio suo Noe: quod tamen non videtur ex Scripturis evidenter posse haberi, quia sequenti capitulo legitur Deus revelasse ipsi Noe de inundatione diluvii tempore suo. Nec legitur hoc alicui alteri antea revelasse statim, quantum ad temporis determinationem.
paras.en: For as in the Acts of the Apostles the glorious and holy Apostles are read to have called Joseph the Cyprian Barnabas, that is, [[Acts 4:36|The son of consolation|filium consolationis]], because the early Church received great consolation from his conversion, holiness and fruitfulness: so Lamech, knowing by God's revelation how virtuously, fruitfully and sweetly his son Noe would live among men, foretold: [[5:29|This same shall comfort us from the works and labours of our hands|Iste consolabitur nos ab operibus et laboribus manuum nostrarum]], that is, by his virtues and fruitful works he will give us relief and solace amid the very labours and works with which we are busied and wearied on this earth, cursed by the Lord for the sins of our first parents, in the sense set out in the exposition of the third chapter. And some say that Lamech foretold these words of Noe because he foresaw that he was to restore the earth and the animals and mankind after the flood; and on this view Lamech would have known that the flood was to come in the time of his son Noe. This, however, does not seem able to be had clearly from the Scriptures, since in the following chapter God is read to have revealed to Noe himself the flood that would come in his time; nor is he read to have revealed it to anyone else beforehand, as to fixing the time.

paras.t: Præterea Lyra dicit quod in Hebræo habetur, Iste quietabit nos. Nam et nomen hoc Noe, requies interpretatur. Et dicunt Hebræi, quod Lamech prædixit hæc verba de Noe, non propter sæculi reparationem post finem diluvii, sed quia primo invenit artem arandi, quum homines antea colerent terram propriis manibus sine subsidio jumentorum, quod erat valde laboriosum: a quo opere et labore relevavit et quietavit eos Noe, inveniendo artem præfatam. Unde infra capitulo nono Noe vocatur agricola. Sed si Lamech prævidit quod Noe esset inventurus hanc artem, ergo et Lamech aliquo modo eam præscivit. Ad quod dici potest, quod non sequitur, ipsum Lamech eam præscivisse in speciali atque distincte. Verum Rabbi Paulus reprehendit utrumque istorum dictorum. Dicit enim quod in Hebræo habetur, Iste consolabitur nos: et non, Iste quietabit nos. Verius tamen reor, quod verbum Hebraicum sit æquivocum ad utrumque. Dixit quoque: Si Noe fuisset primus inventor artis arandi, Scriptura hoc expressisset, sicut præcedenti expressit capitulo de Jabel, quod fuit pater habitantium in tentoriis et pastorum, atque de Jubal, quod fuit pater canentium cithara, etc. Verumtamen dictum illud Hebræorum est satis consonum textui, idcirco argumentum Rabbi Pauli non prævalet. Nam dici potest, quod scriptura ista satis insinuavit hoc, utpote quod Noe invenit artem arandi per verba hæc Lamech. Nec obstaret quod objicit Rabbi Paulus, videlicet quod infra nono capitulo legitur : Cœpit autem Noe vir agricola exercere terram. Hoc enim non dicitur ad hunc sensum, quod tunc et non ante cœpit esse agricola, sed quod tunc cœpit hoc facere, quantum ad tempus post diluvium : imo stare non potest quod Rabbi Paulus ait, ipsum Noe tunc primo cœpisse esse agricolam in plantatione vineæ, et non ante : quoniam etsi artem arandi non reperisset, attamen potuit esse agricola ante diluvium, quum scriptum sit quarto capitulo, quod Cain fuit agricola. Idcirco nec ex ista auctoritate satis probatur, quod Noe invenit artem arandi. Nihilo minus apparentiam potest habere, quod sicut Noe invenit artem plantandi vitem, ita et artem arandi, quum et textus videatur hoc ipsum innuere. Ego tamen de his quæ certitudinem non habent, nil assero.
paras.en: Moreover Lyra says that in the Hebrew it reads, *This one shall give us rest*. For the name Noe means *rest*. And the Hebrews say that Lamech foretold these words of Noe not because of the restoration of the world after the end of the flood, but because he first invented the art of ploughing, since before that men tilled the earth with their own hands, without the help of beasts of burden, which was very laborious; from this work and labour Noe relieved them and gave them rest by inventing the said art. Hence below, in the ninth chapter, Noe is called a husbandman. But if Lamech foresaw that Noe would invent this art, then Lamech too in some way knew it beforehand. To this it can be said that it does not follow that Lamech knew it beforehand specifically and distinctly. But Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a convert from Judaism, whose *Additions* to Lyra's Postill often criticize him] finds fault with both these sayings. For he says that in the Hebrew it reads, [[5:29|This same shall comfort us|Iste consolabitur nos]], and not, *This one shall give us rest*. Yet I think it truer that the Hebrew word is ambiguous between the two. He also said: If Noe had been the first inventor of the art of ploughing, Scripture would have said so, as in the preceding chapter it said of Jabel that he [[Gen 4:20|was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of herdsmen|fuit pater habitantium in tentoriis et pastorum]], and of Jubal that he was [[Gen 4:21|the father of them that play upon the harp|pater canentium cithara]], etc. Yet that saying of the Hebrews agrees well enough with the text; therefore Rabbi Paul's argument does not prevail. For it can be said that this scripture hinted at it sufficiently, namely that Noe invented the art of ploughing, through these words of Lamech. Nor does Rabbi Paul's objection stand in the way, namely that below, in the ninth chapter, one reads: [[Gen 9:20|And Noe a husbandman began to till the ground|Cœpit autem Noe vir agricola exercere terram]]. For this is not said in the sense that he then, and not before, began to be a husbandman, but that he then began to do this, as regards the time after the flood. Indeed what Rabbi Paul says cannot stand, that Noe then first began to be a husbandman, in planting the vineyard, and not before: for even if he had not found the art of ploughing, he could still have been a husbandman before the flood, since it is written in the fourth chapter that Cain was a husbandman[[Gen 4:2||]]. Therefore it is not sufficiently proved from that authority either that Noe invented the art of ploughing. Nonetheless it may seem likely that, as Noe invented the art of planting the vine, so he did that of ploughing, since the text too seems to hint at this very thing. But I assert nothing about things that have no certainty.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur : Primo, quomodo homines potuerunt ante diluvium vivere tamdiu. De isto multa scribit Augustinus ubi enarrat, qualiter quidam fideles considerantes qualiter multi retraherentur a fide, quoniam incredibile reputabant homines tunc tamdiu vixisse, opinati sunt quod anni de quibus loquitur scriptura hæc, non fuerunt anni solares duodecim mensium, secundum quod annos communiter computamus ; sed anni breves, ita quod unus annus solaris comprehenderet decem annos hujusmodi. Diversi enim diversimode computant annos. Istud vero sanctus Augustinus multipliciter reprobat, et specialiter ex duobus. Primo, quoniam Seth quum esset centum et quinque annorum, genuit Enos : ergo secundum illam computationem genuisset filium suum Enos, antequam habuisset undecim annos. Cainan quoque quum esset septuaginta annorum, genuit Malaleel, sicque genuisset, quum erat septem annorum. Secundo, quoniam infra habetur, quod sexcentesimo primo anno vitæ Noe, primo mense, prima die mensis, imminutæ sunt aquæ. Deinde quod mense secundo, vigesima et septima die mensis, arefacta est terra, et paulo ante, Requievit arca mense septimo super montes Armeniæ. Ex quibus constat, quod anni illi computantur sicut et modo.
paras.en: Concerning what has been set out above, it is asked, first, how men before the flood could live so long. Augustine writes much on this, where he relates how certain of the faithful, seeing that many were held back from the faith because they thought it incredible that men lived so long in those days, held that the years of which this scripture speaks were not solar years of twelve months, such as we commonly reckon years, but short years, so that one solar year would contain ten such years; for different people reckon years in different ways. But Saint Augustine refutes this in many ways, and especially by two. First, because Seth, when he was a hundred and five years old, begot Enos: so by that reckoning he would have begotten his son Enos before he was eleven years old. Cainan also, when he was seventy years old, begot Malaleel; and so he would have begotten him when he was seven years old. Secondly, because below it is said that [[Gen 8:13|in the six hundredth and first year|sexcentesimo primo anno]] of Noe's life, [[Gen 8:13|the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were lessened|primo mense, prima die mensis, imminutæ sunt aquæ]]; and then that [[Gen 8:14|in the second month, the seven and twentieth day of the month, the earth was dried|mense secundo, vigesima et septima die mensis, arefacta est terra]]; and a little before, [[Gen 8:4|the ark rested in the seventh month|Requievit arca mense septimo]] [[Gen 8:4|upon the mountains of Armenia|super montes Armeniæ]]. From this it is clear that those years are reckoned just as they are now.

paras.t: Præterea sanctus Thomas dixit simpliciter supernaturale fuisse, quod homines illi tamdiu vixerunt, ita quod Deus supernaturaliter conservavit eos in vita tamdiu propter celeriorem humani generis multiplicationem, præsertim quum sanctus David ante tot millia annorum locutus sit : Dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni : si autem in potentatibus, octoginta anni, et amplius eorum labor et dolor. Propter quod etiam de Berzellai scriptum est, quod erat senex valde, id est octogenarius.
paras.en: Moreover Saint Thomas said that it was simply supernatural that those men lived so long, God preserving them in life supernaturally for so long for the speedier multiplication of mankind; especially since holy David, so many thousands of years ago, said: [[Ps 89:10|The days of our years in them are threescore and ten years. But if in the strong they be fourscore years: and what is more of them is labour and sorrow|Dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni : si autem in potentatibus, octoginta anni, et amplius eorum labor et dolor]] [the margin reads "… 10", its book unread; the words are Ps 89:10]. For this reason it is also written of Berzellai that he [[2 Kings 19:32|was of a great age, that is to say, fourscore years old|erat senex valde, id est octogenarius]] [the margin reads "II Reg. … 32", the chapter unread; the verse is 2 Kings 19:32].

paras.t: Verumtamen aliquæ rationes assignantur, quæ poterant naturaliter conferre ad vitam illorum hominum tam longævam. Prima est, quod homines, potissimum viri isti boni qui tamdiu vixisse leguntur, erant temperatæ ac sobriæ vitæ. Secunda, quoniam terræ nascentia et fructus ac herbæ quibus sustentabantur, erant ante diluvium multo majoris efficaciæ ac virtutis, quam postea. Tertia, quia natura humana quæ paulatim declinat, erat tunc vigorosior in se ipsa. Quarta, quoniam præcipua bonitas complexionis primorum parentum, immediate a Deo factorum, magis remansit in posteris in prima mundi ætate, quam postea. Quinta est bona influentia, conveniensque adspectus stellarum ac planetarum super locum in quo habitaverunt : quæ duo per assiduum motum cœli sunt tempore procedente mutata. Sexta, quoniam Adam qui erat in naturalium rerum scientia multum excellens, scivit, et sobolem suam docuit, vires lapidum ac herbarum, quæ ad vitæ conservationem ac prolongationem plurimum conferunt. Septima, ut homines diu vivendo, magis proficerent in naturali ac morali scientia, præsertim in astronomia. Hinc Josephus primo Antiquitatum libro disseruit : Nemo ex consideratione et comparationem brevitatis vitæ humanæ quæ nunc est, putet falsa esse, quæ de diuturnitate vitæ antiquorum illorum dicuntur. Illi enim quum essent religiosi, et a Deo ipso formati, eisque pabula opportuniora ad manus ad tempus parata exsisterent, tantorum annorum circulis rite vivebant. Deinde propter virtutes et gloriosas utilitates, quas jugiter scrutabantur, id est astrologiam et geometriam, Deus eis vitæ spatia amplius prolongavit : quæ nunquam ediscere potuissent, nisi sexcentis viverent annis. Per tot enim annorum curricula magnus annus impletur. Deinde Josephus probat illos tamdiu vixisse per varia, diversosque historiographos gentium plurimarum.
paras.en: Yet some reasons are given which could naturally have contributed to the long life of those men. The first is that men, above all these good men who are read to have lived so long, were of temperate and sober life. The second, that the produce of the earth, the fruits and the herbs by which they were sustained, were of much greater efficacy and power before the flood than afterwards. The third, that human nature, which declines little by little, was then more vigorous in itself. The fourth, that the outstanding goodness of the complexion [that is, the balance of the bodily humours] of the first parents, made immediately by God, remained more in their descendants in the first age of the world than afterwards. The fifth is the good influence and favourable aspect of the stars and planets over the place where they lived: both of which have been changed in the course of time by the constant motion of the heaven. The sixth, that Adam, who greatly excelled in the knowledge of natural things, knew, and taught his offspring, the powers of stones and herbs, which contribute very much to the preservation and prolonging of life. The seventh, that men, by living long, might make more progress in natural and moral science, especially in astronomy. Hence Josephus discoursed in the first book of the Antiquities: Let no one, from considering and comparing the shortness of human life as it now is, think false what is told of the long life of those ancients. For since they were religious men, and formed by God himself, and more suitable food was at hand and ready for them for the time, they rightly lived through the circles of so many years. Then, because of the virtues and glorious useful arts into which they constantly searched, that is, astrology and geometry, God prolonged the span of their lives further: these they could never have learned had they not lived six hundred years. For in the course of so many years the great year is completed [the "great year" is the period after which the heavenly bodies return to the same positions]. Josephus then proves that they lived so long from various sources and from diverse historians of many nations.

paras.t: Sed Rabbi Paulus, qui ubique satis pronus est reprehendere Nicolaum de Lyra, contra rationes has arguit, et argumentando aliqua dicit, quæ videntur satis faciliter posse redargui. Primo etenim dicit : Nunquam reperitur aliquis a tertia ætate mundi, quæ scilicet incepit ab Abraham et infra, attigisse fere ducentos annos. Contra quod videtur sanctus Job, qui fuit secundum quosdam post Abraham, vixitque post suam percussionem et curationem centum quadraginta annis, qui et ante suam percussionem fuit maturæ ætatis. Unde et omnes pueri ejus qui decem erant, ante ejus percussionem ad virilem ætatem seu annum vicesimum pervenisse videntur, vel saltem multi eorum. Unde probabile est, primogenitum inter eos inter tricesimum et quadragesimum annum fuisse aut circiter, ita quod Job omnibus annis ejus simul acceptis, videtur ad minus fuisse ducentorum annorum. Superius quoque ex epistola Alexandri ad Aristotelem allegatum est, quemadmodum sacerdotes solis et lunæ virtute pomorum, quibus vescuntur, vivant annis quadringentis aut circiter. Legitur item in Chronica Martini, quod tempore Caroli Magni fuit quidam nomine Joannes, qui vixit pene quadringentis annis, propter quod vocabatur Joannes de Tempore. Imo de pluribus legitur qui post Abraham exstiterunt, et plusquam ducentis annis vixerunt.
paras.en: But Rabbi Paul, who is everywhere rather inclined to find fault with Nicholas of Lyra, argues against these reasons, and in arguing says some things which it seems can be refuted easily enough. For first he says: No one from the third age of the world, that is, the one which began from Abraham onwards, is ever found to have reached nearly two hundred years. Against this seems to stand holy Job, who according to some lived after Abraham, and who lived a hundred and forty years after his smiting and healing[[Job 42:16||]], and was already of mature age before his smiting. Hence all his children, who were ten, seem to have reached manhood, or the twentieth year, before his smiting, or at least many of them. So it is probable that the firstborn among them was between his thirtieth and fortieth year, or thereabouts, so that Job, all his years taken together, seems to have been at least two hundred years old. Also above, from the letter of Alexander to Aristotle, it was alleged how the priests of the sun and moon live four hundred years or thereabouts by the power of the fruits they eat. It is also read in the Chronicle of Martin that in the time of Charlemagne there was a certain man named John, who lived nearly four hundred years, for which reason he was called John of the Times. Indeed many are read of who lived after Abraham and lived more than two hundred years.

paras.t: Deinde argumenta quæ facit contra ea quæ dicta sunt de valore terræ nascentium ante diluvium, de bono adspectu atque influxu cœlestium corporum, aliquam apparentiam sortirentur, si unaquæque causarum illarum assignaretur, quasi per se solam sufficiens causa tantæ diuturnitatis vitæ Patrum illorum. Insuper dicit, quod tanta prolongatio vitæ, non contulit ad celerem multiplicationem hominum magis quam brevitas vitæ humanæ in posteris, imo potius minus : in quo non solum contradicit Thomæ, aliisque antiquis doctoribus, sed et experientiæ, ut apparet. Quod vero allegat homines tunc vixisse centum annis antequam genuerunt, non videtur omnifarie rite dictum : quia ut ait Augustinus, Non est putandum, quod illi fuerint semper primogeniti, qui primo nati leguntur ; sed illi primo nati leguntur, per quos ordo successionis ad Abraham est deductus ; ceteri frequenter tacentur.
paras.en: Next, the arguments he makes against what has been said about the virtue of the earth's produce before the flood, and about the good aspect and influence of the heavenly bodies, would have some appearance of truth if each of those causes were assigned as though it alone were a sufficient cause of so long a life of those Fathers. Further he says that so great a lengthening of life did not contribute to the speedy multiplication of men more than the shortness of human life in later generations, but rather less: in which he contradicts not only Thomas and other ancient doctors, but experience too, as is plain. As for his alleging that men then lived a hundred years before they begot, this does not seem rightly said in every respect: because, as Augustine says, It is not to be thought that those who are read to have been born first were always the firstborn; but those are read to have been born first through whom the order of succession is brought down to Abraham; the others are frequently passed over in silence.

paras.t: Præterea dicit : Cursus siderum fuit perfecte declaratus tempore Græcorum, quando Ptolemæus scripsit librum qui dicitur Almagesti, in quo omnes cursus siderum plene traduntur. Istud est contra Ptolemæum et omnes majores astrologos, Albategni, Albumasar, Alfraganum, qui fassi sunt neminem in vita præsenti posse pertingere ad plenam notitiam omnium cursuum et motuum, virtutum, influentiarum, atque effectuum siderum ac cœlorum. Propter quod dixit Sedulius versificator egregius : Qui stellas numeras, quarum tu nomina solus, Signa, potestates, cursus, loca, tempora, nosti. Amplius dicit, quod investigatio Ptolemæi incepit a tempore cujusdam, qui eum præcessit fere per annos trecentos. Istud non potest absolute sic verificari. Consideratio enim astronomiæ incepit plusquam per duo millia annorum ante Ptolemæum, ut patet ex his quæ Augustinus ait in libro de Civitate Dei in multis locis, præsertim quum et Abraham patriarcha fuisse legatur magnus astronomus, imo et multi ante diluvium. Ptolemæus autem studuit libro antiquissimorum astronomorum, quos poterat reperire. Iterum dicit, quod ad cognoscendum effectus siderum sufficit tantum tempus, ut fuit inter prædecessorem Ptolemæi et Ptolemæum, quem iste trecentis annis præcessit. Ad quod reor dicendum, quod nec tria millia annorum cum trecentis annis, sufficiunt ad cognoscendum per investigationem et studium universos effectus stellarum in speciali, præsertim quum nullus valeat naturali investigatione cognoscere numerum ipsum stellarum ac singulas stellas, quarum quælibet propriam virtutem ac influentiam habet, ut in libro de Radiis stellarum ait Alkindus.
paras.en: Moreover he says: The course of the stars was perfectly set forth in the time of the Greeks, when Ptolemy wrote the book called the Almagest, in which all the courses of the stars are fully handed down. This is against Ptolemy and all the greater astrologers, Albategni, Albumasar, Alfraganus, who have confessed that no one in this present life can attain full knowledge of all the courses and motions, powers, influences and effects of the stars and heavens. For which reason Sedulius, that excellent versifier, said: Thou who numberest the stars, whose names thou alone, / Their signs, powers, courses, places and times, dost know. Further he says that Ptolemy's investigation began from the time of a certain man who preceded him by nearly three hundred years. This cannot be verified absolutely in this way. For the study of astronomy began more than two thousand years before Ptolemy, as is plain from what Augustine says in many places in the book of the City of God; especially since the patriarch Abraham too is read to have been a great astronomer, and indeed many before the flood. And Ptolemy studied the book of the most ancient astronomers he could find. Again he says that to know the effects of the stars as much time suffices as there was between Ptolemy's predecessor and Ptolemy, whom that man preceded by three hundred years. To this I think it must be said that not even three thousand years and three hundred suffice to know, by investigation and study, all the effects of the stars in particular; especially since no one can know by natural investigation the very number of the stars, and each single star, every one of which has its own power and influence, as Alkindus says in the book On the Rays of the Stars.

paras.t: Postremo allegat Rabbi Moyses, qui in libro de Directione perplexorum, diuturnitatem illam vitæ Patrum ante diluvium, divino adscribit miraculo, et ait quod Deus voluit viros illos, de quibus in littera scribitur, tamdiu vivere, ut fides de creatione mundi, magis infigeretur cordibus posterorum. Alios vero qui non exprimuntur in littera, dicit Rabbi Moyses non vixisse tamdiu, sed tanto tempore ut post diluvium. Verumtamen huic obviare videtur, quod fuerunt generationes non pauciores ab Adam per Seth, et eos quorum ætas in littera enarratur usque diluvium, quam ab Adam per Cain usque ad illud, quum tamen Cain fuerit plusquam centum annis, ut communiter dicitur, ante Seth natus, imo secundum Methodium, annis centum et quindecim.
paras.en: Lastly he alleges Rabbi Moses, who in the book of the Guide of the Perplexed ascribes that long life of the Fathers before the flood to a divine miracle, and says that God willed those men of whom the letter writes to live so long, so that faith in the creation of the world might be more deeply fixed in the hearts of their descendants. The others, who are not named in the letter, Rabbi Moses says did not live so long, but as long as men after the flood. Yet against this it seems to stand that there were no fewer generations from Adam through Seth, counting those whose age is told in the letter, up to the flood, than from Adam through Cain up to it, although Cain was born more than a hundred years before Seth, as is commonly said, and indeed according to Methodius a hundred and fifteen years before.

6.title: Expositio capituli sexti: Noe vero quum quingentorum esset annorum, genuit Sem, Cham et Japhet
6.title_en: Exposition of the sixth chapter: “And Noe, when he was five hundred years old, begot Sem, Cham, and Japheth”

paras.t: CONSEQUENTER describitur, qualiter mundus diluvio perierit, et prima ætas acceperit finem, et qualiter reparatum sit sæculum. Porro prima ætas sæculi quæ ab Adam usque ad Noe duravit, ita quod Noe cœpit esse in ea, continet duo millia ducentos sexaginta quatuor annos, secundum Septuaginta : secundum Hieronymum vero, non plene duo millia : secundum Methodium autem, duo millia. Methodius tamen per chiliades, hoc est millenarios seu mille annos, sæcula seu ætates disponit et computat : idcirco nil certum de annorum numero tradidit, ut in Scholastica historia scribitur.
paras.en: NEXT is described how the world perished by the flood and the first age came to its end, and how the world was restored. Now the first age of the world, which lasted from Adam to Noe (so that Noe began to be within it), contains two thousand two hundred and sixty-four years according to the Septuagint; but according to Jerome, not fully two thousand; and according to Methodius, two thousand. Methodius, however, arranges and reckons the ages or periods of the world by chiliads, that is, by thousands or spans of a thousand years: and so he handed down nothing certain about the number of the years, as is written in the Scholastic History [the Historia Scholastica of Peter Comestor].

paras.t: Noe vero quum quingentorum esset annorum, genuit Sem, Cham et Japhet, id est, hos tres cœpit generare, seu genuit successive, quum haberet annos quingentos. Quis horum trium fuerit primo natus, infra dicetur. Sed mirum quod Noe tamdiu distulit generare, quum nullus ante eum pro media temporis parte legatur tamdiu continuisse, generationemque distulisse. Ad quod juxta considerationem Augustini superius tactam, posset quis dicere, quod forsan ante hoc tempus generarit alios, quamvis non sint descripti, quia eorum genealogiam non prosequitur hæc scriptura. Porro Hebræi, ut Lyra refert, respondent quod Deus voluit justum Noe cum tota sua posteritate a diluvio præservare. Si autem tam cito generasset, ut alii ante eum, posteri ejus fuissent tam abundanter multiplicati quod inter eos fuissent plurimi mali, quos in arca salvari dignum non exstitisset, et quia tot homines cum necessariis vitæ non potuissent convenienter collocari in arca. His rationibus objici posset, quod etiam inter hos tres, unus, scilicet Cham, exstitit malus, et tamen in arca fuit. Denique quum arca fuerit ita magna, plures homines potuissent in ea facillime contineri : ideo dici potest, quod Noe videns tot scelera fieri, et ea quotidie multiplicari, forsan retrahebatur a generatione, et cogitavit potius continere. Sed quum Deo revelante cognovisset genus humanum diluvio occidendum, et illud per suos posteros reparandum, proposuit generare. Quod tamen adhuc distulit quasi per annos viginti. Deus quippe prædixit ei de adventu diluvii per annos centum et viginti, antequam inundavit, ut infra patebit.
paras.en: [[Gen 5:31|And Noe, when he was five hundred years old, begot Sem, Cham, and Japheth|Noe vero quum quingentorum esset annorum, genuit Sem, Cham et Japhet]]: that is, he began to beget these three, or begot them one after another, when he was five hundred years old. Which of these three was born first will be told below. But it is a wonder that Noe put off begetting for so long, since no one before him is read to have abstained and deferred begetting for even half so long a time. To this, following the consideration of Augustine touched on above, one could say that perhaps he begot others before this time, although they are not recorded, because this Scripture does not follow out their genealogy. The Hebrews, moreover, as Lyra relates, answer that God willed to preserve the just Noe with all his posterity from the flood. But if he had begotten as early as the others before him, his descendants would have been multiplied so abundantly that among them there would have been very many wicked men, whom it would not have been fitting to save in the ark; and also because so many men, with the necessaries of life, could not have been suitably lodged in the ark. Against these reasons it could be objected that even among these three one, namely Cham, was wicked, and yet he was in the ark. And again, since the ark was so great, more men could very easily have been held in it. It can therefore be said that Noe, seeing so many crimes committed and multiplied daily, was perhaps held back from begetting, and thought rather to live in continence. But when by God's revelation he knew that the human race was to be slain by the flood and restored through his descendants, he resolved to beget. This, however, he still put off for about twenty years. For God foretold to him the coming of the flood a hundred and twenty years before it overflowed, as will appear below.

paras.t: Quumque cœpissent homines multiplicari super terram, et filias procreassent. Istud intelligitur de multiplicatione hominum præcipue copiosa atque malitiosa, quæ fuit secundum numerum, non secundum meritum. Alioqui non dubium, quin a tempore quo Adam cœpit generare, homines cœperunt multiplicari. Videntes filii Dei filias hominum quod essent pulchræ, acceperunt uxores sibi ex omnibus quas elegerant : hoc est, unusquisque illorum accepit uxorem pulchram, quæ juxta sensualitatem suam sibi magis complacuit, saltem inter illas quas vidit aut æstimavit se posse acquirere.
paras.en: [[6:1|And after that men began to be multiplied upon the earth, and daughters were born to them,|Cumque cœpissent homines multiplicari super terram, et filias procreassent,]] This is understood of a multiplication of men especially plentiful and wicked, which was in number, not in merit. Otherwise there is no doubt that men began to be multiplied from the time when Adam began to beget. [[6:2|The sons of God seeing the daughters of men, that they were fair, took to themselves wives of all which they chose.|Videntes filii Dei filias hominum quod essent pulchræ, acceperunt uxores sibi ex omnibus quas elegerant]]: that is, each of them took a fair wife who pleased him most according to his sensuality, at least among those whom he saw or thought he could obtain.

paras.t: Circa hæc, antiqua et magna est quæstio, qui fuerunt illi filii Dei. In Scripturis namque filii Dei dici non solent nisi boni, videlicet homines virtuosi, de quibus ait in prima sua epistola Joannes aposto lus, Nunc filii Dei sumus; et angeli san cti, de quibus Dominus ait ad Job, Ubi eras quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei ? Sed nec virtuosis hominibus, nec angelis sanctis competit actus ille libidinosus jam dictus. Et respondendum, quod verba hæc a diversis, tam Hebræis quam christianis, expositoribus ab antiquo diversimode exposita sunt. Quidam namque per filios Dei intellexerunt dæmones incubos, qui dicuntur filii Dei per naturalem similitudinem intellectualis et spiritualis suæ naturæ cum Deo. Unde et Josephus : Multi, inquit, angeli Dei cum mulieribus coierunt. De talibus ait Apostolus : Nescitis quoniam angelos judica bimus ? Sed huic expositioni objicitur, quia diluvium fuit illatum propter peccata istorum, de quibus hic agitur. Et certum est, quod diluvium inflictum est propter vitia hominum, non dæmonum. Præterea, quamvis dæmones incubi interdum mulieribus sint admixti, non tamen leguntur eas duxisse uxores, quamvis quandoque molesti fuerint virorum uxoribus. Iterum de istis filiis Dei filiabusque hominum Dominus subdit : Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est. Quod non competit dæmonibus incubis. Septuaginta quoque pluraliter transtulerunt, In hominibus istis. Hinc expositionem istam reprobat Lyra.
paras.en: Concerning this there is an old and great question: who were those sons of God? For in the Scriptures none but the good are wont to be called sons of God, namely virtuous men, of whom the apostle John says in his first epistle, [[1 John 3:2|we are now the sons of God|Nunc filii Dei sumus]]; and the holy angels, of whom the Lord says to Job, [[Job 38:4|Where wast thou|Ubi eras]] [[Job 38:7|When the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei ?]] But neither to virtuous men nor to holy angels does that lustful act just mentioned belong. And the answer is that these words have been expounded in different ways from of old by different expositors, Hebrew as well as Christian. For some have understood by the sons of God incubus demons [demons said to lie with women in the form of a man], who are called sons of God from the natural likeness of their intellectual and spiritual nature to God. Hence Josephus too says: Many angels of God lay with women. Of such the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 6:3|Know you not that we shall judge angels?|Nescitis quoniam angelos judicabimus ?]] But against this exposition it is objected that the flood was brought on for the sins of those with whom this passage deals; and it is certain that the flood was inflicted for the vices of men, not of demons. Moreover, although incubus demons have sometimes had to do with women, yet they are not read to have taken them as wives, though at times they have molested the wives of men. Again, of these sons of God and daughters of men the Lord goes on to say: [[6:3|My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh|Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est]]. That does not fit incubus demons. The Septuagint, too, translated it in the plural: In these men. Hence Lyra rejects this exposition.

paras.t: Contra quem more solito invehitur Rabbi Paulus. Hæc, inquiens, expositio est consonans litteræ, et etiam sententiæ Augustini. Nam ubi littera nostra habet : Gigantes erant super terram, Hebraica veritas dicit : Nephilim, quod aliud nihil significat nisi cadentes, per quod proprie designantur dæmones lapsi de cœlo. Isti in corporibus assumptis mulieribus commiscebantur. Augustinus quoque de Civitate Dei, dicit esse credendum quod dæmones incubi interdum molesti sunt feminis. Sed mirum apparet, quod Paulus iste sic scribit. In littera enim non dicitur, quod gigantes videntes filias hominum quod essent pulchræ, acceperunt uxores, etc., sed quod videntes filii Dei filias hominum quod essent pulchræ, etc. Deinde littera dicit, quod gigantes nati sunt ex concubitu isto filiorum Dei filiarumque hominum. Et hoc dicunt expositores concorditer, et etiam Josephus, Rabbi Salomon, aliique Hebræi : idcirco de gigantibus constat, quod erant veraciter homines, non dæmones incubi.
paras.en: Against him, as usual, Rabbi Paul inveighs [Paul of Burgos, the converted rabbi, in his Additions to Lyra's Postill]. This exposition, he says, accords with the letter, and also with the opinion of Augustine. For where our text has, [[6:4|giants were upon the earth|Gigantes erant super terram]], the Hebrew verity says Nephilim, which means nothing else than falling ones, by which the demons fallen from heaven are properly designated. These, in assumed bodies, had intercourse with women. Augustine too, in The City of God, says it is to be believed that incubus demons sometimes molest women. But it seems a wonder that this Paul writes thus. For the text does not say that the giants, seeing the daughters of men that they were fair, took wives, etc., but [[6:2|The sons of God seeing the daughters of men, that they were fair|videntes filii Dei filias hominum quod essent pulchræ]], etc. Then the text says that the giants were born of this union of the sons of God and the daughters of men. And this the expositors say with one accord, and so do Josephus, Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] and other Hebrews: it is therefore certain of the giants that they were truly men, not incubus demons.

paras.t: Amplius quoque quod Rabbi Paulus dicit expositionem illam esse consonam Augustino, manifeste erroneum est : quamvis etenim Augustinus fateatur dæmones incubos interdum misceri cum feminis, non tamen fatetur quod filii Dei de quibus hic agitur, erant dæmones incubi ; imo ex proposito et assertive hoc reprobat. Siquidem quintodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur : Non autem illos ita fuisse angelos aut filios Dei, ut homines non essent, sicut quidam putant : sed homines procul dubio fuisse, Scriptura ipsa sine ambiguitate declarat. Quum enim præmissum est, quod videntes angeli Dei filias hominum, quia bonæ, id est pulchræ, sunt, sumpserunt sibi uxores, etc., mox adjunctum est, Et dixit Dominus Deus : Non permanebit spiritus meus in hominibus istis in æternum, eo quod caro sunt. Rursus in eodem libro asserit Augustinus : In apocryphis legitur, quod Enoch scripsit, quod gigantes, de quibus habetur in Genesi, non sunt nati ex hominibus ; sed quia hoc falsum est, non creditur Enoch istud scripsisse. Hæc Augustinus.
paras.en: Further, what Rabbi Paul says, that that exposition accords with Augustine, is plainly mistaken: for although Augustine admits that incubus demons sometimes have to do with women, yet he does not admit that the sons of God here treated of were incubus demons; nay, he rejects this of set purpose and in plain terms. For in the fifteenth book of The City of God he says: But that they were not angels or sons of God in such a way as not to be men, as some think, but were beyond doubt men, Scripture itself declares without ambiguity. For when it had first been said that the angels of God, seeing the daughters of men that they were good, that is, fair, took them wives, etc., there was at once added: And the Lord God said: [[6:3|My spirit shall not remain|Non permanebit spiritus meus]] in these men for ever, because they are flesh. Again in the same book Augustine asserts: It is read in the apocrypha that Enoch wrote that the giants of whom Genesis speaks were not born of men; but because this is false, it is not believed that Enoch wrote it. Thus Augustine.

paras.t: Ut autem hæc clarius pateant, advertendum quod Thomas ait in prima parte, quæstione 51 : Teste Augustino, multi se expertos affirmant, vel ab expertis audisse, Sylvanos et Faunos, quos vulgus incubos vocat, mulieribus frequenter improbos exstitisse, atque earum expetisse et peregisse concubitum : ideo hoc negare, impudentiæ ac imprudentiæ est. Si ergo ex coitu dæmonum aliqui interdum nascuntur, hoc non erit per semen decisum ab eis, aut eorum corporibus, sed aliunde acceptum, ita quod dæmon qui viro est succubus, mulieri sit incubus, quemadmodum aliarum rerum semina congregant ad producendum quosdam effectus, ut tertio de Trinitate Augustinus testatur. Idcirco sic natus, non est filius dæmonis, sed viri cujus semen dæmon accepit, et mulieri infudit. Hæc Thomas. Hinc super Lucam loquitur Beda : Quidam dæmones dicuntur succubi, qui supponunt se viris in specie mulieris ; quidam incubi, qui cognoscunt mulieres in specie viri, forte non luxuria tracti, sed ut hominibus illudant, nec tamen emittunt. Istud autem quod Beda ait, quod non emittunt semen, intelligi potest, quod non emittunt proprium semen, et forte interdum non emittunt. Porro Hieronymus ait : Verbum Hebraicum Elohim, utriusque est numeri, ita quod significat Deum aut deos : ideo Aquila ausus est transferre, Filios deorum, deos intelligens sanctos vel angelos : quem sequens Symmachus, transtulit, Videntes filii potentum filias hominum. Hinc quidam dixerunt, quod in Hebræo habeatur : Filii judicum potentum. Et ita exponunt, quod potentes et judices, corruperunt sponsas et filias subditorum : quod quamvis potuerit esse verum, non tamen fuisset sufficiens ratio generalis diluvii.
paras.en: To make this clearer, note what Thomas says in the First Part, question 51: On the testimony of Augustine, many affirm that they have experienced, or have heard from those who have experienced it, that Sylvans and Fauns, whom the common people call incubi, have often behaved wantonly towards women, and have sought and accomplished intercourse with them: hence to deny this is a mark of shamelessness and of senselessness [impudentiæ ac imprudentiæ, a play on words in the Latin]. If therefore some are sometimes born of the intercourse of demons, this will not be through seed shed by them or from their bodies, but taken from elsewhere, so that the demon who is succubus to a man becomes incubus to a woman; just as they gather the seeds of other things to bring about certain effects, as Augustine testifies in the third book On the Trinity. Therefore one so born is not the son of the demon, but of the man whose seed the demon took and poured into the woman. Thus Thomas. Hence Bede says on Luke: Some demons are called succubi, who lie under men in the form of a woman; some incubi, who know women in the form of a man, perhaps not drawn by lust, but to make sport of men; and yet they do not emit. Now what Bede says, that they do not emit seed, can be understood to mean that they do not emit seed of their own, and perhaps sometimes emit none at all. Jerome, further, says: The Hebrew word Elohim is of either number, so that it means God or gods: hence Aquila ventured to translate, Sons of the gods, understanding by gods the saints or angels; and Symmachus, following him, translated: The sons of the mighty seeing the daughters of men. Hence some have said that the Hebrew has: Sons of the mighty judges. And they expound it thus: that the mighty and the judges defiled the brides and daughters of their subjects; which, although it may have been true, would yet not have been sufficient reason for a general flood.

paras.t: Est ergo absolute tenendum, quod isti filii Dei, fuerunt posteri nati ex semine Seth et filiorum ejus. Erantque primo devoti vel ipsi, vel patres eorum : idcirco vocati sunt filii Dei seu angeli eo modo, quo in Scripturis quidam homines, ratione vitæ aut officii, nuncupati sunt angeli, sicut sacerdotes vocantur in Malachia propheta, angeli Domini exercituum. Et de beatissimo Joanne Baptista prædictum est : Ecce mitto angelum meum. Dicuntur quoque filii deorum, id est hominum divinorum. Per filias autem hominum, intelliguntur filiæ natæ ex semine Cain, quæ erant lascivæ, superbæ, curiosæ et pulchræ, quarum amore capti filii Seth, duxerunt eas conjuges ; tuncque communiter invaluerunt vitia super terram, ita quod paucissimi boni manserunt.
paras.en: It must therefore be held absolutely that these sons of God were descendants born of the seed of Seth and of his sons.
