paras.t: De animantibus quoque mundis et immundis, et de volucribus, et ex omni quod movetur super terram, id est ex omni genere animalium terrenorum, quæ in se ipsis habent principium vitæ et motus, videlicet animam, duo et duo, id est combinata, juxta duplicem expositionem præhabitam, seu potius juxta unam earum, quoniam simul stare non possunt, ingressa sunt in arcam ad Noe. Ex quo constat, quod Noe ea non attulit nec collegit, sed nutu divino, angelorumque ministerio sponte et supernaturaliter, quantum ad inductivum motus, venientia introire permisit, intrantiaque suscepit, et congruis mansionibus collocavit, cum adjutorio filiorum suorum. Unde et ipse Noe videtur ante animalia ista arcam ingressus. Forsitan tamen accepit per se et filios suos aliqua animalia domita ex propriis gregibus.
paras.en: [[7:8|And of beasts clean and unclean, and of fowls, and of every thing that moveth upon the earth|De animantibus quoque mundis et immundis, et de volucribus, et ex omni quod movetur super terram]], that is, of every kind of earthly animals that have within themselves the principle of life and movement, namely a soul, [[7:9|Two and two|duo et duo]], that is, paired, according to the twofold exposition given above, or rather according to one of them, since both cannot stand together, [[7:9|went in to Noe into the ark|ingressa sunt in arcam ad Noe]]. From which it is clear that Noe did not bring them or gather them; but as they came of their own accord, by the will of God and the ministry of angels, and supernaturally as to what set them moving, he let them come in, received them as they entered, and settled them in fitting quarters, with the help of his sons. Hence Noe himself seems to have gone into the ark before these animals. Perhaps, however, he and his sons took some tame animals from their own flocks.

paras.t: Anno sexcentesimo vitæ Noe, mense secundo, id est in Maio, qui ab Hebræis dicitur Nisan, ut in Glossa atque Scholastica historia fertur. Quidam tamen dicunt, quod Martius ab Hebræis Nisan vocetur. Hebræi autem Aprilem vocant primum mensem. Verumtamen inter Hebræos est diversa opinio et varius modus loquendi de primo mense anni, ut in expositione primi capituli tactum est. Josephus quoque affirmat, quod in legitimis, id est descriptione præceptorum legalium, præsertim quantum ad esum agni paschalis, Moyses ponit Aprilem primum mensem. In contractibus vero et gubernatione sæculi, id est solutione debitorum et locatione domorum, servavit solita decreta temporum, et usualem ordinem mensium, qui scilicet a calendis Januarii aliquando inchoat, prout in Scholastica historia, ejusque glossa habetur.
paras.en: [[7:11|In the six hundredth year of the life of Noe, in the second month|Anno sexcentesimo vitæ Noe, mense secundo]], that is, in May, which the Hebrews call Nisan, as is said in the Gloss and the Scholastic History. Some, however, say that March is called Nisan by the Hebrews. But the Hebrews call April the first month. Yet among the Hebrews there is differing opinion and a varied way of speaking about the first month of the year, as was touched on in the exposition of the first chapter. Josephus also affirms that in matters of the Law, that is, in setting out the legal precepts, especially as regards the eating of the paschal lamb, Moses puts April as the first month; but in contracts and the governing of the world, that is, the payment of debts and the letting of houses, he kept the accustomed reckoning of times and the usual order of the months, which sometimes begins from the calends of January, as is found in the Scholastic History and its gloss.

paras.t: Septimodecimo die mensis præfati, rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ. Magna abyssus vocatur Oceanus, ex quo omnes fontes et fluvii ac particularia maria originaliter oriri dicuntur. Unde Salomon ait: Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant. Et rursus: Omnia flumina intrant mare. Fontes ergo abyssi magnæ, appellantur aquæ inclusæ in visceribus terræ, quæ ex Oceano ducunt originem. Hi fontes tunc rumpebantur, id est repente eruperunt, ruptis receptaculis suis, seu præfatis terræ visceribus in quibus continebantur. Et recte rupti dicuntur, ad insinuandum, quod non effluxerunt sensim solito more, sed repentina inundatione terram operuerunt, ut ait Glossa. Et cataractæ cœli apertæ sunt. Per cataractas cœli, intelligit aperturas meatusque nubium, seu loca cœli aerei, per quæ aquæ pluviales descendunt: quæ cataractæ tunc apertæ fuerunt, quia ex nubibus aquæ superabundantissime descenderunt. Cataractæ autem secundum Rabanum, sunt proprie ostia, id est capita Nili, sed abusive pro omnibus fenestris ponuntur. Hinc ait auctor Scholasticæ historiæ: Cataractæ proprie sunt meatus Nili, quum in septem ostia separatur, id est, in septem partes seu capita dividitur, vel loca ejusdem.
paras.en: [[7:11|in the seventeenth day of the month|Septimodecimo die mensis]] just named, [[7:11|all the fountains of the great deep were broken up|rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ]]. The great deep is the name for the Ocean, from which all fountains and rivers and particular seas are said to take their first rise. Hence Solomon says: [[Eccles 1:7|unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again|Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant]]. And again: [[Eccles 1:7|All the rivers run into the sea|Omnia flumina intrant mare]]. So the fountains of the great deep is the name for the waters shut up in the bowels of the earth, which take their origin from the Ocean. These fountains were then broken up, that is, they suddenly burst out, their receptacles being broken, that is, the bowels of the earth just mentioned, in which they were held. And they are rightly said to be broken up, to suggest that they did not flow out little by little in the usual way, but covered the earth in a sudden inundation, as the Gloss says. [[7:11|and the floodgates of heaven were opened|Et cataractæ cœli apertæ sunt]]. By the floodgates of heaven [Latin cataractæ, which also means the cataracts of a river] he understands the openings and passages of the clouds, or the places of the airy heaven through which the rain waters come down; and these floodgates were then opened, because the waters came down most superabundantly from the clouds. Now cataracts, according to Rabanus, are properly the mouths, that is, the heads, of the Nile, but by an extension of the word they are used for all windows. Hence the author of the Scholastic History says: Cataracts are properly the channels of the Nile where it is separated into seven mouths, that is, divided into seven parts or heads, or the places of the same.

paras.t: Et facta est pluvia super terram, hoc est, impetuosissime ac […] cadens in terram ubique, quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, puta tandiu, quousque aquæ in tantum ascenderunt quantum omnipotens Deus decrevit. Secundum Josephum, ab Adam usque ad inundationem diluvii, fluxerunt anni duo millia sexcenti quinquaginta sex.
paras.en: [[7:12|And the rain fell upon the earth|Et facta est pluvia super terram]], that is, falling upon the earth everywhere most violently and […], [[7:12|forty days and forty nights|quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus]], namely for as long as it took for the waters to rise as far as almighty God had decreed. According to Josephus, from Adam to the coming of the flood two thousand six hundred and fifty-six years passed.

paras.t: In articulo illius diei ingressus est Noe, etc. De quo die hoc dicitur, quum jam pluraliter dictum sit, quadraginta diebus? Respondendum, quod per diem illum potest intelligi tempus seu prima dies, in quibus sic pluit. Itaque in articulo, id est in parte seu hora clara vel necessitate diei illius, ingressus est arcam cum suis, et omne animal secundum genus suum, id est quædam de omni animalium genere, intelligendo per animal feras atque reptilia. De aliis quippe subjungitur, universaque jumenta in genere suo, id est quædam animalia domestica seu domita hominibus deservientia, de omni specie jumentorum, juxta quem sensum nunc subditur: cunctumque volatile secundum genus suum, id est universæ aves, omnesque volucres. Unum horum frequenter pro alio ponitur, nunc tamen accipiuntur distincte, secundum quod aves sunt diversarum proprietatum et naturarum, quemadmodum animalia terræ. De qua re in expositione primi capituli est tractatum.
paras.en: [[7:13|In the selfsame day Noe|In articulo illius diei ingressus est Noe]] went in, etc. Of which day is this said, since it has already been said in the plural, forty days? It must be answered that by that day can be understood the time, or the first day, of those on which it rained so. So in the selfsame day [Latin in articulo, literally at the point or moment], that is, in the part, or the clear hour, or the pressing moment of that day, he went into the ark with his own, [[7:14|and every beast according to its kind|et omne animal secundum genus suum]], that is, some of every kind of animal, understanding by beast [Latin animal] the wild beasts and the creeping things. For of the others it is added, [[7:14|and all the cattle in their kind|universaque jumenta in genere suo]], that is, some domestic animals, tamed and serving men, of every species of cattle [Latin jumenta, beasts of burden and draught]; in keeping with which sense it now adds: [[7:14|and every fowl according to its kind|cunctumque volatile secundum genus suum]], that is, [[7:14|all birds, and all that fly|universæ aves, omnesque volucres]]. The one of these [that is, aves and volucres] is often put for the other, but here they are taken distinctly, inasmuch as birds are of different properties and natures, like the animals of the earth; this matter was treated in the exposition of the first chapter.

paras.t: Bina et bina ex omni carne ingressa sunt arcam, hoc est, omnia introierunt combinata, quantum ad sexuum distinctionem, quia sive septena et septena de mundis, sive bina et bina de immundis, omnia quantum ad sexum fuerunt distincta et combinata. Itaque ex omni carne in qua erat spiritus vitæ, id est, ex omni genere animalis, in quo erat spiritus vitalis, videlicet anima sensitiva, ingressa sunt bina et bina. Et inclusit eum Dominus deforis, id est, Deus ministerio angeli clausit ab extra ostium arcæ, liniendo illud bitumine, ne ingredi possent aquæ per aliquas rimas. Sic autem non potuit Noe intus existens ostium claudere, seu deforis bituminare: idcirco ubi defuit humanum subsidium adfuit divinum.
paras.en: [[7:15|two and two of all flesh|Bina et bina ex omni carne]] went into the ark, that is, all went in paired as to the distinction of the sexes: for whether seven and seven of the clean or two and two of the unclean, all were distinguished and paired as to sex. So of all flesh [[7:15|wherein was the breath of life|in qua erat spiritus vitæ]], that is, of every kind of animal in which there was the vital spirit, namely a sensitive soul, they went in two and two. [[7:16|and the Lord shut him in on the outside|Et inclusit eum Dominus deforis]], that is, God by the ministry of an angel closed the door of the ark from outside, smearing it with bitumen, so that the waters could not get in through any chinks. For Noe, being inside, could not close the door in this way, or pitch it from outside; and so where human help was lacking, divine help was at hand.

paras.t: Et multiplicatæ sunt aquæ, quoniam a sursum ac deorsum venerunt ad superficiem terræ, et aqua magni maris exivit terminos suos, et fusa est super terram; et elevaverunt arcam in sublime, a terra, utpote super omnes turres seu ædificia ac arbores terræ. Porro arca ferebatur super aquas hinc inde, non recto processu, juxta impulsum ventorum ac gurgitum. Erat tamen pro magna parte profundata in aqua, ex magnitudine et gravitate oneris quod gestabat.
paras.en: [[7:17|and the waters increased|Et multiplicatæ sunt aquæ]], since they came from above and from below to the face of the earth, and the water of the great sea went out of its bounds and was poured over the earth; [[7:17|and lifted up the ark on high from the earth|et elevaverunt arcam in sublime, a terra]], namely above all the towers or buildings and the trees of the earth. [[7:18|and the ark was carried upon the waters|Porro arca ferebatur super aquas]] hither and thither, not on a straight course, as the winds and the eddies drove it. Yet it was for the most part sunk deep in the water, from the size and weight of the load it carried.

paras.t: Opertique sunt omnes montes excelsi sub universo cœlo. Quindecim cubitis altior fuit aqua super montes quos operuerat. Voluit namque Dominus aerem quasi purgare a sordibus, quibus impiissimi homines illum suis vitiis, clamoribus, operibus, fumis, fœtoribus inquinarunt. Idcirco tam alte ascendit diluvium, sicut illa ascendere potuerunt. Creditur quoque, quod ignis conflagrationis in die judicii tam alte ascendet. Qualiter autem poterat aqua in tantum multiplicari atque ascendere, præhabitum est. Verumtamen Glossa ait: Sunt qui putant ante diluvium non fuisse talem terræ qualitatem, hoc est bassitudinem: nec tantam montium altitudinem, qualis et quanta est postea. Nec sine ratione hoc dicitur. Ex confluxu namque et residentia aquarum in aliquibus locis terra consumpta est pro aliqua parte deorsum, et bassior facta: quod circa loca montium qui tunc erant, potissime accidere poterat. Sicque ex tunc montes hujusmodi altiores apparuerunt. Unde nec certum est, quod mons Olympus tunc fuerit tam sublimis ut modo. De quo monte in Scholastica narratur historia: Mons Olympus usque ad liquidum aerem tenditur, super quem litteræ scriptæ in pulvere, repertæ sunt mansisse immotæ; ubi præ nimia aeris raritate, nec aves vivere queunt, neque philosophi ascendentes potuerunt ibi aliquantulum manere sine spongiis aqua plenis, quas suis naribus apponentes, crassiorem inde aerem extraxerunt. His verbis in Glossa adjicitur, quod nec nubes ibi videntur, nec ventus sentitur.
paras.en: [[7:19|and all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered|Opertique sunt omnes montes excelsi sub universo cœlo]]. [[7:20|The water was fifteen cubits higher than the mountains which it covered|Quindecim cubitis altior fuit aqua super montes quos operuerat]]. For the Lord willed, as it were, to purge the air of the filth with which those most impious men had defiled it by their vices, clamours, works, smokes and stenches; and so the flood rose as high as these could rise. It is believed too that the fire of the burning on the day of judgement will rise as high. How the water could increase and rise so far was treated above. Yet the Gloss says: There are some who think that before the flood the earth was not of such a quality, that is, lowness, nor were the mountains of such height, as they were afterwards. And this is not said without reason. For through the flowing together and the settling of the waters in some places the earth was worn away downward in part and made lower; which could have happened most of all about the places of the mountains that then were. And so from then on such mountains appeared higher. Hence it is not certain either that Mount Olympus was then as lofty as now. Of which mountain the Scholastic History relates: Mount Olympus reaches up to the clear air; letters written in the dust on top of it have been found to have remained undisturbed; and there, because of the great thinness of the air, neither can birds live, nor could the philosophers who climbed it stay there for any while without sponges full of water, which they put to their nostrils and so drew thicker air from them. To these words the Gloss adds that neither are clouds seen there nor is wind felt.

paras.t: Quæri potest, de quibus intelligendum sit cubitis, quod aqua fertur fuisse quindecim cubitis altior montibus cunctis. Si enim de cubitis geometricis hoc dicatur, fuisset valde mirabile, ideo creditur esse intelligendum de cubitis usualibus. Nec irrationabile, si in descriptione ejusdem materiæ, idem diversimode accipiatur, præsertim quando ea de quibus tractatur, et materiam illam concernunt, satis ostendunt, unum illud, utpote pondus seu mensuram, diversimode esse accipiendum, et ita est in proposito. Dum enim arca fertur fuisse trecentorum cubitorum in longitudine, et quinquaginta in latitudine, et triginta in altitudine, et tamen tot animalia totque cibaria in ea fuisse scribuntur, satis innuitur de majoribus cubitis id esse intelligendum; dum vero describitur ipsa aqua fuisse altior omnibus montibus, satis insinuatur sufficere, si de usualibus et minoribus cubitis exponatur.
paras.en: It may be asked of what cubits it is to be understood that the water is said to have been fifteen cubits higher than all the mountains. For if this were said of geometrical cubits [that is, the larger cubit of measurement, reckoned by some, after Origen and Augustine, at six common cubits], it would have been very wonderful; so it is believed that it is to be understood of common cubits. Nor is it unreasonable that in describing the same matter the same thing should be taken in different ways, especially when the things treated, which concern that matter, show well enough that one and the same thing, such as a weight or a measure, is to be taken in different ways; and so it is here. For when the ark is said to have been three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth and thirty in height, and yet so many animals and so much food are written to have been in it, it is hinted clearly enough that this is to be understood of the larger cubits; but when the water itself is described as higher than all the mountains, it is suggested clearly enough that it is sufficient if it be expounded of the common and smaller cubits.

paras.t: Consumptaque est omnis caro quæ movebatur super terram, volucrum, animantium, bestiarum, omniumque reptilium, etc., hoc est, omnia ista occisa sunt, et forte pro magna parte penitus putrefacta, et motu aquarum sublata de terra. Obtinueruntque aquæ diluvii terram centum quinquaginta diebus, id est, tot diebus operuerunt et occupaverunt totam terram. Quod tamen dupliciter potest intelligi. Primo, incipiendo computationem horum dierum a die quo ingressus est Noe arcam, quo et aqua diluvii cœpit diffundi, usque ad diem quo cœpit aqua diluvii minui sive decrescere. Unde sequenti capitulo legitur: Post dies centum quinquaginta cœperunt aquæ minui. Et ita exponitur in Scholastica historia. Secundo, incipiendo computationem horum dierum, ab eo die quo diluvium factum est tam altum, quod operuit montes altitudine quindecim cubitorum, hoc est a fine defluxus pluvialis: ut sit sensus, quod aquæ in tanta altitudine terram operuerunt per dies centum quinquaginta; quibus expletis, cœperunt decrescere.
paras.en: [[7:21|And all flesh was destroyed that moved upon the earth, both of fowl and of cattle, and of beasts, and of all creeping things|Consumptaque est omnis caro quæ movebatur super terram, volucrum, animantium, bestiarum, omniumque reptilium]], etc., that is, all these were killed, and perhaps for the most part utterly putrefied, and carried off the earth by the movement of the waters. [[7:24|And the waters prevailed upon the earth a hundred and fifty days|Obtinueruntque aquæ diluvii terram centum quinquaginta diebus]], that is, for so many days they covered and occupied the whole earth. This, however, can be understood in two ways. First, beginning the count of these days from the day on which Noe went into the ark, on which the water of the flood also began to spread, up to the day on which the water of the flood began to lessen or decrease. Hence in the following chapter we read: [[Gen 8:3|after a hundred and fifty days|Post dies centum quinquaginta]] the waters [[Gen 8:3|began to be abated|cœperunt aquæ minui]]. And so it is expounded in the Scholastic History. Second, beginning the count of these days from the day on which the flood had become so high that it covered the mountains to a height of fifteen cubits, that is, from the end of the outpouring of rain: so that the sense is that the waters covered the earth at such a height for a hundred and fifty days, and when these were completed they began to decrease.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, an universale diluvium posset naturaliter evenire. Et videtur quod sic, auctoritate Avicennæ, et quorumdam astronomorum hoc sententium. Præterea, conjunctio planetarum humidorum in pluvialibus signis videtur hoc posse efficere. Aristoteles quoque in libro Meteororum testatur, quod particularia maria post aliqua tempora spatia variant sua loca. Ergo apparet idem posse in toto contingere, quod fit in parte. Et respondendum, quod universale diluvium, nequaquam possibile est per naturam. Læset enim corruptivum ordinis universi. Et multa ex ista opinione sequuntur absurda, per quæ et Averroes Avicennam satis redarguit. Insuper Aristoteles libro præallegato edocuit, quod dum aliqua terra seu regio operitur de novo aquis maris particularis, terra in qua prius mare fuit, siccatur. Et hoc naturaliter fit ex influxu et diverso respectu cœlesti. Totam vero terram aquis simul cooperiri, docet impossibile esse. Et præsertim impossibile est per naturam fieri diluvium tantum, ut montes universos quindecim cubitis sit transcendens.
paras.en: Concerning what has been said, it is asked whether a universal flood could come about naturally. And it seems that it could, on the authority of Avicenna and of certain astronomers who hold this. Besides, a conjunction of the moist planets in the rainy signs seems able to bring this about. Aristotle too, in the book of the Meteorologica, testifies that particular seas change their places after certain spaces of time. So it appears that what happens in a part can happen in the whole. And it must be answered that a universal flood is by no means possible by nature, for it would be destructive of the order of the universe [the printed Læset is unclear; the sense seems to be this]. And many absurdities follow from that opinion, by which Averroes too sufficiently refutes Avicenna. Moreover Aristotle, in the book cited above, taught that when some land or region is newly covered by the waters of a particular sea, the land where the sea was before is dried; and this happens naturally from the influence and the varying aspect of the heavens. But that the whole earth should be covered with waters at once, he teaches is impossible. And above all it is impossible by nature for a flood so great to come about as to rise above all the mountains by fifteen cubits.

7.title: Elucidatio spiritualis ejusdem capituli septimi
7.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same seventh chapter

paras.t: Spiritualis intelligentia hujus capituli, magna ex parte inducta est, patuitque in mystica expositione præcedentis capituli.
paras.en: The spiritual understanding of this chapter has in great part been brought forward already, and became plain in the mystical exposition of the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad eum, hoc est ad Christum secundum naturam assumptam. Ingredere tu et omnis domus tua, hoc est cuncti discipuli tui, in arcam, id est Ecclesiam universalem, cujus primitiva ista Ecclesia fuit pars atque primitiæ, et Christus caput. Te enim vidi justum coram me. Christus, in quantum Deus, est substantialiter ipsa justitia. Porro secundum naturam humanam, universis ac singulis ineffabiliter justior est, quippe qui nunquam peccavit, et tanta æquitate ac gratia exstitit plenus, quod natura creata majoris gratiæ et justitiæ capax non fuit. Ipse etenim Patrem perfectissime honoravit, et pro communi bono totius generis humani laboravit, et dedit se ipsum in mortem.
paras.en: [[7:1|And the Lord said to him|Dixitque Dominus ad eum]], that is, to Christ according to the nature he assumed: [[7:1|Go in, thou and all thy house|Ingredere tu et omnis domus tua]], that is, all thy disciples, [[7:1|into the ark|in arcam]], that is, into the universal Church, of which that primitive Church was a part and the first-fruits, and Christ the head. [[7:1|for thee I have seen just before me|Te enim vidi justum coram me]]. Christ, inasmuch as he is God, is substantially justice itself. And according to his human nature he is ineffably more just than all men together and each one singly, since he never sinned, and was so full of righteousness and grace that no created nature was capable of greater grace and justice. For he honoured the Father most perfectly, and laboured for the common good of the whole human race, and gave himself up to death[[Is 53:12||]] [the margin gives Is. liii without a verse; 53:12, "he hath delivered his soul unto death", is the nearest].

paras.t: Denique Noe interpretatur requies, quod potissime competit Salvatori, qui tulit peccata mundi. Et in Evangelio protestatur: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Jugum enim meum suave est. De hoc loquitur Origenes: Noe interpretatur requies vel justus, qui est Christus Jesus. Neque enim illi Noe convenit quod dixit Lamech pater ipsius: Iste dabit nobis requiem ab operibus et tristitiis manuum nostrarum in terra cui maledixit Dominus. Quomodo enim ille Noe dedit requiem patri suo Lamech, aut populo qui tunc fuit, quum illis temporibus iracundia Dei magis ostensa est, et Deus ipse locutus est. Pœnitet me fecisse hominem, et super omnia datur signum summæ offensæ Dei universalis interitus cunctorum in terra viventium? Si vero respicias ad Dominum nostrum Jesum, de quo dicitur, Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi: et iterum, Factus est pro nobis maledictum, ut nos a maledicto legis redimeret: qui etiam ait, Venite ad me, et invenietis requiem animabus vestris, invenies honeste esse qui vere requiem dedit hominibus, liberavitque terram de maledicto quo maledixerat ei Deus. Hæc verba Origenis non sunt sic intelligenda, quasi prœallegata verba nullo modo convenerint ipsi Noe ad litteram, sed quia non convenerunt ei ita perfecte ut Christo.
paras.en: Further, Noe is interpreted *rest*, which belongs most of all to the Saviour, who took away the sins of the world. And in the Gospel he declares: [[Matt 11:28|Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you|Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos]]. [[Matt 11:30|For my yoke is sweet|Jugum enim meum suave est]]. Of this Origen speaks: Noe is interpreted *rest* or *just*, and this is Christ Jesus. For what Lamech his father said does not suit that Noe: [[Gen 5:29|This same shall comfort us from the works and labours of our hands on the earth, which the Lord hath cursed|Iste dabit nobis requiem ab operibus et tristitiis manuum nostrarum in terra cui maledixit Dominus]] [Origen's text reads "This same shall give us rest from the works and sorrows of our hands", where the Douay-Rheims has "comfort" and "labours"]. For how did that Noe give rest to his father Lamech, or to the people of that time, when in those days the wrath of God was shown the more, and God himself said: [[Gen 6:7|it repenteth me that I have made them|Pœnitet me fecisse hominem]] [Origen has "made man"], and, above all, the universal destruction of everything living on the earth is given as the sign of God's utmost displeasure? But if you look to our Lord Jesus, of whom it is said, [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God. Behold him who taketh away the sin of the world|Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi]]; and again, [[Gal 3:13|being made a curse for us|Factus est pro nobis maledictum]], that he [[Gal 3:13|redeemed us from the curse of the law|nos a maledicto legis redimeret]]; who also says, [[Matt 11:28|Come to me|Venite ad me,]] and [[Matt 11:29|you shall find rest to your souls|invenietis requiem animabus vestris]]: you will find that it is he who truly gave rest to men, and freed the earth from the curse with which God had cursed it. These words of Origen are not to be understood as though the words cited above did not in any way suit Noe himself according to the letter, but because they did not suit him as perfectly as they suit Christ.

paras.t: Insuper, sicut Noe tantum invenit gratiam coram Deo, quod propter merita ejus Deus pepercit domesticis ejus qui secum fuerunt in arca, sic propter Christum misertus est Dominus universis qui per Christum salvantur in Ecclesia: imo secundum Apostolum, Deus elegit nos in Christo, de quo Joannes ait: Gratia et veritas per Jesum facta est. Christus enim ut homo salvator, est causa meritoria omnis gratiæ quæ membris suis confertur. Unde in ipso ponitur gratia capitis, qua influit membris suis.
paras.en: Moreover, just as Noe found so much grace before God that for his merits God spared his household who were with him in the ark[[Gen 6:18||]], so for Christ's sake the Lord has had mercy on all who are saved through Christ in the Church: indeed, according to the Apostle, God [[Eph 1:4|chose us|elegit nos]] in Christ, of whom John says: [[John 1:17|grace and truth came by Jesus|Gratia et veritas per Jesum facta est]]. For Christ as man and Saviour is the meritorious cause of all the grace that is bestowed on his members. Hence there is placed in him the grace of the head [that is, the grace Christ has as head of the Church, from which grace flows into all its members], by which he flows into his members.

paras.t: E omnibus animantibus mundis tolle septena et septena, masculum et feminam. De animantibus vero immundis duo et duo, masculum et feminam. Sed et de volatilibus cœli septena et septena, masculum et feminam, ut salvetur semen super faciem universæ terræ. Per animalia munda, intelligi possunt hi, qui ante evangelicæ legis prædicationem aliquo modo honeste vixerunt in lege naturæ, aut etiam in lege scripta, ita quod comparatione aliorum quasi mundi fuerunt. Isti in majori numero fuerunt conversi tempore evangelicæ prædicationis, in quantum se præparaverunt ad gratiam Christi. Et recte per septenarium numerum exprimuntur, quoniam septiformi gratia Sancti Spiritus sunt repleti. Et qui inter eos fuerunt perfectiores, significantur per mares, alii per femellas. Porro per animalia immunda insinuantur carnales et prorsus indigni, quorum nonnulli sunt misericordissime præventi atque conversi, qui binario designantur, quia binarius primo ab unitate recedens, divisionem et infirmitatem frequenter significat. Per volatilia quoque ingeniosi, periti, et contemplativi intelliguntur, inter quos nullus appellatur immundus, quum omnes tales dicantur suo modo perfecti, quamvis non æque perfecta. Unde et inter eos masculus et femina reperiuntur. Per hos Deus salvavit semen super terram, quia per eos convertit alios multos, qui adoptivi filii Dei exstiterunt.
paras.en: [[7:2|Of all clean beasts take seven and seven, the male and the female|E omnibus animantibus mundis tolle septena et septena, masculum et feminam]]. [[7:3|But of the beasts that are unclean two and two, the male and the female|De animantibus vero immundis duo et duo, masculum et feminam]]. [[7:3|Of the fowls also of the air seven and seven, the male and the female: that seed may be saved upon the face of the whole earth|Sed et de volatilibus cœli septena et septena, masculum et feminam, ut salvetur semen super faciem universæ terræ]]. By the clean animals may be understood those who before the preaching of the gospel law lived in some way uprightly under the law of nature, or also under the written law, so that in comparison with others they were as it were clean. These were converted in greater number at the time of the gospel preaching, inasmuch as they had prepared themselves for the grace of Christ. And they are rightly expressed by the number seven, since they were filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]][[Acts 2:4||]]. And those among them who were more perfect are signified by the males, the others by the females. But by the unclean animals are suggested the carnal and the wholly unworthy, some of whom were most mercifully forestalled [by grace] and converted; they are designated by the number two, because two, as the first number to depart from unity, often signifies division and weakness. By the fowls, too, are understood the gifted, the learned and the contemplative, among whom none is called unclean, since all such are said to be perfect in their own way, though not equally perfect. Hence among them too male and female are found. Through these God saved seed upon the earth, because through them he converted many others, who became adopted sons of God[[Rom 8:15||]].

paras.t: Post dies septem ego pluam super terram quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, hoc est, post tempus evangelicæ legis ac gratiæ, infligam obstinatis atque incredulis et ingratis plagas temporalis interitus et æternæ damnationis. Septenario quippe exprimitur tempus gratiæ et salutis. Per quadraginta vero, tempus punitionis eorum, qui decem præcepta et quatuor Evangeliorum doctrinam per quatuor mundi partes spreverunt.
paras.en: [[7:4|after seven days, I will rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights|Post dies septem ego pluam super terram quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus]]: that is, after the time of the gospel law and of grace, I will inflict on the obstinate, the unbelieving and the ungrateful the plagues of temporal destruction and of eternal damnation. For by seven is expressed the time of grace and salvation; and by forty, the time of the punishment of those who have spurned the ten commandments and the teaching of the four Gospels throughout the four parts of the world [ten times four makes forty].

paras.t: Rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ, et cataractæ cœli apertæ sunt. Per hoc figuratum est, quod tribulatio super iniquos consurget desuper ac deorsum, ita quod elementa et mixta atque cœlestia ad eorum punitionem excitabuntur, sicut et Dominus in Evangelio pandit: Erunt, inquiens, terræ motus magni per loca, et pestilentiæ et fames, terroresque de cœlo. Unde in libro Sapientiæ habetur: Armabit creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum, et pugnabit cum illo orbis terrarum contra insensatos. Et rursus in eodem libro legitur: Creatura enim tibi factori deserviens, exardescit in tormentum adversus injustos, et lenior fit ad benefaciendum pro his qui in te confidunt. Itaque fontes abyssi sunt inundationes tribulationum magnarum. Et cataractæ cœli, sunt aperturæ quæ videntur in cœlis, dum fulgura et cœlestes impressiones apparent. Propter quod stellæ cœli dicuntur casuræ.
paras.en: [[7:11|all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened|Rupti sunt omnes fontes abyssi magnæ, et cataractæ cœli apertæ sunt]]. By this it was figured that tribulation will rise up against the wicked from above and from below, so that the elements and the mixed bodies [that is, bodies compounded of the elements] and the heavenly bodies will be stirred up to punish them; as the Lord too makes known in the Gospel: [[Luke 21:11|And there shall be|Erunt]], he says, [[Luke 21:11|great earthquakes in divers places and pestilences and famines and terrors from heaven|terræ motus magni per loca, et pestilentiæ et fames, terroresque de cœlo]]. Hence it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:18|he will arm the creature for the revenge of his enemies|Armabit creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum]], and [[Wis 5:21|the whole world shall fight with him against the unwise|pugnabit cum illo orbis terrarum contra insensatos]]. And again in the same book we read: [[Wis 16:24|For the creature serving thee, the Creator, is made fierce against the unjust for their punishment: and abateth its strength for the benefit of them that trust in thee|Creatura enim tibi factori deserviens, exardescit in tormentum adversus injustos, et lenior fit ad benefaciendum pro his qui in te confidunt]]. So the fountains of the deep are floods of great tribulations; and the floodgates of heaven are the openings that are seen in the heavens when lightnings and heavenly signs [*impressiones*: the phenomena of the upper air, such as meteors] appear. For this reason the stars of heaven are said to be about to fall[[Mark 13:25||]].

paras.t: In articulo illius diei ingressus est Noe, etc., id est, in exordio evangelicæ legis ingressus est Christus et ejus familia sanctam Ecclesiam, juxta sensum præhabitum.
paras.en: [[7:13|In the selfsame day Noe|In articulo illius diei ingressus est Noe]] went in, etc.: that is, at the outset of the gospel law Christ and his household entered holy Church, according to the sense given above.

paras.t: Bina et bina ingressa sunt ex omni carne, id est gemina caritate conjuncti. Unde et Christus misit discipulos suos combinatos in omnem civitatem et locum quo ipse erat venturus.
paras.en: [[7:15|two and two|Bina et bina]] went in [[7:15|of all flesh|ex omni carne]]: that is, joined by the twofold charity [of God and of neighbour]. Hence Christ too sent his disciples two by two [[Luke 10:1|into every city and place whither he himself was to come|in omnem civitatem et locum quo ipse erat venturus]].

paras.t: Et inclusit eum Dominus deforis, id est, Deus Pater Christum secundum ipsius humanitatem ab omni adversitate protexit, ab omni vitio præservavit, ab omni tribulatione eripuit: non quod adversitates et tribulationes perpessus non sit, sed quia ei nil nocuerunt, sed maxime profuerunt; non ei dumtaxat, quantum ad cumulum præmii accidentalis, quod per talia ei accrevit, sed et toti generi humano, quod per ipsius passionem salvatum est. Nihil enim profecit inimicus in eo. Propter quod Isaias testatur: In umbra manus suæ protexit me. Nam et anima Christi a suæ creationis exordio confirmata fuit perfecte in bono, quemadmodum comprehensores in cœlo, imo præ omnibus illis.
paras.en: [[7:16|and the Lord shut him in on the outside|Et inclusit eum Dominus deforis]]: that is, God the Father protected Christ according to his humanity from all adversity, preserved him from every fault, and delivered him from every tribulation: not that he did not suffer adversities and tribulations, but because they did him no harm, and rather profited him greatly; and not him only, as to the increase of his accidental reward [that is, the added joy beyond the essential reward of the vision of God] which accrued to him through such things, but also the whole human race, which was saved through his passion. For [[Ps 88:23|The enemy shall have no advantage over him|Nihil enim profecit inimicus in eo]] [Denis has the past tense: the enemy had no advantage over him]. Wherefore Isaias testifies: [[Is 49:2|in the shadow of his hand he hath protected me|In umbra manus suæ protexit me]]. For the soul of Christ was, from the beginning of its creation, perfectly confirmed in good, as the comprehensors [that is, the blessed who already see God] are in heaven, nay, beyond all of them.

paras.t: Et multiplicatæ sunt aquæ, et elevaverunt arcam in sublime, a terra. Istæ sunt aquæ tribulationis, quibus fideles exercentur in terra. De quibus canit Psalmista: Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam. Denique, aquæ istæ elevant arcam in altum, quando fideles in tentationibus et afflictionibus ad Deum confugiunt, eumque invocant, et omne gaudium arbitrantur dum in varias tentationes et adversitates labuntur. Tunc quoque arca fertur super aquas hujusmodi, quia non vincitur eis Ecclesia, sed prævalet, Deo juvante. Quod totum ad tempus Antichristi apte refertur, quando gravissima tribulatio erit, nec tamen Ecclesia in toto deficiet.
paras.en: [[7:17|and the waters increased, and lifted up the ark on high from the earth|Et multiplicatæ sunt aquæ, et elevaverunt arcam in sublime, a terra]]. These are the waters of tribulation by which the faithful are exercised on earth, of which the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 68:2|Save me, O God: for the waters are come in even unto my soul|Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam]]. And these waters lift the ark on high when the faithful in temptations and afflictions flee to God and call upon him, and [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy|omne gaudium arbitrantur]] when they fall into divers temptations and adversities. Then too [[7:18|the ark was carried upon the waters|arca fertur super aquas]] of this kind, because the Church is not overcome by them but prevails, with God's help. All this is fitly referred to the time of Antichrist, when the tribulation will be most grievous, and yet the Church will not wholly fail.

paras.t: Opertique sunt montes excelsi, etc. Per hoc datur intelligi, quod prælati et spirituales viri in persecutionibus, tentationibus et tribulationibus opprimuntur. Quod maxime fiet sub persecutione impiissimi Antichristi, qui erit homo peccati, filius perditionis, vasque principis dæmoniorum.
paras.en: [[7:19|all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered|Opertique sunt montes excelsi]], etc. By this we are given to understand that prelates and spiritual men are overwhelmed in persecutions, temptations and tribulations. This will happen most of all under the persecution of the most wicked Antichrist, who will be [[2 Thess 2:3|the man of sin|homo peccati]], [[2 Thess 2:3|the son of perdition|filius perditionis]], and the vessel of the prince of the demons.

paras.t: Obtinuerantque aquæ diluvii terram centum quinquaginta diebus. Per dies illos intelligi potest tempus quo persecutio Antichristi durabit. Quæ tamen diutius quam per tot dies creditur duratura. Attamen breviabuntur illi dies propter electos.
paras.en: [[7:24|And the waters prevailed upon the earth a hundred and fifty days|Obtinuerantque aquæ diluvii terram centum quinquaginta diebus]]. By those days may be understood the time that the persecution of Antichrist will last; which, however, is believed likely to last longer than so many days. Yet [[Matt 24:22|for the sake of the elect those days shall be shortened|breviabuntur illi dies propter electos]].

8.title: Explanatio litteralis capituli octavi: Recordatus autem Dominus Noe, cunctorumque animantium, etc.
8.title_en: Literal explanation of the eighth chapter: “And the Lord remembered Noe, and all the living creatures, etc.”

paras.t: Præsenti capitulo narrat Scriptura, qualiter cessavit diluvium, et quomodo Noe egressus est arcam. Recordatus autem Dominus Noe, cunctorumque animantium et omnium jumentorum, quæ erant cum eo in arca, hoc est, per pium effectum ostendit se memorem ejus, minorando diluvium, ut exsistentes in arca, consolationem et habitationem in terra reciperent. Porro in invariabili Deo non cadit recens recordatio, neque oblivio, sed Scriptura loquitur de incomprehensibili Deo more humano, condescendens infirmitati intelligentiæ nostræ. Itaque recordatus Dominus ipsius Noe, et omnium animalium brutorumque quæ erant cum eo, adduxit spiritum, id est ventum siccantem super terram, ut flatu venti aquæ impellerentur ad redeundum in propria loca, quia tantus locus in aere non fuit eis connaturalis. De tali spiritu fertur in Psalmo: Dixit, et stetit spiritus procellæ. Itemque: Flavit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ. Et imminutæ sunt aquæ, hoc est, paulatim cœperunt decrescere; et clausi sunt fontes abyssi, id est, viscera seu ventriculi terræ, in quibus continentur subterraneæ aquæ, reclusi sunt, ita quod non emanaverunt aquas ex se super terram, sed effusas potius resorbuerunt; et cataractæ cœli sunt clausæ; et prohibitæ sunt pluviæ de cælo: hoc est, aperturæ et meatus nubium cessaverunt, et loca cœli aerei per quæ pluvia descenderat, in se ipsis reclusa sunt, ita quod aer non dividebatur ut prius per pluvias.
paras.en: In the present chapter Scripture relates how the flood ceased, and how Noe went out of the ark. [[8:1|And God remembered Noe, and all the living creatures, and all the cattle which were with him in the ark|Recordatus autem Dominus Noe, cunctorumque animantium et omnium jumentorum, quæ erant cum eo in arca]], that is, by a merciful effect He showed Himself mindful of him, by lessening the flood, so that those who were in the ark might receive comfort and a dwelling on the earth. Now in the unchangeable God there falls no fresh remembering, nor forgetting; but Scripture speaks of the incomprehensible God in human fashion, condescending to the weakness of our understanding. So the Lord, remembering Noe himself and all the animals and brute beasts that were with him, [[8:1|brought a wind|adduxit spiritum]], that is, a drying wind, [[8:1|upon the earth|super terram]], so that by the blowing of the wind the waters might be driven to return to their proper places, since so great a place in the air was not natural to them. Of such a wind it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 106:25|He said the word, and there arose a storm of wind|Dixit, et stetit spiritus procellæ]]. And again: [[Ps 147:7|his wind shall blow, and the waters shall run|Flavit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlvii, 18, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate it is Ps 147:7, and Denis has *flavit*, "blew", where the Vulgate reads *flabit*, "shall blow"]. [[8:1|and the waters were abated|Et imminutæ sunt aquæ]], that is, little by little they began to decrease; [[8:2|The fountains also of the deep|et clausi sunt fontes abyssi]] were shut up, that is, the bowels or hollows of the earth in which the underground waters are held were closed again, so that they did not pour waters out of themselves upon the earth, but rather drank back those that had been poured out; [[8:2|and the floodgates of heaven|et cataractæ cœli]] were shut; [[8:2|and the rain from heaven was restrained|et prohibitæ sunt pluviæ de cælo]]: that is, the openings and passages of the clouds ceased, and the places of the airy heaven through which the rain had come down were closed up in themselves, so that the air was no longer parted by rains as before.

paras.t: Reversæque sunt aquæ de terra euntes et redeuntes, id est, hinc inde se concutientes atque fluctuantes, et ad loca Oceani particulariumque marium revertentes. Non enim omnes aquæ in Oceanum decurrebant, sed multæ in particularibus maribus remanserunt, et in subterraneis locis ac fluviis, præsertim in quatuor fluviis paradisi. Et cœperunt minui post centum quinquaginta dies, quibus obtinuerant et operuerant terram, prout in fine præcedentis capituli dictum est, dupliciterque expositum. Requievitque arca mense septimo, vicesima septima die mensis, hoc est vicesima septima die mensis septimi illius anni quo fuit diluvium; super montes Armeniæ, quæ alio nomine dicitur Ararat, secundum doctores. At vero aquæ ibant et decrescebant usque ad decimum mensem ejusdem anni. Non quod decimo mense illo completa sit decrescentia, seu recessus aquarum a terra, ut statim patebit ex textu, sed decimo mense facta est tanta diminutio aquæ, quod cacumina montium apparuerunt, sicut subjungitur: Decimo enim mense, prima die mensis decimi apparuerunt cacumina montium; et tunc totum corpus arcæ fuit extra aquam, quando resedit super montes Armeniæ. Et aqua descenderat ad minus per quindecim cubitos, et forte aliqui montium illorum erant sibi invicem tam propinqui in situ, quod arca ista longissima simul requievit super capita duorum aut plurium montium; vel si requievit super unum montem, ponitur plurale pro singulari. Eratque mons iste magnæ extensionis in vertice, ita quod super eum potuit arca quiescere.
paras.en: [[8:3|And the waters returned from off the earth going and coming|Reversæque sunt aquæ de terra euntes et redeuntes]], that is, dashing this way and that and surging, and returning to the places of the Ocean and of the particular seas. For not all the waters ran down into the Ocean, but many remained in the particular seas, and in underground places and rivers, especially in the four rivers of paradise. [[8:3|and they began to be abated after a hundred and fifty days|Et cœperunt minui post centum quinquaginta dies]], during which they had prevailed over and covered the earth, as was said at the end of the preceding chapter and expounded in two ways. [[8:4|And the ark rested in the seventh month, the seven and twentieth day of the month|Requievitque arca mense septimo, vicesima septima die mensis]], that is, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month of that year in which the flood was, [[8:4|upon the mountains of Armenia|super montes Armeniæ]], which by another name is called Ararat, according to the doctors. [[8:5|And the waters were going and decreasing until the tenth month|At vero aquæ ibant et decrescebant usque ad decimum mensem]] of the same year. Not that the decrease, or the withdrawal of the waters from the earth, was completed in that tenth month, as will at once be clear from the text; but in the tenth month the waters were so far lessened that the tops of the mountains appeared, as is added: [[8:5|for in the tenth month, the first day of the month|Decimo enim mense, prima die mensis]], the tenth, [[8:5|the tops of the mountains appeared|apparuerunt cacumina montium]]. And by then the whole body of the ark, which had settled upon the mountains of Armenia, was out of the water. And the water had gone down by at least fifteen cubits; and perhaps some of those mountains stood so close to one another that this very long ark rested at once upon the tops of two or more mountains; or, if it rested upon one mountain, the plural is put for the singular. And that mountain was of great extent at its summit, so that the ark could rest upon it.

paras.t: De hac re in Scholastica recitatur historia: Arca requievit super montes Armeniæ, ubi usque nunc provinciales ostendunt reliquias arcæ. Denique ut Josephus refert, historiographi Barbarorum mentionem faciunt hujus arcæ atque diluvii. Scribit enim Berosus Chaldæus: Dicitur quædam pars esse navis illius quæ in Armeniam venit, et quoddam bitumen tolli ex ea, quo homines maxime ad piandum utuntur. De eodem scribit Hieronymus Ægyptius, Manasseus quoque Damascenus: Est, inquit, excelsus mons in Armenia, qui Baris appellatur, in quo sermo est, quemdam devectum in arca, etc. Ex quibus etiam constat, arcam venisse ad ipsam Armeniam, et requievisse in montibus ejus, et mentitos esse hæreticos, qui dixerunt historiam istam de arca, esse fabulam fictam: propter quod etiam errant Judæi, qui (ut Lyra refert) affirmant, arcam quievisse in alia terra, cujus montes usque Armeniam protenduntur, et ideo montes Armeniæ nominantur.
paras.en: Of this matter the Scholastic History relates: [[8:4|the ark rested|Arca requievit]] [[8:4|upon the mountains of Armenia|super montes Armeniæ]], where to this day the people of the province show remains of the ark. Further, as Josephus reports, the historians of the barbarians make mention of this ark and of the flood. For Berosus the Chaldean writes: It is said that a certain part of that ship which came into Armenia still exists, and that a kind of bitumen is taken from it, which men use chiefly for expiation. Of the same thing write Hieronymus the Egyptian and also Manaseas of Damascus: There is, he says, a lofty mountain in Armenia which is called Baris, on which, the story goes, a certain man was carried in an ark, etc. From these it is also established that the ark came to Armenia itself and rested on its mountains, and that the heretics lied who said that this history of the ark is an invented fable; and on the same account the Jews are also in error, who (as Lyra reports) affirm that the ark rested in another land, whose mountains stretch as far as Armenia, and are therefore called the mountains of Armenia.

paras.t: Quumque transissent quadraginta dies, a die quo apparuerunt primo cacumina montium, aperiens Noe fenestram arcæ, quam fecerat, quæ fenestra fuit facta in tecto arcæ, ut dictum est in expositione sexti capituli, dimisit corvum, ut per eum exploraret, an terra esset siccata in sua planitie; qui egrediebatur et non revertebatur, donec siccarentur aquæ super terram, id est, donec terra siccaretur ab aquis, quæ defluxerunt a terra: non quod corvus post illam siccationem ad Noe redierit, sed quia nec ante eam, nec postea est reversus ad arcam. Sicque Donec, excludit tempus præcedens, nec statuit sequens, juxta quem modum fertur in Psalmo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos, etc. Atque in Matthæo: Non cognovit eam, scilicet Joseph Mariam, donec peperit filium suum primogenitum. Juxta hanc expositionem corvus nunquam reversus est: ideo secundum Augustinum intelligendum est, quod mansit alicui cadaveri insidens. Verumtamen Josephus dicit, quod rediit. Et Lyra dicit quod in Hebræo habetur, Qui egrediebatur exiens et revertens. Et idem ait Hieronymus libro de Hebraicis quæstionibus. Circa quod dicunt Hebræi, quod corvus legationem suam non fecit, sed circa arcam volitans, eo quod undique aquam conspiceret, quæsivit reingredi, et intravit ut nutrimentum haberet. In Glossa vero sic dicitur: In Hebræo habetur, Egressus est exiens et non revertens, donec siccarentur aquæ.
paras.en: [[8:6|And after that forty days were passed|Quumque transissent quadraginta dies]], from the day on which the tops of the mountains first appeared, [[8:6|Noe opening the window of the ark, which he had made|aperiens Noe fenestram arcæ, quam fecerat]] (this window was made in the roof of the ark, as was said in the exposition of the sixth chapter), [[8:6|sent forth a raven|dimisit corvum]], to find out through it whether the earth was dried on its level ground; [[8:7|Which went forth and did not return, till the waters were dried up upon the earth|qui egrediebatur et non revertebatur, donec siccarentur aquæ super terram]], that is, until the earth was dried of the waters, which flowed away from the earth: not that the raven came back to Noe after that drying, but because it went back to the ark neither before it nor afterwards. And so *till* [Latin *donec*] excludes the time before and does not decide the time after, in the way in which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 109:1|Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies|Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos]], etc. And in Matthew: [[Matt 1:25|he knew her not|Non cognovit eam]], that is, Joseph knew not Mary, [[Matt 1:25|till she brought forth her first born son|donec peperit filium suum primogenitum]]. According to this exposition the raven never returned: therefore, according to Augustine, it is to be understood that it stayed perched on some carcass. Josephus, however, says that it returned. And Lyra says that in the Hebrew it reads: Which went forth going out and returning. And Jerome says the same in the book of Hebrew Questions. On this the Hebrews say that the raven did not carry out its errand, but flying about the ark, because it saw water on every side, sought to go back in, and entered so as to have food. But in the Gloss it is said thus: In the Hebrew it reads, It went forth going out and not returning, till the waters were dried up.

paras.t: Emisit quoque columbam post eum, ut videret, id est, ex columbæ effectu cognosceret, si jam cessassent aquæ super faciem terræ, id est, an a superficie terræ omnino abiissent. Sive enim corvus dicatur statim reversus ad Noe, sive nunquam reversus, non scivit ex corvi effectu an planities terræ esset siccata. Poterat enim manere super cadaver natans in aqua, aut circa alicujus montis cacumen jacens. Quæ quum non invenisset ubi requiesceret pes ejus, quia columba abhorret super cadaver sedere, montium quoque capita adhuc erant lutosa ac nimium humida, reversa est ad eum in arcam, propter quietem et pastum. Aquæ enim erant super universam terram, hoc est, adhuc operuerant totam terram planam, non montuosam. Terra etenim montuosa, fuit pro magna parte jam nudata ab aquis. Extenditque manum suam, et apprehensam intulit in arcam; forte enim sedebat super tectum arcæ juxta fenestram. Unde quod jam ante scriptum est, eam rediisse in arcam, intelligendum est, quod rediit usque ad tectum arcæ per se, et tunc Noe apprehendit eam ac introduxit. Exspectatis autem ultra septem diebus aliis: ex quo sequitur, quod Noe post emissionem corvi exspectavit septem dies, antequam emisit columbam; et ea reversa, rursus denuo evolutis tot diebus, rursum dimisit columbam ex arca.
paras.en: [[8:8|He sent forth also a dove after him, to see|Emisit quoque columbam post eum, ut videret]], that is, to learn from what the dove did, [[8:8|if the waters had now ceased upon the face of the earth|si jam cessassent aquæ super faciem terræ]], that is, whether they had wholly gone from the surface of the earth. For whether the raven is said to have returned to Noe at once or never to have returned, he did not learn from what the raven did whether the level ground of the earth was dried; for it could have stayed upon a carcass floating in the water, or lying about the top of some mountain. [[8:9|But she not finding where her foot might rest|Quæ quum non invenisset ubi requiesceret pes ejus]], because the dove shrinks from settling on a carcass, and the tops of the mountains too were still muddy and too wet, [[8:9|returned to him into the ark|reversa est ad eum in arcam]], for rest and food. [[8:9|for the waters were upon the whole earth|Aquæ enim erant super universam terram]], that is, they still covered all the level land, though not the mountainous; for the mountainous land was already for the most part laid bare of the waters. [[8:9|and he put forth his hand, and caught her, and brought her into the ark|Extenditque manum suam, et apprehensam intulit in arcam]]: for perhaps she was sitting on the roof of the ark beside the window. Hence what was written just before, that she returned into the ark, is to be understood to mean that she came back by herself as far as the roof of the ark, and then Noe caught her and brought her in. [[8:10|And having waited yet seven other days|Exspectatis autem ultra septem diebus aliis]]: from which it follows that after sending out the raven Noe waited seven days before he sent out the dove; and when she had returned, after as many days had again gone by, [[8:10|he again sent forth the dove out of the ark|rursum dimisit columbam ex arca]].

paras.t: At illa venit ad eum ad vesperam, forte ejusdem diei, quo eam emisit, portans ramum olivæ virentibus foliis in ore suo. An columba tulit ramum illum de arbore olivæ adhuc stante, an potius reperit eum in terra, non exprimit textus. Et videtur quod tulit eum de arbore, quoniam ramus iste fuit foliis virens. Oppositum tamen apparet, quia subjungitur: Intellexit ergo Noe quod cessassent aquæ super terram: quod non potuisset, si ramus fuisset sublatus de arbore. Quocirca rursus inquiritur, quia si columba jam reperit ubi requiesceret pes suus, cur revertebatur ad arcam. Dici potest, quod terra erat adhuc nimis mollis ac lutea ad manendum in ea, prout infra clarebit. Nutu tamen divino creditur factum, ut ita rediret cum ramo pro certificatione ipsius Noe.
paras.en: [[8:11|And she came to him in the evening|At illa venit ad eum ad vesperam]], perhaps of the same day on which he sent her out, [[8:11|carrying a bough of an olive tree, with green leaves, in her mouth|portans ramum olivæ virentibus foliis in ore suo]]. Whether the dove took that bough from an olive tree still standing, or rather found it on the ground, the text does not say. And it seems that she took it from the tree, since the bough was green with leaves. Yet the opposite appears, because it is added: [[8:11|Noe therefore understood that the waters were ceased upon the earth|Intellexit ergo Noe quod cessassent aquæ super terram]]: which he could not have done if the bough had been taken from a tree. Here it is asked again: if the dove had now found where her foot might rest, why did she go back to the ark? It can be said that the earth was still too soft and muddy to stay on, as will be clear below. Yet it is believed to have come about by God's will that she came back thus with the bough, to give Noe himself assurance.

paras.t: Exspectavitque nihilo minus septem alios dies, ut post tantum tempus majorem certificationem de terræ siccatione acciperet; et emisit columbam tertia vice, quæ non est reversa ultra ad eum, quoniam terra fuit jam satis solida pro columba, et potuit in ea invenire necessaria pabula. Igitur sexcentesimo primo anno vitæ Noe, primo mense anni apud Hebræos, puta Aprili, secundum doctores præallegatos, vel Martio, ut aliqui dicunt, prima die mensis illius, imminutæ sunt aquæ super terram, ita quod totaliter recesserunt a terra ad habitandum præordinata. Corvus namque fuit emissus undecimo mense, utpote evolutis quadraginta diebus a decimo mense. Post emissionem autem corvi usque ad tertiam columbæ emissionem, fluxerunt tres hebdomadæ, sic quod columba fuit tertio emissa duodecimo mense. Et aperiens Noe tectum arcæ, adspexit, id est fenestram quæ erat in tecto, sicut aliquis dicitur aperire domum dum aperit januam domus. Aliqui tamen dicunt, quod nunc aliud designatur per apertionem tecti arcæ, quam supra per apertionem fenestræ, quod ad litteram non videtur. Poterat enim per fenestram satis circumspicere terram. Viditque quod exsiccata esset superficies terræ: nondum tamen exivit de arca, quoniam terra non erat adhuc satis dura et solida facta pro inhabitatione animalium terrestrium et hominum; et quoniam exspectavit revelationem Dei de tempore exeundi. Mense secundo anni præfati, septimo et vicesimo die mensis secundi, arefacta est terra, id est, satis siccata et indurata ad habitandum et operandum in ea. Siquidem quasi duo menses fluxerunt interim a prima die primi mensis anni illius.
paras.en: [[8:12|And he stayed yet other seven days|Exspectavitque nihilo minus septem alios dies]], so that after so long a time he might receive greater assurance of the drying of the earth; [[8:12|and he sent forth the dove|et emisit columbam]] a third time, [[8:12|which returned not any more unto him|quæ non est reversa ultra ad eum]], because the earth was now firm enough for the dove, and she could find on it the food she needed. [[8:13|Therefore in the six hundredth and first year|Igitur sexcentesimo primo anno]] of Noe's life, [[8:13|the first month|primo mense]] of the year among the Hebrews, that is, April, according to the doctors cited above, or March, as some say, [[8:13|the first day of the month|prima die mensis]], that is, of that month, [[8:13|the waters were lessened upon the earth|imminutæ sunt aquæ super terram]], so that they had wholly withdrawn from the land ordained for dwelling in. For the raven was sent out in the eleventh month, forty days having passed from the tenth month; and from the sending out of the raven to the third sending out of the dove three weeks went by, so that the dove was sent out the third time in the twelfth month. [[8:13|and Noe opening the covering of the ark, looked|Et aperiens Noe tectum arcæ, adspexit]], that is, opening the window which was in the roof, as someone is said to open a house when he opens the door of the house. Some, however, say that something different is now meant by the opening of the roof of the ark from what was meant above by the opening of the window; which does not appear so according to the letter, for through the window he could look about over the land well enough. [[8:13|and saw that the face of the earth was dried|Viditque quod exsiccata esset superficies terræ]]: yet he did not yet go out of the ark, because the earth had not yet become hard and firm enough for land animals and men to dwell on, and because he was waiting for God's revelation of the time to go out. [[8:14|In the second month|Mense secundo]] of the said year, [[8:14|the seven and twentieth day of the month|septimo et vicesimo die mensis]], the second month, [[8:14|the earth was dried|arefacta est terra]], that is, dried and hardened enough to be lived on and worked. For about two months had meanwhile gone by from the first day of the first month of that year.

paras.t: Locutus est autem Deus ad Noe, dicens: Egredere de arca, tu et uxor tua, et filii tui et uxores filiorum tuorum tecum. Cuncta animantia quæ sunt apud te ex omni carne, tam in volatilibus quam in bestiis et universis reptilibus quæ reptant super terram, educ tecum, et ingredimini super terram. Itaque, sicut ex Dei imperio arcam intravit, ita ex Dei imperio est egressus: atque ut dictum est, quando jussit eum exire, mixtim expressit eum et conjugem ejus, ejusque filios et eorum uxores, ad innuendum quod de cetero esset tempus maritalis amplexus. Dicunt quoque expositores concorditer, quod Noe cum suis fuit integro anno in arca, eodemque die exiit quo intravit. Nec obstat, quod in præcedenti capitulo legitur, diluvium incepisse anno sexcentesimo vitæ Noe, mense secundo, septimadecima die mensis illius; nunc vero dicitur exivisse anno sexcentesimo primo vitæ Noe, mense secundo, vicesima septima die mensis: quoniam annus solaris excedit lunarem in diebus, qui supercrescunt in mense isto secundo sexcentesimi primi anni vitæ Noe, ultra dies taxatos in mense secundo anni sexcentesimi vitæ illius. Judæi autem computant menses secundum lunationes. Crescite et multiplicamini super terram, id est, per generationem augeantur individua vestra: quod dictum est ad Noe pro omnibus domesticis ejus qui secum erant in arca, et animantibus universis, ut scilicet de cetero generationi insisterent. An vero et ipse Noe postea genuerit, postea inquiretur.
paras.en: [[8:15|And God spoke to Noe, saying|Locutus est autem Deus ad Noe, dicens]]: [[8:16|Go out of the ark, thou and thy wife, thy sons and the wives of thy sons with thee|Egredere de arca, tu et uxor tua, et filii tui et uxores filiorum tuorum tecum]]. [[8:17|All living things that are with thee of all flesh, as well in fowls as in beasts, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth, bring out with thee, and go ye upon the earth|Cuncta animantia quæ sunt apud te ex omni carne, tam in volatilibus quam in bestiis et universis reptilibus quæ reptant super terram, educ tecum, et ingredimini super terram]]. And so, as he entered the ark at God's command, so at God's command he went out; and, as was said, when He bade him go out He named him and his wife, and his sons and their wives, mixed together, to hint that from then on it would be a time for the marriage embrace. The expositors also say with one accord that Noe with his family was in the ark a whole year, and went out on the same day on which he went in. Nor is it an objection that in the preceding chapter we read that the flood began in the six hundredth year of Noe's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of that month, while now he is said to have gone out in the six hundred and first year of Noe's life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month: for the solar year exceeds the lunar by days, and these run over in this second month of the six hundred and first year of Noe's life beyond the days counted in the second month of the six hundredth year of his life. For the Jews reckon the months by the moons. [[8:17|increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]] upon the earth, that is, let your individuals be increased by generation: which was said to Noe for all his household who were with him in the ark, and for all the living creatures, so that from then on they might give themselves to generation. Whether Noe himself also begot children afterwards will be inquired into later.

paras.t: Ædificavit autem Noe altare Domino: quia in lege naturæ offerebantur sacrificia Deo, ut dictum est de Abel et Cain. Ædificavit autem altare istud statim post egressionem de arca, de qua exivit in Armenia, atque ut in Scholastica fertur historia, Armenii vocant locum ubi exivit, egressorum. Filii vero Noe vocaverunt eum Thanon, id est octo, eo quod octo homines ibi exierint arcam. Unde et aliqui imaginati sunt, quod Noe fecit altare illud de octo lapidibus, atque (ut Josephus ait) provinciales ibidem nunc usque ostendunt reliquias arcæ. In eadem Historia legitur, quod uxor Noe vocata sit Puarphara; uxor Sem, Pharsia; uxor Cham, Cathaflua; uxor Japhet, Flua. Et tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis: quæ cur munda vocata sint, patuit in expositione præcedentis capituli; obtulit holocausta super altare; et hoc pro gratiarum actione liberationis suæ et domesticorum suorum, atque in recognitionem summi et universalis ac independentis Domini Dei, beneficiorumque ejus. Porro holocaustum proprie appellatur sacrificium, quod ad divinæ reverentiam majestatis totum comburitur. Aliqui quoque dicunt, quod de qualibet specie pecorum, volatiliumque mundorum obtulit individuum unum, ut tactum est, exponendo præcedens capitulum, et successive hoc facere potuit, adjuveruntque eum filii sui in ædificando altare et immolatione, in quantum fuerat opportunum, applicando seu præparando materiam.
paras.en: [[8:20|And Noe built an altar unto the Lord|Ædificavit autem Noe altare Domino]]: for in the law of nature sacrifices were offered to God, as was said of Abel and Cain. And he built this altar immediately after going out of the ark, from which he went out in Armenia; and, as is told in the Scholastic History, the Armenians call the place where he went out *Egressorum* [that is, "of those who went out"]. But the sons of Noe called it Thanon, that is, eight, because eight persons went out of the ark there. Hence some have also imagined that Noe made that altar of eight stones; and (as Josephus says) the people of the province show remains of the ark there to this day. In the same History we read that the wife of Noe was called Puarphara; the wife of Sem, Pharsia; the wife of Cham, Cathaflua; the wife of Japhet, Flua. [[8:20|and taking of all cattle and fowls that were clean|Et tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis]] (why these are called clean was made plain in the exposition of the preceding chapter), [[8:20|offered holocausts upon the altar|obtulit holocausta super altare]]; and this in thanksgiving for the deliverance of himself and his household, and in acknowledgment of the supreme, universal and independent Lord God and of His benefits. Now a holocaust is properly the name of a sacrifice which is wholly burnt for reverence of the divine majesty. Some also say that of every species of clean cattle and fowls he offered one individual, as was touched on in expounding the preceding chapter; and he could do this one after another, and his sons helped him in building the altar and in the sacrifice as far as was fitting, by bringing or preparing the material.

paras.t: Odoratusque est Dominus odorem suavitatis, id est, holocaustum istud complacuit ei non secundum se, seu ex opere operato, sed ex opere operante, videlicet fide et devotione offerentis; et ait ad eum: Nequaquam ultra maledicam terræ propter homines, id est, propter vitia hominum non inducam de cetero habitatoribus terræ, ipsique terræ et brutis tam gravem et universalem vindictam seu plagam, nec ipsos homines propter eorum peccata ita simul plagabo, usque in finem mundi exclusive, quia in fine sæculi erit horribilior plaga quam fuit diluvium, utpote conflagratio mundi per ignem, quo tunc omnes in terra viventes exstinguentur. Denique Josephus refert, quod Noe formidans, ne Deus rursus induceret humano generi diluvium, Dominum exoravit ne hoc amplius faceret, et sacrificavit ei pro causa hac. Tunc Deus respondit se exaudisse preces illius, et cetera quæ hic leguntur.
paras.en: [[8:21|And the Lord smelled a sweet savour|Odoratusque est Dominus odorem suavitatis]], that is, this holocaust pleased Him, not in itself, or *ex opere operato*, but *ex opere operante* [that is, not by the mere performance of the rite but by the disposition of the one who performs it], namely by the faith and devotion of the offerer; [[8:21|and said|et ait]] to him: [[8:21|I will no more curse the earth for the sake of man|Nequaquam ultra maledicam terræ propter homines]], that is, for the vices of men I will not henceforth bring upon the dwellers on the earth, and upon the earth itself and the brute beasts, so heavy and universal a vengeance or plague; nor will I so strike men themselves all together for their sins until the end of the world, that end excluded; for at the end of the world there will be a more terrible plague than the flood was, namely the burning of the world by fire, by which all then living on the earth will be destroyed. Further, Josephus reports that Noe, fearing lest God should again bring a flood upon the human race, besought the Lord not to do this any more, and offered sacrifice to Him for this cause. Then God answered that He had heard his prayers, and the rest that is read here.

paras.t: Sensus enim, non solum exteriores, sed etiam interiores, et cogitatio humani cordis, hoc est ipsa vis cogitativa seu intellectiva, et item voluntas, in malum prona sunt culpæ, utpote ad peccandum, præsertim ex infectione originalis peccati seu fomite. Præsertim quoque quatuor vires hominis sunt infectæ et pronæ ad vitia, scilicet vis concupiscibilis, irascibilis, rationalis et voluntas. In quibus ponuntur quatuor vulnera animæ, quæ sunt, concupiscentia, infirmitas, error, malitia. Concupiscibilis, prona est nimis ad appetendum illicita. Irascibilis, debilis est ad resistendum prohibitis. Intellectus, pronus est ad errores et falsa; voluntas, ad perversa ac vitiosa. Et pronitas ista ad vitia, partim alleviat et aliquo modo excusat hominum culpas, quia diminuit rationem voluntarii, quod proprie est de ratione peccati. Prona sunt ergo hæc ad malum ab adolescentia sua, id est a tempore quo homo uti incipit ratione. Tunc enim radicalia mala illa incipiunt in actum erumpere, nisi per Dei gratiam et virtutes frenentur. Non igitur ultra percutiam omnem animam viventem, id est omne animatum tam rationale quam irrationale in terra, sicut feci, perpaucis individuis demptis. Quocirca posset quis dicere: Nonne Deus ante diluvium scivit hanc hominum pronitatem in malum? quare ergo tunc induxit diluvium? Et respondendum, quod Deus interdum ostendit rigorem suæ justitiæ, interdum vero dulcorem suæ clementiæ, secundum beneplacitum et ordinem imperscrutabilis atque immensæ sapientiæ suæ. Omnia etenim facit, ut sua perfectio in rebus resplendeat.
paras.en: [[8:21|for the imagination|Sensus enim]] [Latin *sensus*, "sense", hence Denis's gloss], not only the outward senses but also the inward, [[8:21|and thought of man's heart|et cogitatio humani cordis]], that is, the cogitative or intellective power itself, and likewise the will, [[8:21|are prone to evil|in malum prona sunt]], the evil of guilt, that is, to sinning, especially from the infection of original sin, or the *fomes* [the "tinder" of sin: the inclination to evil left by original sin]. And especially four powers of man are infected and prone to vices, namely the concupiscible power, the irascible, the rational, and the will. In these are placed the four wounds of the soul, which are concupiscence, weakness, error, malice. The concupiscible is too prone to desire unlawful things; the irascible is weak in resisting forbidden things; the intellect is prone to errors and falsehoods; the will, to perverse and vicious things. And this proneness to vices partly lightens and in some way excuses men's faults, because it lessens the character of the voluntary, which properly belongs to the nature of sin. These, then, are prone to evil [[8:21|from his youth|ab adolescentia sua]], that is, from the time when a man begins to use reason. For then those root evils begin to break out into act, unless they are curbed by God's grace and the virtues. [[8:21|therefore I will no more destroy every living soul|Non igitur ultra percutiam omnem animam viventem]], that is, every animate thing on earth, rational as well as irrational, [[8:21|as I have done|sicut feci]], except for a very few individuals. Whereupon someone might say: Did not God know this proneness of men to evil before the flood? Why then did He bring on the flood at that time? And the answer is that God sometimes shows the rigour of His justice, and sometimes the sweetness of His clemency, according to the good pleasure and the order of His unsearchable and immeasurable wisdom. For He does all things so that His perfection may shine forth in things.

paras.t: Cunctis diebus terræ, sementis et messis, id est semen seu seminatio ac seges seu fructificatio terræ, frigus et æstus, æstas et hiems, nox et dies non requiescent, id est, non cessabunt in toto, sed usque in finem mundi successive et ordinate evenient.
paras.en: [[8:22|All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest|Cunctis diebus terræ, sementis et messis]], that is, the seed or sowing and the crop or fruiting of the earth, [[8:22|cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease|frigus et æstus, æstas et hiems, nox et dies non requiescent]], that is, they will not cease altogether, but will come in succession and in order until the end of the world.

paras.t: Solemus autem frigus et hiemem pro eodem accipere, seu unum pro qualitate alterius, similiter æstum atque æstatem; sic et nunc potest frigus pro qualitate seu rigore hiemis accipi, et hiems pro parte anni seu tempore hiemali. Similiterque dicendum est de æstate et æstu. Vel frigus sumitur pro frigidiori hiemis parte, et æstus pro calidiori æstatis parte; sicque residuum tempus hiemis et æstatis, accipi posset quasi pro tempore quod in ver et autumnum dividimus, potissimum juxta vulgarem modum loquendi, quo totum annum in hiemem et æstatem distinguimus. Distinctio autem istorum, quam introducit hic Lyra, secundum Hebræos non habet generaliter veritatem nec locum, nisi in certis terris: quod brevitati studens, declarare omitto quum parvi sit ponderis.
paras.en: Now we are accustomed to take cold and winter for the same thing, or the one for the quality of the other, and likewise heat and summer; so here too cold can be taken for the quality or harshness of winter, and winter for the part of the year, or winter time; and the same is to be said of summer and heat. Or cold is taken for the colder part of winter, and heat for the hotter part of summer; and so the rest of the time of winter and summer could be taken as it were for the time which we divide into spring and autumn, chiefly according to the common way of speaking in which we divide the whole year into winter and summer. But the distinction of these which Lyra brings in here, following the Hebrews, does not hold true or have a place generally, but only in certain lands: which, aiming at brevity, I omit to explain, since it is of little weight.

paras.t: Postremo, in expositione hujus capituli facit Lyra grandem discussionem, quam profunde seu per quot cubitos arca intravit aquas diluvii. Et primo dicit, quod non intravit quindecim cubitis: quia si sic, non potuisset super aquas flotare, sed tetigisset capita montium, quoniam aqua erat altior montibus quindecim cubitis tantum. Secundo dicit, quod arca tantum præcise intravit aquam, quantum aqua excedebat montes, quando arca primo requievit super montes. Tertio tandem concludit, quod arca intravit aquam tredecim cubitis et parum plus, secundum textum nostræ translationis.
paras.en: Lastly, in the exposition of this chapter Lyra holds a long discussion of how deep, or by how many cubits, the ark entered the waters of the flood. And first he says that it did not enter by fifteen cubits: because if so it could not have floated upon the waters, but would have touched the tops of the mountains, since the water was higher than the mountains by fifteen cubits only. Secondly he says that the ark entered the water by exactly as much as the water exceeded the mountains when the ark first rested upon the mountains. Thirdly he finally concludes that the ark entered the water by thirteen cubits and a little more, according to the text of our translation.

paras.t: Circa hæc Rabbi Paulus scribit, quod inquisitio ista sit magis curiosa quam utilis, quia non confert cognitionem utilem in credendis, nec requiritur ad plenam litteræ expositionem.
