For the glorious Virgin He protected not only from all mortal sin, but also from all venial sin; while those sanctified in the womb and confirmed in grace He protected only from all mortal sin, that they might not fall into it. And Abram needed the divine protection above all because he was then dwelling in the midst of idolaters and very wicked men, lest he be perverted along with those perverse men[[Ps 17:27||]] [the margin gives "Ibid. 2", that is, the same Psalm; Denis echoes Ps 17:27, with the perverse thou wilt be perverted]. [[15:1|and thy reward exceeding great|Et merces tua magna nimis]], that is, a very great reward is prepared for thee for thy obedience and thy other virtues. Further, that [[15:1|reward exceeding great|merces illa magna nimis]] could not be merely a temporal or outward good, since such a good is not a sufficient reward for a virtuous work; it is the beatific enjoyment of the Godhead, which is an incomparable good, and in a way infinite, being the immediate, secure and everlasting possession of the infinite and uncreated good.

paras.t: Dixitque Abram: Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi? Ego vadam absque liberis. Circa hoc quidam exponendo sic ait: Ac si dicat, Parum valebunt ista, ex quo filium non habeo. Sed non videtur, quod Abram vir spiritualis et sapiens, magnam illam mercedem æternæ felicitatis atque divinæ fruitionis taliter parvipendit, quod parum reputaverit eam, nisi prolem haberet antequam moreretur. Præterea, rursus mirum apparet, qualiter Abram vir fidelis dixerit, Ego vadam absque liberis: quum jam ante Deus promiserit ei semen et copiosam posteritatem, terram Chanaan possessuram. Itaque quod Abram ait, Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi? non dixit parvipendendo præmium istud magnum nimis sibi promissum, nisi haberet et filium. Sed dixit hoc quasi admirando et pie conquerendo et quodammodo per locum a minori argumentando, tanquam diceret: Quid est quod promittis mihi illa bona futura, quam maxima, qui non confers mihi bonum multo minus ac temporale, videlicet prolem, pro qua toties oro, et quam ardenter desidero? Potest quoque sic exponi: Abram enim ex revelatione divina noverat mundi Salvatorem ex suo semine nasciturum, sine cujus adventu et salvatione noverat genus humanum non esse redimendum: quoniam ergo vidit se nondum habere filium, neque secundum inferiorum naturaliumque causarum processum ac ordinem habiturum, admirando et pie conquerendo, non discredendo, locutus est: Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi? quasi dicat: Æternam illam beatitudinem qualiter possum sperare? Ego enim vadam sine liberis, hoc est, ad aliam vitam quæ erit mihi in limbo patrum, transibo per mortem temporalem, non relinquendo nec habendo semen seu filium. Et hoc secundum processum inferiorum causarum, quum uxor mea sit sterilis, et ita Salvator mundi non orietur ex semine meo, nec per eum adepturus sum maximum præmium illud. Itaque verba hæc, Ego vadam absque liberis, Abram non protulit absolute asserendo, quia sic fuisset mentitus, et divinæ promissioni incredulus, sed secundum quemdam particularem respectum, loquendo.
paras.en: [[15:2|And Abram said: Lord God, what wilt thou give me?|Dixitque Abram: Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi?]] [[15:2|I shall go without children|Ego vadam absque liberis]]. On this someone, expounding it, speaks thus: As if he should say: These things will be of little worth, since I have no son. But it does not seem that Abram, a spiritual and wise man, made so little of that great reward of eternal happiness and of the enjoyment of God as to reckon it of little worth unless he had offspring before he died. Besides, it again seems strange how Abram, a man of faith, could have said, [[15:2|I shall go without children|Ego vadam absque liberis]], when God had already promised him seed and a numerous posterity that would possess the land of Chanaan. So when Abram says, [[15:2|Lord God, what wilt thou give me?|Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi?]], he did not say it making light of that reward exceeding great promised him, unless he should also have a son. He said it rather as one wondering and lovingly complaining, and in a way arguing from the lesser [that is, from the smaller good to the greater], as if he were saying: How is it that Thou promisest me those future goods, the greatest of all, Thou who dost not bestow on me a good far less and temporal, namely offspring, for which I so often pray and which I so ardently desire? It can also be expounded thus. Abram knew by divine revelation that the Saviour of the world was to be born of his seed, and that without His coming and saving work the human race was not to be redeemed. Since, then, he saw that he did not yet have a son, nor would have one according to the course and order of lower and natural causes, he spoke wondering and lovingly complaining, not disbelieving: [[15:2|Lord God, what wilt thou give me?|Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi?]]; as if to say: How can I hope for that eternal beatitude? For [[15:2|I shall go without children|vadam sine liberis]], that is, I shall pass by temporal death to the other life, which will be mine in the limbo of the fathers, neither leaving nor having seed or a son. And this according to the course of lower causes, since my wife is barren; and so the Saviour of the world will not spring from my seed, nor shall I obtain through Him that greatest reward. So Abram did not utter these words, [[15:2|I shall go without children|Ego vadam absque liberis]], as an absolute assertion, for then he would have lied and disbelieved the divine promise, but speaking with regard to one particular respect.

paras.t: Et filius procuratoris domus meæ iste Damascus Eliezer, hoc est, juvenis iste nomine Damascus, est filius procuratoris domus meæ, qui vocatur Eliezer; quasi dicat: Dispensator domus meæ filium habet, non ego; et ita quantum ad hoc, sum miserior eo. Vel, Damascus iste, filius Eliezer procuratoris mei, supple, Erit mihi pro libero, seu filio adoptivo, et ita erit heres meus. Lot etenim nepos Abræ, nondum habebat prolem, quando hæc dixit Abram. Hinc subditur: Mihi autem non dedisti semen, quum tamen tantam benedictionem promiseris mihi. Et ecce vernaculus meus, videlicet præfatus Damascus, qui vocatur vernaculus, id est servus in domo Abræ domini sui natus, erit hæres meus. Intendebat namque Abram illum adoptare in filium, si proprium semen non obtineret. Unde hæc verba protulit, secundum inferiorum causarum considerationem et æstimationem humanam. Damascus iste (ut in Glossa et Scholastica historia recitatur) condidit urbem, quæ ab ejus nomine Damascus vocata est, et postea regnavit in ea. Hæc est Damascus illa famosa. Præterea, S. Patriarchæ ardentissime optaverunt Christum ex eorum semine nasci. Quumque Christus sit Deus et homo, poterant omnia alia pro modico reputare, nisi Christus ex eorum semine nasceretur.
paras.en: [[15:2|and the son of the steward of my house is this Damascus Eliezer|Et filius procuratoris domus meæ iste Damascus Eliezer]], that is, this young man named Damascus is the son of the steward of my house, who is called Eliezer; as if to say: The steward of my house has a son, and I have not; and so in this respect I am more wretched than he. Or: this Damascus, son of Eliezer my steward (supply: shall be to me as a child [libero: the word of “without children”, absque liberis], or adopted son), and so shall be my heir. For Lot, Abram's nephew, did not yet have offspring when Abram said this. Hence there follows: [[15:3|But to me thou hast not given seed|Mihi autem non dedisti semen]], though thou hast promised me so great a blessing. [[15:3|and lo my servant born in my house|Et ecce vernaculus meus]], namely the aforesaid Damascus, who is called vernaculus, that is, a servant born in the house of Abram his master, [[15:3|shall be my heir|erit hæres meus]]. For Abram meant to adopt him as his son if he did not obtain seed of his own. So he spoke these words according to a consideration of the lower causes and by human reckoning. This Damascus (as is related in the Gloss and in the Scholastic History [the Historia scholastica of Peter Comestor]) founded the city which was called Damascus after his name, and afterwards reigned in it. This is that famous Damascus. Moreover, the holy Patriarchs most ardently desired that Christ should be born of their seed. And since Christ is God and man, they could count everything else as little unless Christ were born of their seed.

paras.t: Statimque sermo Domini factus est ad eum, dicens: Non erit hic hæres tuus: sed qui egredietur de utero tuo, id est ex semine corporis tui gignetur. Nec est imaginandum cum Apollinari hæresiarcha rudissimo, quod anima rationalis sit ex traduce, aut simul cum semine resolvatur et producatur ab anima generantis, quum et Aristoteles satis demonstret, quod intellectus sit omnino ab extra. Ipsum habebis heredem. Educitque eum foras, id est, Dominus præcepit Abræ ut egrederetur. Ex quo constat, quod visio et allocutio ista cœpit in domo. Et reor quod in aliquo loco domus secretiori, in quo Abram vacabat orationi et devotioni. Sic et Ezechieli jussit Dominus, Egredere in campum, et ibi loquar tecum. Et ait illi: Suspice cœlum, et numera stellas, si potes, id est, universitatem stellarum numerando perstringe et apprehende: quasi dicat, Hoc non potes præ multitudine earumdem, imo hoc Deo adscribitur tanquam præcipuum aliquid, juxta illud Psalmi: Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum, et omnibus eis nomina vocat. Verumtamen cives superni sciunt numerum siderum, sed homo viator naturaliter nequit sidera plenarie computare. Hinc Augustinus loquitur: Auctoritas libri hujus (id est Genesis) contemnit eos, qui universum stellarum numerum comprehendisse et conscripsisse jactantur, sicut Aratus vel Eudoxus, vel et qui alii sunt: quia nec omnes stellæ videri possunt. Nam quantum quisque acutius intuetur, tanto plures videt, exceptis sideribus, quæ in alia orbis parte a nobis remotissima, oriri et occidere perhibentur. Patet quoque ex isto, quod revelatio ista facta sit Abræ in nocte, quando sincero aere videri poterant stellæ, quanquam omnipotenti Creatori exstet facillimum etiam in die clarissimo stellas ad oculum demonstrare.
paras.en: [[15:4|And immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying|Statimque sermo Domini factus est ad eum, dicens]]: [[15:4|He shall not be thy heir|Non erit hic hæres tuus]]: [[15:4|but he that shall come out of thy bowels|sed qui egredietur de utero tuo]], that is, he that shall be begotten of the seed of thy body. Nor are we to imagine, with Apollinaris, that most ignorant heresiarch, that the rational soul is by propagation [ex traduce: handed on from the parents' souls as the body is from their seed], or that it is released together with the seed and produced by the soul of the one begetting; for even Aristotle shows well enough that the intellect is wholly from outside. [[15:4|him shalt thou have for thy heir|Ipsum habebis heredem]]. [[15:5|And he brought him forth abroad|Educitque eum foras]], that is, the Lord commanded Abram to go out. From this it is clear that this vision and speaking began in the house; and I think it was in some more secret place of the house, where Abram gave himself to prayer and devotion. So too the Lord commanded Ezechiel: [[Ezech 3:22|go forth into the plain, and there I will speak to thee|Egredere in campum, et ibi loquar tecum]]. [[15:5|and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars if thou canst|Et ait illi: Suspice cœlum, et numera stellas, si potes]], that is, run through and grasp by counting the whole number of the stars; as if to say: This thou canst not do, for their multitude; nay, this is ascribed to God as something belonging to Him alone, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 146:4|Who telleth the number of the stars: and calleth them all by their names.|Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum, et omnibus eis nomina vocat]] Yet the citizens on high know the number of the stars; but man in this life [homo viator: man as a wayfarer, still on the way to his heavenly home] cannot by nature count the stars completely. Hence Augustine says: The authority of this book (that is, of Genesis) scorns those who boast that they have grasped and written down the whole number of the stars, as Aratus or Eudoxus, or whoever else there are; for not even all the stars can be seen. For the more keenly anyone looks, the more he sees; to say nothing of the stars which are said to rise and set in the other part of the world, most remote from us. It is plain from this also that this revelation was made to Abram at night, when the stars could be seen in the clear air; though it is most easy for the almighty Creator to show the stars to the eye even in the brightest day.

paras.t: Et dixit ei: Sic erit semen tuum, id est, posteritas tua innumerabilis erit instar stellarum, quod tamen hyperbolice dictum est, utpote per excessum. Absolute enim loquendo, semen Abræ non esset tam innumerabile, si totum simul esset collectum, ut sidera cœli. Circa hunc locum scribit Lyra, quod Deus per hanc promissionem principaliter intendebat promittere Abræ et semini ejus vitam beatam, quæ erit in resurrectione futura perfecte, quando resurgentes distabunt ab invicem in splendore quemadmodum stellæ, secundum illud Apostoli: Stella differt a stella in claritate, sic erit et resurrectio mortuorum. Atque ad istud probandum allegat quod ait Salvator: Abraham pater vester exsultavit ut videret diem meum: vidit, et gavisus est. Dies autem Christi vocatur tempus suæ passionis et resurrectionis, in qua aperta est janua regni cœlestis, et patres de limbo educti sunt. Idcirco in offertorio Missæ defunctorum cantatur: Signifer Sanctus Michael repræsentet eas in lucem sanctam, quam olim Abrahæ promisisti et semini ejus.
paras.en: [[15:5|And he said to him: So shall thy seed be|Et dixit ei: Sic erit semen tuum]], that is, thy posterity shall be beyond number like the stars; which, however, is said hyperbolically, that is, by way of exaggeration. For, speaking absolutely, the seed of Abram would not be as innumerable as the stars of heaven, if it were all gathered together at once. On this place Lyra writes that by this promise God chiefly meant to promise Abram and his seed the blessed life, which will be perfect in the resurrection to come, when those who rise will differ from one another in splendour as the stars do, according to that word of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 15:41|star differeth from star in glory|Stella differt a stella in claritate]] [claritas: brightness]: [[1 Cor 15:42|So also is the resurrection of the dead|sic erit et resurrectio mortuorum]]. And to prove this he cites what the Saviour says: [[John 8:56|Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day: he saw it and was glad.|Abraham pater vester exsultavit ut videret diem meum: vidit, et gavisus est]] Now the day of Christ is the name given to the time of His passion and resurrection, in which the gate of the heavenly kingdom was opened and the fathers were led out of limbo. Therefore in the offertory of the Mass for the dead it is sung: May Saint Michael the standard-bearer bring them into the holy light, which thou didst promise of old to Abraham and to his seed.

paras.t: Sed contra hæc arguit Rabbi Paulus, quia (ut ait) præallegata Christi verba non sunt referenda ad visionem Abræ, de qua agitur in hoc loco, quoniam hic non fit mentio de Christi passione aut resurrectione, nec in re nec in figura. Ad quod dicere potest, qui vult verba Lyræ salvare, quod hic fit mentio de Christi passione et resurrectione in earum effectu, videlicet de felicitate æterna, quam Christus sua passione generi humano promeruit et recuperavit. Verum est tamen, quod prædicta Salvatoris verba, Abraham pater vester exsultavit, etc. aptius referuntur ad aliam visionem Abræ factam quam istam, præsertim quantum ad id quod dictum est Abræ: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes, quod Abram de Christo ad litteram intellexit, et tunc diem Christi spiritualiter vidit. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus concedit, quod Abram intellexit sibi et semini suo, hoc loco esse promissa, non solum bona terrena, sed item cœlestia. Unde et Augustinus: Videtur, inquit, mihi hoc loco promissa posteritas cœlesti felicitate sublimis: quia non dixit Dominus, Erit semen tuum innumerabile, sicut arena terræ: sed dictum est, Sic erit semen tuum sicut stellæ cœli. Circa quod Rabbi Paulus scribit: Quasi dicat, Cœleste, lucidum, et incorruptibile erit semen tuum, juxta illud Danielis: Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates.
paras.en: But against this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, whose Additions are printed with Lyra's Postill] argues that (as he says) the words of Christ cited above are not to be referred to the vision of Abram treated in this place, since here no mention is made of Christ's passion or resurrection, either in reality or in figure. To which one who wishes to save Lyra's words can say that here mention is made of Christ's passion and resurrection in their effect, namely of the eternal happiness which Christ merited and recovered for the human race by His passion. It is true, however, that the Saviour's words quoted above, [[John 8:56|Abraham your father rejoiced|Abraham pater vester exsultavit]], etc., are more fittingly referred to another vision made to Abram than this one, above all as regards what was said to Abram: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]], which Abram understood literally of Christ, and then saw the day of Christ in spirit. Yet Rabbi Paul grants that Abram understood that in this place not only earthly goods were promised to him and to his seed, but heavenly ones too. Hence Augustine also says: It seems to me that in this place a posterity is promised that is lofty in heavenly happiness; for the Lord did not say, Thy seed shall be innumerable as the sand of the earth, but it was said, [[15:5|So shall thy seed be|Sic erit semen tuum]] as the stars of heaven. On which Rabbi Paul writes: As if to say: Heavenly, shining and incorruptible shall thy seed be; according to that word of Daniel: [[Dan 12:3|they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity|Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]] [Denis joins the two halves of the verse: they that instruct many to justice shall shine as stars for all eternity].

paras.t: Credidit Abram Deo sibi hæc promittenti, quæ erant supernaturalia potissime, quantum ad bona æterna. Posteritas quoque carnalis ex sterili conjuge fuit supernaturalis, quantum ad modum acquirendi eamdem. Et ita hæc credere ex caritate, fuit meritorium, propter quod subditur: Et reputatum est illi ad justitiam, id est, Deus judicavit eum juste egisse ita credendo, et justificatus est credendo hoc ipsum, non quod ante non fuerit justus, sed quia nunc justior factus est. Sumitur autem justitia hic, prout est virtus communis. Nam omnis virtus est quædam justitia, in quantum homo per eam se habet ut debet aut decet. Hanc quoque auctoritatem allegat Apostolus ad Romanos, et item ad Galatas, ad probandum quod Abraham per fidem placuit Deo, etiam ante suam circumcisionem. Patet insuper ex hoc loco, quod fides justificat hominem: quod intelligendum est de fide per dilectionem formata, et de justificatione formali. Idcirco in Actis scriptum est: In hoc, scilicet in Christo, omnis qui credit, justificatur. Fides namque est fundamentum virtutum, et justificationis exordium.
paras.en: [[15:6|Abram believed God|Credidit Abram Deo]], who promised him these things, which were supernatural, above all as regards the eternal goods. And his posterity according to the flesh, from a barren wife, was also supernatural as regards the way of obtaining it. And so to believe these things out of charity was meritorious; and therefore there follows: [[15:6|and it was reputed to him unto justice|Et reputatum est illi ad justitiam]], that is, God judged that he had acted justly in so believing, and he was justified by believing this very thing: not that he was not just before, but because he was now made more just. Justice is taken here as the general virtue [that is, justice in the wide sense, the whole of virtue, not the particular virtue that gives each his due]. For every virtue is a kind of justice, inasmuch as by it a man stands as he ought or as is fitting. The Apostle cites this authority too, in the Epistle to the Romans[[Rom 4:3||]] and again in that to the Galatians[[Gal 3:6||]], to prove that Abraham pleased God by faith, even before his circumcision. It is plain, moreover, from this place that faith justifies a man; which is to be understood of faith formed by charity [that is, faith made living by charity], and of formal justification [that is, by the grace that is in the soul and makes it just]. Therefore it is written in the Acts: [[Acts 13:39|In him|In hoc]], that is, in Christ, [[Acts 13:39|every one that believeth is justified|omnis qui credit, justificatur]]. For faith is the foundation of the virtues and the beginning of justification.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur, id est igne seu regione Chaldæorum, sicut hoc supra fuit diffusius expositum, ut darem tibi terram istam, et possideres eam: tibi, inquam, id est posteris tuis. Non tamen possessio terræ hujus, fuit principalis finalisque causa eductionis Abræ de Chaldæa; sed expletio mysteriorum Christi, qui ex semine Abræ voluit incarnari, conversari, et genus humanum in terra promissionis salvare.
paras.en: [[15:7|And he said to him: I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur|Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur]], that is, from the fire or region [[15:7|of the Chaldees|Chaldæorum]] [ur is Hebrew for fire], as was set out more fully above, [[15:7|to give thee this land, and that thou mightest possess it|ut darem tibi terram istam, et possideres eam]]: to thee, I say, that is, to thy posterity. Yet the possession of this land was not the chief and final cause of Abram's being led out of Chaldea, but the fulfilment of the mysteries of Christ, who willed to be incarnate of the seed of Abram, to live among men, and to save the human race in the land of promise.

paras.t: At ille ait: Domine Deus, unde scire possum quod possessurus sim eam in posteris meis? Jam dictum est, quod Abram credidit Deo. Quod ergo nunc ait, Unde scire possum, non venit ex incredulitate aut diffidentia, sed desiderio informationis majoris de modo quo fieret, quemadmodum beatissima Virgo, audita annuntiatione superincomprehensibilis incarnationis Filii Dei, ait: Quomodo fiet istud? Ideo loquitur Augustinus, quod ideo dixit Abram hæc verba, quatenus rei quam credidit, aliqua similitudo adhiberetur, qua ejus modus agnosceretur. Et quoniam Abram quæsivit hoc signum, inolevit Judæis mos signa quærendi, ut in Scholastica historia dicitur.
paras.en: [[15:8|But he said: Lord God, whereby may I know that I shall possess it|At ille ait: Domine Deus, unde scire possum quod possessurus sim eam]] in my posterity? It has already been said that Abram believed God. So what he now says, [[15:8|whereby may I know|Unde scire possum]], does not come from unbelief or mistrust, but from a desire for fuller instruction about the way it would come about; just as the most blessed Virgin, on hearing the announcement of the more than incomprehensible incarnation of the Son of God, said: [[Luke 1:34|How shall this be done|Quomodo fiet istud]]? Therefore Augustine says that Abram spoke these words so that some likeness might be given of the thing he believed, by which the manner of it might be known. And because Abram asked for this sign, the custom of seeking signs grew up among the Jews, as is said in the Scholastic History.

paras.t: Et respondens Dominus : Sume, inquit, mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam, hoc est trium annorum, et arietem annorum trium, turturem quoque et columbam. Ideo Dominus specialiter jussit ista animalia irrationalia, videlicet tria terrestria, et duo aerea accipi et offerri, quoniam erat futurum, ut ex eis dumtaxat fierent sacrificia in lege per Moysen data, excepto quod in emundatione leprosi, fiebat de passeribus oblatio. Sicque oblatio illa non fuit communis, propter quod non fit nunc sermo de ea. Cur autem præcipit Deus, ut tria animalia ista terrestria essent triennia ? Respondetur ex Augustino, quod ideo, quia populus Israel in tertia mundi ætate, quæ cœpit ab Abraham, et duravit usque ad David, adolevit seu crevit. Potest etiam dici, quod animalia illa in triennio majorem habent aptitudinem, vivacitatem, robur, aut proprietatem ad immolandum, et propter commendandum superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mysterium, propter quod etiam tria jussa sunt accipi.
paras.en: [[15:9|And the Lord answered|Et respondens Dominus]]: [[15:9|Take|Sume]], he said, [[15:9|me a cow of three years old, and a she-goat of three years|mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam]], that is, three years old, [[15:9|and a ram of three years, a turtle also, and a pigeon|et arietem annorum trium, turturem quoque et columbam]]. The Lord specially commanded these irrational animals to be taken and offered, namely three land animals and two of the air, because it was to come about that the sacrifices in the law given through Moses would be made of these alone, except that in the cleansing of a leper an offering was made of sparrows. And so that offering was not a common one, which is why no mention is made of it here. But why does God command that these three land animals be three years old? The answer, from Augustine, is: because the people of Israel grew up, or increased, in the third age of the world, which began from Abraham and lasted until David. It can also be said that in their third year those animals have greater fitness, liveliness, strength or suitability for being sacrificed; and it was done also to set forth the mystery of the more than most blessed Trinity, for which reason too three were commanded to be taken.

paras.t: Qui tollens universa hæc : non in ipsa nocte, qua facta est ei revelatio ista, sed die immediate sequente ; divisit ea per medium, utpote tria animalia illa terrestria, et utrasque partes contra se altrinsecus posuit, utpote ambas partes seu medietates cujuslibet animalis occisi, ita quod una animalis occisi medietas, sic jacuit ex opposito alterius medietatis, quod inter eas potuit quis transire, propter causam infra tangendam ; aves autem, scilicet turturem et columbam, non divisit per medium, ut animalia alia. Videtur tamen quod eas occidit, et forsitan unam occisam posuit juxta unam partem animalium divisorum, et aliam avem occisam juxta aliam illorum animalium partem. Cur aves non divisit ? De hoc spiritualis ratio assignatur. Primo, quod per animalia designantur carnales, qui dividuntur per schismata et peccata : per aves vero, spirituales, qui solliciti sunt servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis. Secundo, quod per animalia designantur activi, qui circa plurima distrahuntur, quemadmodum Dominus dixit ad sanctam Martham, Sollicita es, et turbaris erga plurima ; per aves, contemplativi, qui circa unum intenti sunt, et recolligunt se in Deum.
paras.en: [[15:10|And he took all these|Qui tollens universa hæc]]: not on the very night in which this revelation was made to him, but on the day immediately following; [[15:10|and divided them in the midst|divisit ea per medium]], namely those three land animals, [[15:10|and laid the two pieces of each one against the other|et utrasque partes contra se altrinsecus posuit]], namely both parts or halves of each slain animal, so that one half of the slain animal lay opposite the other half in such a way that a man could pass between them, for a reason to be touched on below; [[15:10|but the birds|aves autem]], that is, the turtle and the pigeon, [[15:10|he divided not|non divisit]] down the middle, as he did the other animals. It seems, however, that he killed them, and perhaps he laid one, slain, beside one part of the divided animals, and the other bird, slain, beside the other part of those animals. Why did he not divide the birds? A spiritual reason is given for this. First, that by the animals are signified the carnal, who are divided by schisms and sins; but by the birds the spiritual, who are [[Eph 4:3|careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace|solliciti sunt servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis]]. Second, that by the animals are signified the active, who are drawn apart about many things, as the Lord said to Saint Martha: [[Luke 10:41|thou art careful and art troubled about many things|Sollicita es, et turbaris erga plurima]]; by the birds, the contemplative, who are intent upon one thing and gather themselves up into God.

paras.t: Descenderuntque volucres super cadavera, hoc est super carnes illas occisas, ut ex eis comederent. Et dicit quidam, quod aves istæ erant de nocte volantes. Quod non videtur consonare verbis, nam subditur : et abigebat eas Abram. Quo constat, quod in die descenderunt super sacrificia ejus. Quumque sol occumberet, pavor irruit super Abram. Ex quibus apparet, quod clara die volucres super carnes illas descenderant, quia et Abram vidit eas, et ante solis occubitum fuit hoc.
paras.en: [[15:11|And the fowls came down upon the carcasses|Descenderuntque volucres super cadavera]], that is, upon that slain flesh, to eat of it. And someone says that these were birds that fly by night. That does not seem to agree with the words, for there follows: [[15:11|and Abram drove them away|et abigebat eas Abram]]. From which it is plain that they came down upon his sacrifices by day. [[15:12|And when the sun was setting|Quumque sol occumberet]], dread [[15:12|fell upon Abram|irruit super Abram]] [Denis's text reads pavor, "dread", where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "a deep sleep" (sopor); he discusses the readings in the next paragraph]. From these words it appears that the birds had come down upon that flesh in broad daylight, since Abram both saw them, and this happened before the setting of the sun.

paras.t: Itaque quum sol occubuisset, pavor irruit super Abram. Aliqui textus habent, Sopor irruit, etc. Circa quod Lyra ait, quod in Hebræo habetur, Ecstasis irruit, etc. Et per ecstasim intelligit raptum seu alienationem ab exterioribus sensibus. Porro, secundum Rabbi Paulum, in Hebræo habetur proprie, Sopor, sicut in translatione nostra, in qua secundum Lyram dicitur, Sopor irruit : ex quo etiam satis apparet, quod Lyra frequenter dicit aliter haberi in Hebræo, quam in nostra translatione, quum tamen ita non sit absolute loquendo. Dicitque Rabbi Paulus, quod in Hebræo eadem dictio ponitur hic, quæ supra secundo capitulo habetur : Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam. Verumtamen omnia concordando, dici potest quod verbum Hebraicum exstet æquivocum. Nam et in verbis illis, Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam, per soporem illum intelligitur ad litteram, non somnus quicumque naturalis aut solitus, sed potius raptus aut ecstasis, ut dictum est ibi. Septuaginta quoque transtulerunt, Pavor irruit, etc. Et potuit esse, ut Abram gravaretur naturaliter quodam somno, aut supernaturaliter perduceretur ad raptum aut ecstasim, per quem raptum disponeretur ad revelationem mox subditam.
paras.en: [[15:12|And when the sun was setting|Itaque quum sol occubuisset]], dread [[15:12|fell upon Abram|irruit super Abram]]. Some texts have: [[15:12|a deep sleep fell|Sopor irruit]], etc. On this Lyra says that in the Hebrew there is: An ecstasy fell, etc. And by ecstasy he understands rapture, or withdrawal from the outward senses. But according to Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, whose Additions accompany Lyra's Postill], the Hebrew properly has "deep sleep", as in our translation, in which, according to Lyra, it says: [[15:12|a deep sleep fell|Sopor irruit]]. From this too it is clear enough that Lyra often says the Hebrew has otherwise than our translation, when, speaking absolutely, this is not so. And Rabbi Paul says that in the Hebrew the same word is used here as is found above in the second chapter: [[Gen 2:21|the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam|Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam]]. Yet, to bring all these into agreement, it can be said that the Hebrew word is equivocal [that is, it has more than one meaning]. For in those words too, [[Gen 2:21|the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam|Immisit Dominus soporem in Adam]], that deep sleep is understood according to the letter not as any natural or ordinary sleep, but rather as a rapture or ecstasy, as was said there. The Septuagint also translated: Dread fell, etc. And it may be that Abram was weighed down naturally by a kind of sleep, or was carried supernaturally into a rapture or ecstasy, by which rapture he was made ready for the revelation that follows straight after.

paras.t: Et horror magnus et tenebrosus invasit eum. Quæri potest, ex qua causa oriebatur in Abram horror iste tam magnus et tenebrosus, id est afflictivus et gravis seu in tenebris ortus. Respondetur, quod passiones animæ communiter generantur ex aliqua prævia sensitiva apprehensione seu sensatione. Interdum vero oriuntur ex causis valde occultis, aut supernaturalibus, ita quod homo ipse qui patitur eas, cognoscere nequit causam immediatam et propriam unde nascuntur ; sic dum aliquis tremit et pavet ex appropinquatione seu præsentia hostis sive latronis aut periculi imminentis, quum tamen ignoret se illis appropinquare. Sicque ad propositum dici potest, quod ex operatione occulta angelici spiritus, oriebatur in Abram magnus pavor iste. Potest enim angelus bonus, imo et angelus malus, corporalem hominis naturam faciliter ac multipliciter ac fortiter immutare. Probabiliter quoque dici potest, quod in hujusmodi tremefactione atque formidine præsit et adsit interior quædam imaginatio saltem occulta cujusdam mali sive adversitatis. Sicque fuisse in Abram videtur. Nam et in Scholastica fertur historia, quod horror iste tam ingens, fuit pars signi quod petiit Abram, ut factum est. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod fuit quodammodo supernaturalis, utpote præfigurativus futurorum : idcirco subjungitur, quod timor iste significavit.
paras.en: [[15:12|and a great and darksome horror seized upon him|Et horror magnus et tenebrosus invasit eum]]. It may be asked from what cause this horror, so great and so darksome, arose in Abram: darksome, that is, afflicting and heavy, or arising in the darkness. The answer is that the passions of the soul are commonly produced by some foregoing apprehension or sensation of the senses. Sometimes, however, they arise from causes that are very hidden, or supernatural, so that the man who undergoes them cannot know the immediate and proper cause from which they spring; as when someone trembles and is afraid at the approach or presence of an enemy or a robber or of some imminent danger, while not knowing that he is drawing near to them. And so, to the point, it can be said that this great dread arose in Abram by the hidden working of an angelic spirit. For a good angel, and indeed a bad angel too, can easily, in many ways and strongly alter the bodily nature of man. It can also be said with probability that in trembling and fear of this kind there is present and at work some inward imagining, at least a hidden one, of some evil or adversity. And so it seems to have been in Abram. For the Scholastic History [Peter Comestor's Historia Scholastica] also reports that this horror, so immense, was part of the sign that Abram asked for, as was done. From which it seems to follow that it was in some way supernatural, as foreshadowing things to come: therefore what this fear signified is added next.

paras.t: Dictumque est ad eum, puta ad Abram a Domino : Scito prænoscens, id est prophetaliter jam prænoscas, quod peregrinum futurum sit semen tuum in terra non sua, hoc est, quod posteritas tua habitabit in terra aliena : et subjicient eos servituti, et affligent, id est, hi in quorum regionibus posteri tui erunt peregrini, subdent posteros tuos famulatui gravi et tribulationi multiplici, quadringentis annis : non quod servitus et afflictio tot annis durabunt, sed quia peregrinatio præfata erit tam diuturna, et infra annos illos evenient et complebuntur prædicta servitus atque afflictio. Itaque quod ait, quadringentis annis, determinat complexum illud, Peregrinum futurum sit ; non autem verbum illud, Subjicient eos servituti.
paras.en: [[15:13|And it was said unto him|Dictumque est ad eum]], namely to Abram by the Lord: [[15:13|Know thou beforehand|Scito prænoscens]], that is, know now beforehand by prophecy, [[15:13|that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own|quod peregrinum futurum sit semen tuum in terra non sua]], that is, that thy posterity shall dwell in a foreign land: [[15:13|and they shall bring them under bondage, and afflict them|et subjicient eos servituti, et affligent]], that is, those in whose countries thy posterity shall be strangers shall subject thy posterity to heavy service and to manifold tribulation, [[15:13|four hundred years|quadringentis annis]]: not that the bondage and affliction will last so many years, but because the sojourning spoken of will be so long, and within those years the said bondage and affliction will come about and be fulfilled. So when he says [[15:13|four hundred years|quadringentis annis]], this qualifies the phrase [[15:13|shall be a stranger|Peregrinum futurum sit]], and not the words [[15:13|they shall bring them under bondage|Subjicient eos servituti]].

paras.t: Denique, quod semen Abræ seu filii Israel non habitaverint in Ægypto tot annis, facile est ex textu probare. Nam infra habetur, quod Jacob descendit in Ægyptum cum filiis suis et filiis filiorum suorum, hoc est, verbi gratia, cum filio suo Levi, et cum Caath filio Levi. Caath vero genuit Amram, cujus filii fuerunt Moyses et Aaron, qui eduxerunt filios Israel de Ægypto. Caath vero vixit annis centum triginta tribus, Amram autem centum triginta septem, ut legitur in Exodo. Moyses demum, quum esset octoginta annorum, filios Israel de Ægypto eduxit : sicque totum tempus vitæ Caath et Amram ac Moysis usque ad octogesimum vitæ suæ annum, non fuit nisi trecenti et quinquaginta anni. Nec tamen filii Israel fuerunt tam diu in terra Ægypti : imo ab annis præfatis oportet subtrahere totum tempus quo vixit Caath, antequam introivit Ægyptum, et annos quibus vixit postquam genuit Amram, tempus quoque quo vixit Amram postquam Moysen generavit. Idcirco, ut dicunt Hebræi et multi Catholici, filii Israel non fuerunt in Ægypto, nisi annis ducentis et decem. Nec tamen toto tempore illo fuerunt servituti et afflictioni ibidem subjecti ; imo multis annis ibi in honore fuerunt sub Joseph et fratribus ejus, ut infra patebit.
paras.en: Next, that the seed of Abraham, or the children of Israel, did not dwell in Egypt for so many years is easy to prove from the text. For it is found below that Jacob went down into Egypt with his sons and his sons' sons[[Gen 46:7||]]: that is, for example, with his son Levi and with Caath, the son of Levi. Now Caath begot Amram, whose sons were Moses and Aaron, who led the children of Israel out of Egypt. And Caath lived a hundred and thirty-three years, and Amram a hundred and thirty-seven, as we read in Exodus[[Ex 6:18||]][[Ex 6:20||]]. Moses, lastly, led the children of Israel out of Egypt when he was eighty years old; and so the whole time of the lives of Caath and Amram, and of Moses up to the eightieth year of his life, was no more than three hundred and fifty years. And yet the children of Israel were not in the land of Egypt for so long: rather, from the said years one must subtract the whole time Caath lived before he entered Egypt, and the years he lived after he begot Amram, and also the time Amram lived after he begot Moses. Therefore, as the Hebrews and many Catholics say, the children of Israel were in Egypt only two hundred and ten years. Nor were they subject to bondage and affliction there for the whole of that time; on the contrary, for many years they were held in honour there under Joseph and his brethren[[Gen 47:11||]][[Gen 47:12||]], as will appear below.

paras.t: Præterea anni hi quadringenti, computari possunt a nativitate Isaac, qui proprie dictus est filius Abrahæ præelectus, et per repromissionem concessus, propter quod dictum est Abrahæ : In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen. Isaac autem sexagenarius genuit Jacob, qui quum esset centum triginta annorum, Ægyptum ingressus est, ut infra in textu habetur : qui anni ducentis et decem annis præfatis appositi, faciunt adæquate annos quadringentos, quibus semen Abrahæ exstitit peregrinum in terra non sua, partim in Palæstina, videlicet in terra Chanaan et Geraræ, partimque in Ægypto. Verumtamen Augustinus ab anno nativitatis Isaac usque ad annum egressionis de Ægypto, computat annos quadringentos et quinque, et dicit quod Scriptura non facit mentionem de illis quinque annis, quia consuetudo est Scripturæ, non curare minutias numeri aut temporis. Computat autem Augustinus secundum translationem Septuaginta. Sed circa hæc oritur difficultas, quoniam in Actis loquitur Paulus apostolus : Deus sorte distribuit eis terram, quasi post quadringentos et quinquaginta annos. Porro ad Galatas ait : Quæ post quadringentos et triginta annos facta est lex, non irritum facit, etc. Respondetur, quod tempus illud quadringentorum quinquaginta annorum, computatur a nativitate Isaac usque ad divisionem terræ promissionis factum sub Josue, ut in Josue libro legitur; anni vero quadringenti et triginta, computantur a tempore quo ista promissio facta est Abræ. Sed rursus objicitur contra prædicta, quoniam in Exodi libro scriptum est : Habitatio filiorum Israel, qua manserunt in Ægypto, fuit quadringentorum triginta annorum. Ergo non solum annis ducentis et decem, sed amplius quam quadringentis in Ægypto morati sunt. Hujus solutionem usque ad locum illum suspendo, quanquam breviter dici posset, quod in auctoritate hac Exodi, per habitationem in Ægypto, datur intelligi habitatio filiorum Israel in Ægypto, et habitatio patrum eorum in Chanaan.
paras.en: Moreover, these four hundred years can be counted from the birth of Isaac, who is properly called the chosen son of Abraham, granted by promise, for which reason it was said to Abraham: [[Gen 21:12|in Isaac shall thy seed be called|In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen]]. Now Isaac at sixty begot Jacob, who entered Egypt when he was a hundred and thirty years old, as is found below in the text; and these years, added to the said two hundred and ten, make exactly the four hundred years during which the seed of Abraham was a stranger in a land not its own: partly in Palestine, namely in the land of Chanaan and of Gerara, and partly in Egypt. Augustine, however, counts four hundred and five years from the year of Isaac's birth to the year of the going out of Egypt, and says that Scripture makes no mention of those five years because it is the custom of Scripture not to care about the small details of a number or of time. But Augustine counts according to the Septuagint translation. Here, though, a difficulty arises, since in the Acts the apostle Paul says: God [[Acts 13:19|divided their land among them by lot|sorte distribuit eis terram]], [[Acts 13:20|as it were, after four hundred and fifty years|quasi post quadringentos et quinquaginta annos]]. And again, to the Galatians he says: [[Gal 3:17|the law which was made after four hundred and thirty years doth not disannul|Quæ post quadringentos et triginta annos facta est lex, non irritum facit]], etc. The answer is that that time of four hundred and fifty years is counted from the birth of Isaac to the division of the land of promise made under Josue, as is read in the book of Josue[[Jos 13:7||]]; but the four hundred and thirty years are counted from the time at which this promise was made to Abraham. But again an objection is raised against what has been said, since it is written in the book of Exodus: [[Ex 12:40|the abode of the children of Israel that they made in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years|Habitatio filiorum Israel, qua manserunt in Ægypto, fuit quadringentorum triginta annorum]]. Therefore they stayed in Egypt not only two hundred and ten years but more than four hundred. I put off the answer to this until we reach that place, though it could be said briefly that in this text of Exodus, by the abode in Egypt is to be understood the abode of the children of Israel in Egypt together with the abode of their fathers in Chanaan.

paras.t: Verumtamen gentem cui servituri sunt, puta Ægyptios, ego judicabo, id est, juste indurabo, reprobabo, ac puniam plagis temporalibus, quæ in Exodo describuntur; deinde damnatione æterna, quia per plagas temporales non erunt conversi et emendati. Istud Dominus dixit ad Abram pro consolatione ipsius, qui de futuris suæ posteritatis tribulationibus poterat contristari. Et post hoc egredientur cum magna substantia. Nam multi filiorum Israel egredientium de Ægypto, fuerunt divites valde, habueruntque pecora multa, et ultra hoc, Deo jubente, egressuri mox de Ægypto, mutuarunt ab Ægyptiis vasa aurea atque argentea, vestesque pretiosas ac plurimas, prout in Exodi libro recitatur.
paras.en: But [[15:14|the nation which they shall serve|gentem cui servituri sunt]], namely the Egyptians, [[15:14|I will judge|ego judicabo]]: that is, I will justly harden, reprobate and punish them with the temporal plagues described in Exodus, and afterwards with eternal damnation, since they will not be converted and amended by the temporal plagues. The Lord said this to Abram for his comfort, since he could be saddened by the future tribulations of his posterity. [[15:14|and after this they shall come out with great substance|Et post hoc egredientur cum magna substantia]]. For many of the children of Israel who went out of Egypt were very rich and had many flocks; and besides this, at God's command, when they were about to go out of Egypt, they borrowed from the Egyptians vessels of gold and silver and very many precious garments, as is related in the book of Exodus[[Ex 12:35||]].

paras.t: Tu autem ibis ad patres tuos in pace, hoc est, per mortem temporalem transibis ad sanctos Patriarchas in limbo patrum detentos, de quorum semine natus es, quamvis aliqui patrum tuorum qui fuerunt post illos, fuerint vitiosi, et item idololatræ : sepultus in senectute bona, hoc est, virtuoso senio consummatus, et in statu salutis defunctus. Verumtamen ante corporis sepulturam discessit anima sancti viri ad limbum, si tamen nihil purgandum detulit secum. Denique per hunc modum loquendi insinuavit Moyses animæ immortalitatem, et vitam aliam post præsentem, quoniam mortem nominat transitum ad prædecessores defunctos, qui nihil essent post mortem, nullus iret ad eos post mortem. Rursus per verba hæc Deus assecuravit Abram de sua salute, præsertim si verba hæc intellexit per modum absolutæ assertionis absque conditione implicita.
paras.en: [[15:15|And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace|Tu autem ibis ad patres tuos in pace]]: that is, by temporal death thou shalt pass over to the holy Patriarchs held in the limbo of the fathers, of whose seed thou wast born, although some of thy fathers who came after them were wicked men, and idolaters too: [[15:15|and be buried in a good old age|sepultus in senectute bona]], that is, brought to completion in a virtuous old age, and dying in the state of salvation. Yet before the burial of the body the soul of the holy man departed to limbo, provided that he carried nothing with him needing to be purged [that is, nothing to be cleansed in purgatory]. Further, by this manner of speaking Moses hinted at the immortality of the soul and at another life after the present one, since he calls death a passing over to one's forebears who have died; and if they were nothing after death, no one would go to them after death. Again, by these words God assured Abram of his salvation, especially if he understood them as an absolute assertion, without an implied condition.

paras.t: Generatione autem quarta revertentur huc, hoc est, quarto viro nato post eum, qui simul cum sobole sua intrabit Ægyptum, redibunt posteri tui ad terram hanc Chanaan, et hoc in computatione successionis tribus sacerdotalis sive Leviticæ. Levi enim genuit Caath, Caath Amram, Amram Aaron, Aaron Eleazarum, qui cum patre suo Aaron exivit Ægyptum. Sicque Eleazarus fuit quartus post Levi, ipso Levi excluso. Quidam computationem istam a Levi incipiunt inclusive, et dicunt quod secundum successionem tribus sacerdotalis, quinta generatione egressi sunt : secundum quod Septuaginta translatio continet, Quinta generatione redibunt. Alii vero dicunt hoc adimpletum in regia tribu, videlicet generatione Judæ, qui genuit Phares patrem Aram, qui Aram genuit Aminadab, patrem Naasson, qui cum patre suo Ægyptum est egressus. Computationum vero diversitas faciliter concordatur per diversam inceptionem, atque per terminorum inclusionem aut exclusionem.
paras.en: [[15:16|But in the fourth generation they shall return hither|Generatione autem quarta revertentur huc]]: that is, in the fourth man born after him who, together with his offspring, shall enter Egypt, thy posterity shall return to this land of Chanaan; and this in reckoning the succession of the priestly, or Levitical, tribe. For Levi begot Caath, Caath Amram, Amram Aaron, Aaron Eleazar, who went out of Egypt with his father Aaron. And so Eleazar was the fourth after Levi, Levi himself not counted. Some begin this count from Levi inclusively, and say that by the succession of the priestly tribe they went out in the fifth generation, in keeping with what the Septuagint translation has: In the fifth generation they shall return. Others, however, say that this was fulfilled in the royal tribe, namely in the line of Juda, who begot Phares, the father of Aram [so the text; in Ruth and Matthew Aram is the son of Esron, the son of Phares], and this Aram begot Aminadab, the father of Naasson[[Ruth 4:18||]][[Ruth 4:19||]][[Ruth 4:20||]][[Matt 1:3||]][[Matt 1:4||]], who went out of Egypt with his father. But the differences between the reckonings are easily reconciled by starting at different points, and by counting or not counting the end terms.

paras.t: Porro quidam incipit computationem istam a Jacob, et dicit quod si computentur generationes ab eo per lineam generationum, inveniuntur quatuor usque ad reditum in terram promissionis, quoniam Jacob genuit Judam, Judas vero Phares, Phares autem Esron, Esron vero Caleb, qui terram promissionis intravit. Quod autem Caleb sit filius Esron, probatur ex primo libro Paralipomenon. Sed advertendum, quod istud stare non potest, quoniam Caleb ille filius Esron, alius fuit ab isto Caleb, qui terram promissionis ingressus est. Siquidem Caleb iste, fuit pater ipsius Hur, qui genuit Uri patrem Beseleel, qui Beseleel exivit Ægyptum cum patre suo, fuitque quartus vel saltem tertius post illum Caleb. Caleb vero qui terram promissionis intravit, erat solum quadraginta annorum, vel potius minus, quando exivit Ægyptum. Nam quadragenarius erat, quando cum ceteris ad explorandum terram a Moyse missus est.
paras.en: Someone, again, begins this count from Jacob, and says that if the generations from him are counted along the line of descent, four are found up to the return into the land of promise, since Jacob begot Juda, Juda Phares, Phares Esron, and Esron Caleb, who entered the land of promise. And that Caleb was the son of Esron is proved from the first book of Paralipomenon. But it must be noted that this cannot stand, since that Caleb, the son of Esron, was another than the Caleb who entered the land of promise. For that Caleb was the father of Hur, who begot Uri, the father of Beseleel[[1 Par 2:18||]][[1 Par 2:19||]][[1 Par 2:20||]][[1 Par 2:21||]]; and this Beseleel went out of Egypt with his father, and was the fourth, or at least the third, after that Caleb. But the Caleb who entered the land of promise was only forty years old, or rather less, when he went out of Egypt. For he was forty when he was sent by Moses with the others to spy out the land[[Jos 14:7||]] [the margin reads Jerem. 2, which does not fit; the passage is Jos 14:7].

paras.t: Deinde subditur causa tantæ dilationis, qua filii Israel protracti sunt ab ingressu terræ eis promissæ. Necdum enim completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum usque ad præsens tempus, id est, nondum impleverunt mensuram seu pondus facinorum, quod ab eis pietas mea sustinere decrevit, antequam ejiciantur de terra sua. Ex hoc accipit Augustinus, quod scribit in libro de Doctrina christiana, quod Deus dignatur ab unoquoque homine seu populo sustinere certam mensuram culparum, qua impleta, non tolerat eum diutius. Exspectat enim ut misereatur, ut loquitur Isaias, hoc est, ut homines se emendent, quibus misericordia Dei abutentibus adhibet ultionem. Propter quod asserit Jeremias : Non poterat vos Dominus ultra sustinere propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum. Verumtamen quicumque peccat mortaliter, non solum meretur damnationem æternam, sed etiam immediate mortem corporalem, et omnium exteriorum rerum privationem. Estque indignus pane quo vescitur, et omnium creaturarum obsequio, usu, ac ope.
paras.en: Then is added the cause of so long a delay, by which the children of Israel were held back from entering the land promised them: [[15:16|for as yet the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not at the full until this present time|Necdum enim completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum usque ad præsens tempus]]; that is, they have not yet filled up the measure or weight of crimes that my goodness has decided to bear from them before they are cast out of their land. From this Augustine takes what he writes in the book On Christian Doctrine: that God deigns to bear from each man or people a certain measure of faults, and when it is filled He bears with him no longer. For [[Is 30:18|the Lord waiteth that he may have mercy|Exspectat enim ut misereatur]], as Isaias says: that is, for men to amend themselves; and on those who abuse the mercy of God He brings vengeance. For this reason Jeremias declares: [[Jer 44:22|the Lord could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings|Non poterat vos Dominus ultra sustinere propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum]]. Yet whoever sins mortally deserves not only eternal damnation but also immediate bodily death and the loss of all outward things. And he is unworthy of the bread he eats, and of the service, use and help of all creatures.

paras.t: Consequenter redit Moyses ad prosecutionem historiæ. Quum ergo occubuisset sol, ut dictum est paulo ante, facta est caligo tenebrosa. Hoc non fuit mirum, quod post solis occasum caligo inducta est, sed caligo ista fuit tenebrosior solito, et forte apparuit densissima nubes, quæ fuit pars signi petiti, et significavit vehementiam adversitatum tribulationumque filiorum Israel in Ægypto. Et apparuit clibanus fumans, et lampas ignis. Istud fuit signum veritatis divinæ promissionis præfatæ.
paras.en: Next Moses returns to carrying on the story. [[15:17|And when the sun was set|Quum ergo occubuisset sol]], as was said a little before, [[15:17|there arose a dark mist|facta est caligo tenebrosa]]. It was no wonder that darkness came on after sunset; but this darkness was darker than usual, and perhaps a very thick cloud appeared, which was part of the sign asked for and signified the violence of the adversities and tribulations of the children of Israel in Egypt. [[15:17|and there appeared a smoking furnace, and a lamp of fire|Et apparuit clibanus fumans, et lampas ignis]]. This was the sign of the truth of the divine promise spoken of above.

paras.t: Circa verba hæc duo quæruntur. Primo, an ista fuerunt ibi realiter, scilicet fornax fumans, et lampas ignis, an per similitudinem et imaginariam visionem dumtaxat. Secundo, an ibi apparuerunt duo ignes, videlicet ignis fornacis, et ignis lampadis. Ad primum istorum videtur quibusdam dicendum, quod ibi apparebat realiter ignis, ut dicunt nonnulli quod apparuit ibi ad repræsentandum divinæ majestatis præsentiam, sicut in rubo monteque Sinai. His consonat quod in Scholastica historia fertur, quod ignis ille consumpsit sacrificium Abræ, hoc est carnes illas divisas. Unde si realem habuit ignis actionem, videtur fuisse realiter ignis, non similitudo dumtaxat. Ad secundum aliqui dicunt, quod non fuit nisi unus ignis. Ait namque præfata Historia, quod apparuit ignis quasi clibani ; verumtamen textui magis consonare censetur, quod duo ignes ibi fuerunt : unus fornacis ardentis ac fumigantis, stans fixe in loco suo ; alter lampadis, qui pertransivit inter partes prædictas. Subditur enim in textu : Et lampas ignis transiens inter divisiones illas, utpote inter carnes ab invicem divisas ac positas. Nam et Septuaginta transtulerunt : Quum autem jam sol erat ad occasum, flamma facta est, et fornax fumibunda, et lampades ignis, quæ pertransierunt per media illa divisa. Et forsitan ex clibano illo ardente erumpebant quasi lampades ignis, volitantes inter carnes illas, et comburentes easdem : in signum, quod sacrificium Abræ exstitit Deo acceptum. Fuit itaque ibi reale aliquid simile clibano, et ministerio angeli tota visio ista exhibebatur.
paras.en: Two questions are asked about these words. First, whether these things, namely the smoking furnace and the lamp of fire, were really there, or only by a likeness and an imaginary vision. Second, whether two fires appeared there, namely the fire of the furnace and the fire of the lamp. To the first of these, some think the answer is that fire really appeared there, as several say that it appeared there to represent the presence of the divine majesty, as in the bush and on Mount Sinai[[Ex 3:2||]][[Ex 19:18||]]. With this agrees what the Scholastic History reports, that that fire consumed Abraham's sacrifice, that is, that divided flesh. Hence if the fire really acted, it seems to have been really fire, and not only a likeness. To the second, some say that there was only one fire; for the History already mentioned says that there appeared a fire as of a furnace. Yet it is judged to agree better with the text that there were two fires there: one of the burning and smoking furnace, standing fixed in its place; the other of the lamp, which passed between the said parts. For there follows in the text: [[15:17|and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions|Et lampas ignis transiens inter divisiones illas]], that is, between the pieces of flesh divided from one another and laid out. For the Septuagint too translated: And when the sun was now at its setting, a flame arose, and a smoking furnace, and lamps of fire, which passed through the midst of those divided pieces. And perhaps from that burning furnace there burst forth, as it were, lamps of fire, flitting among those pieces of flesh and burning them up: in sign that Abraham's sacrifice was acceptable to God. So there was something real there like a furnace, and this whole vision was shown by the ministry of an angel.

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, cur ignis lampadis pertransivit partes præfatas. Respondetur, quoniam inter antiquos fuit consuetudo, ut percutientes pactum seu fœdus pariter ineuntes, occiderent atque dividerent aliquod animal, et inter partes divisas transirent, quasi ad innuendum quod morte efficerentur condigni, qui pactum infringerent. Hinc apud Jeremiam ait Dominus de obstinatis Judæis : Non observaverunt verba fœderis mei, in quibus assensi sunt; vitulum quem consciderunt in duas partes, et transierunt inter divisiones ejus. Quoniam itaque Dominus in hac visione pepigit fœdus cum Abram, ut protinus subjungetur, idcirco ignis iste Dei præsentiam repræsentans, transivit inter illa divisa, sicque Deus cum Abram agens, habuit se modo humano.
paras.en: It is further asked why the fire of the lamp passed between the said parts. The answer is that it was a custom among the ancients that those who struck a pact, entering together into a covenant, should kill and divide some animal and pass between the divided parts, as if to signify that those who broke the pact would deserve death. Hence in Jeremias the Lord says of the obstinate Jews: They [[Jer 34:18|have not performed the words of the covenant which they agreed to|Non observaverunt verba fœderis mei, in quibus assensi sunt]]; [[Jer 34:18|when they cut the calf in two and passed between the parts thereof|vitulum quem consciderunt in duas partes, et transierunt inter divisiones ejus]]. Since, then, the Lord in this vision made a covenant with Abram, as is added straight after, this fire, representing the presence of God, passed between those divided pieces; and so God, in dealing with Abram, behaved in a human way.

paras.t: In die illo. Istud quod subditur, videtur factum in nocte, sicut et visio jam descripta, idcirco per diem illum intelligitur dies naturalis, qui noctem includit. Pepigit Dominus fœdus cum Abram, id est, firmiter ei promisit, dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc a fluvio Ægypti usque ad fluvium magnum Euphraten. Secundum Augustinum, non dixit, A flumine magno Ægypti, hoc est a Nilo, sed a fluvio parvo, qui dividit inter Ægyptum et Palæstinam, et vocatur fluvius iste Rhinocolura, estque terminus terræ promissionis a parte australi versus Ægyptum : Euphrates vero est terminus terræ ejusdem ex parte opposita versus Chaldæos, inter quos Euphrates currit.
paras.en: [[15:18|That day|In die illo]]. What follows seems to have been done at night, as was the vision just described; therefore by that day is understood the natural day, which includes the night. [[15:18|God made a covenant with Abram|Pepigit Dominus fœdus cum Abram]], that is, He firmly promised him, [[15:18|saying: To thy seed will I give this land, from the river to Egypt even to the great river Euphrates|dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc a fluvio Ægypti usque ad fluvium magnum Euphraten]]. According to Augustine, He did not say, From the great river of Egypt, that is, from the Nile, but from a small river which divides Egypt from Palestine; this river is called Rhinocolura, and it is the boundary of the land of promise on the southern side, towards Egypt; while the Euphrates is the boundary of the same land on the opposite side, towards the Chaldeans, among whom the Euphrates runs.

paras.t: Cinæos et Cenezæos et Cedmonæos et Hethæos, etc. Nominantur hic decem gentes, quarum terras Deus promisit semini Abræ. Et est sensus : Gentes has, id est terram earum, dabo posteris tuis. Prænominatæ quoque gentes istæ, sunt ex Chanaan natæ, ut superius dictum est, quamvis aliqua nomina varientur.
paras.en: [[15:19|The Cineans, and Cenezites, the Cedmonites|Cinæos et Cenezæos et Cedmonæos]], [[15:20|And the Hethites|et Hethæos]], etc. Ten nations are named here, whose lands God promised to the seed of Abraham. And the sense is: These nations, that is, their land, I will give to thy posterity. These nations named before were also born of Chanaan, as was said above[[Gen 10:15||]][[Gen 10:16||]][[Gen 10:17||]], although some of the names vary.

15.title: De spirituali sensu ejusdem capituli quintidecimi
15.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same fifteenth chapter

paras.t: His itaque transactis, factus est sermo Domini ad Abram, dicens : Noli timere. Quemadmodum Deus confortavit et consolatus est Abram quum infideles vicisset, sic admonet et consolatur unumquemque fidelem, qui tentationibus viriliter restitit, et vitia expugnavit, ne timeat inordinate ob hoc, quod invisibiles hostes semel victi solent acrius impugnare, atque callidius impetuosiusque insurgere ac tentare. Tali ergo fideli loquitur Dominus : Ego protector tuus sum, qui conteram Satanam sub pedibus tuis velociter ; et merces tua magna nimis, quemadmodum ait Apostolus : Id quod in præsenti est modicum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis. Itemque : Stabiles, inquit, estote et immobiles, abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino. Talis ergo Dei pugnator indiget assidua armatura virtutum, ut cum omni humilitate et firmitate speret in Domino, et jugiter invocet eum, nec unquam inani securitate torpescat, imo quotidie custoditior ferventiorque reddatur, atque quod non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam, efficaciter contempletur.
paras.en: [[15:1|Now when these things were done|His itaque transactis]], [[15:1|the word of the Lord came to Abram|factus est sermo Domini ad Abram]], [[15:1|saying: Fear not|dicens : Noli timere]]. As God strengthened and consoled Abram when he had conquered the unbelievers, so he admonishes and consoles every faithful man who has manfully resisted temptations and overcome vices, that he should not fear inordinately because the invisible enemies, once beaten, are wont to attack more fiercely, and to rise up and tempt more cunningly and more violently. To such a faithful man, then, the Lord says: [[15:1|I am thy protector|Ego protector tuus sum]], who will [[Rom 16:20|crush Satan under your feet speedily|conteram Satanam sub pedibus tuis velociter]] [Denis turns the Apostle's words to God speaking: ‘I will crush Satan under thy feet’]; [[15:1|and thy reward exceeding great|et merces tua magna nimis]], as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation worketh for us above measure, exceedingly an eternal weight of glory|Id quod in præsenti est modicum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis]]. And again: [[1 Cor 15:58|be ye steadfast|Stabiles]], he says, [[1 Cor 15:58|and unmoveable: always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord|estote et immobiles, abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino]]. Such a fighter for God, then, needs the constant armour of the virtues, so that with all humility and firmness he may hope in the Lord and call upon him unceasingly, and never grow sluggish in idle security, but rather become every day more watchful and more fervent, and effectually contemplate that [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]].

paras.t: Dixitque Abram : Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi ? Ego vadam absque liberis. Vir fidelis per Abram designatus, divini amoris ardore succensus, et fraternæ salutis zelo transverberatus, propria salute nequaquam contentus est, et quidquid sibi pro præmio desuper promittatur, non conquiescit nisi et alios verbo aut oratione, bonæque vitæ exemplis ac meritis trahat ad Creatorem, et quasi spiritualiter pariat Christo : quod dum se videt aut arbitratur non facere, conqueritur se sine spirituali semine recedere de hac vita, quum tamen videat seu confidat quosdam bonos activos et sæculares, trahere proximos ad salutem. Et ecce vernaculus meus erit heres meus : id est, proximus meus servus, sanguine Christi emptus, in domo Ecclesiæ constitutus, obtinebit, alios convertendo, munera gratiarum quæ mihi dedisti, quibus privatum modo me vereor, eo quod nullum tibi gignere queam.
paras.en: [[15:2|And Abram said: Lord God, what wilt thou give me? I shall go without children|Dixitque Abram : Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi ? Ego vadam absque liberis]]. The faithful man signified by Abram, kindled with the ardour of divine love and pierced through with zeal for his brethren's salvation, is by no means content with his own salvation; and whatever is promised him from on high as a reward, he does not rest unless he also draws others to the Creator by word or prayer, and by the examples and merits of a good life, and as it were brings them forth spiritually to Christ. And when he sees, or thinks, that he is not doing this, he complains that he is departing this life without spiritual seed, while yet he sees, or trusts, that certain good men of the active life, and men living in the world, draw their neighbours to salvation. [[15:3|and lo my servant born in my house, shall be my heir|Et ecce vernaculus meus erit heres meus]]: that is, my neighbour, a servant bought with the blood of Christ and set in the house of the Church, will obtain, by converting others, the gifts of graces which thou gavest me, of which I fear I am now deprived, because I can beget none for thee.

paras.t: Nempe vir talis dum se putat non fructificare in aliis, æstimat Deum sibi iratum, seque pristina gratia destitutum, quem Dominus protinus per inspirationem internam aut alio modo consolatur, dicendo : Non erit hic heres tuus, sed qui egredietur de utero tuo, id est, quem semine verbi cælestis ex corde tuo egredientis converteris, et caritate mentis tuæ spiritualiter generaris, ipsum habebis heredem, gratiam tibi collatam administrando in ipsum, et communicando eidem, et relinquendo eum post te in Ecclesia militante successorem tuæ gratiæ ac virtutis, ita quod quasi stella pulcherrima fulgebit in ea, imo et plures convertes, quod credens vir talis, justificatur a Deo.
paras.en: For such a man, when he thinks he is bearing no fruit in others, supposes God to be angry with him and himself stripped of his former grace; and the Lord at once consoles him by an inward inspiration or in some other way, saying: [[15:4|He shall not be thy heir|Non erit hic heres tuus]]: [[15:4|but he that shall come out of thy bowels|sed qui egredietur de utero tuo]], that is, he whom thou shalt convert by the seed of the heavenly word coming forth from thy heart, and beget spiritually by the charity of thy mind, [[15:4|him shalt thou have for thy heir|ipsum habebis heredem]], by ministering to him the grace conferred on thee, imparting it to him, and leaving him after thee in the Church militant as the successor of thy grace and virtue, so that he will shine in it like a most beautiful star; nay, thou shalt convert many more. And believing this, such a man is justified by God.

paras.t: Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum, ut darem tibi terram, et possideres eam, id est, de igne carnalium desideriorum et fervore tentationum te erui, ut terrenos et carnales meritis tuis converterem, et eos in spirituales filios possideres : quod fructuosis pastoribus ac prædicatoribus virtuosis potissimum condonatur et competit.
paras.en: [[15:7|I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees|Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum]], [[15:7|to give thee this land, and that thou mightest possess it|ut darem tibi terram, et possideres eam]], that is, I rescued thee from the fire [*Ur* means ‘fire’ in Hebrew] of carnal desires and from the heat of temptations, so that by thy merits I might convert the earthly and carnal, and thou mightest possess them as spiritual sons: which is granted to, and befits, fruitful pastors and virtuous preachers above all.

paras.t: Præterea vir talis, propriam fragilitatem insufficientiamque perpendens, ait : Domine Deus, unde scire possum quod possessurus sim eam? id est, quod terrenos sic traham ad te, spiritualesque natos habebo eos, quod non nisi per specialem atque præcipuam tuam gratiam fieri valet.
paras.en: Further, such a man, weighing his own frailty and insufficiency, says: [[15:8|Lord God, whereby may I know that I shall possess it?|Domine Deus, unde scire possum quod possessurus sim eam?]] that is, that I shall so draw the earthly to thee and have them as spiritual children, which cannot be done except by thy special and singular grace.

paras.t: Et respondens Dominus : Sume, inquit, mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam, et arietem annorum trium, id est propriam carnem tuam, ex se ipsa instar vaccæ pigram ac tardam ad bona, et quasi capram ad prava pronam ac prosilientem, lascivam quoque tanquam arietem : turturem quoque et columbam, id est spiritum tuum rationalem, instar turturis ad futura suspirantem, et propter mala gementem, ac simplicem veluti columbam. Hæc, inquam, tolle et offer mihi in holocaustum, ut te totum meo cultui mancipans, merearis tanta gratia adimpleri, quod in alios possis eam transfundere. Hoc itaque ait vir talis, carnemque propriam dividit, castigando et flagellando eam quotidie, ita ut dicat : Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die. Sed spiritum suum non dividit, imo eum totum in Deo recolligit, integrat et adunat.
paras.en: [[15:9|And the Lord answered|Et respondens Dominus]]: [[15:9|Take|Sume]], he says, [[15:9|me a cow of three years old, and a she-goat of three years. and a ram of three years|mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam, et arietem annorum trium]], that is, thine own flesh, of itself sluggish like a cow and slow to good, and like a she-goat prone to evil and leaping forth to it, and wanton too like a ram; [[15:9|a turtle also, and a pigeon|turturem quoque et columbam]], that is, thy rational spirit, sighing like the turtle-dove after the things to come and groaning because of evils, and simple as the dove. These, I say, take and offer to me as a holocaust, that, giving thyself over wholly to my service, thou mayest deserve to be filled with grace so great that thou canst pour it into others. This, then, such a man does [the printed text has *ait*, ‘says’, apparently for *agit*, ‘does’], and he divides his own flesh by chastising and scourging it every day, so that he may say: [[Ps 43:22|Because for thy sake we are killed all the day long|Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die]]. But his spirit he does not divide; rather he gathers it wholly together in God, makes it whole and one.

paras.t: Descenderuntque volucres super cadavera. Volucres istæ sunt dæmones, qui semen verbi ac gratiæ Dei nituntur de agro cordis auferre, et sacrificia orationum nostrarum contaminare, corpus et animam inquinare, atque per evagationes et pravas affectiones, ac sinistras intentiones, quidquid Deo offerimus, facere inacceptum. Quas aves pestiferas volitantes, oportet nos cum omni agilitate et diligentia semper abigere, ut stabiles simus ac puri, præsertim in deitatis obsequio Sacrificioque altaris.
paras.en: [[15:11|And the fowls came down upon the carcasses|Descenderuntque volucres super cadavera]]. These fowls are the demons, who strive to take away the seed of God's word and grace from the field of the heart[[Luke 8:5||]][[Luke 8:12||]], to defile the sacrifices of our prayers, to pollute body and soul, and, by wanderings of mind, evil affections and crooked intentions, to make unacceptable whatever we offer to God. These pestilent birds, as they fly about, we must always drive away with all quickness and diligence, that we may be steadfast and pure, above all in the service of the Godhead and in the Sacrifice of the altar.

paras.t: Quumque sol occumberet, pavor, seu sopor, irruit super Abram. Sic plane dum Sol sapientiæ atque justitiæ Christus Dominus paululum subtrahit homini spirituali lucem contemplationis et rorem consolationis supernæ, irruit super eum sopor pigritiæ, negligentiæ somnus, et multiplex timor gravis. Nam et interdum veretur se divinitus derelictum ac periturum.
paras.en: [[15:12|And when the sun was setting|Quumque sol occumberet]], a dread, or [[15:12|a deep sleep fell upon Abram|sopor, irruit super Abram]] [Denis gives two readings, *pavor*, ‘dread’, and *sopor*, ‘deep sleep’, which is the Vulgate's]. So plainly, when Christ the Lord, the Sun of wisdom and of justice, withdraws for a little from the spiritual man the light of contemplation and the dew of heavenly consolation, there falls upon him the deep sleep of sloth, the slumber of negligence, and fear, grave and manifold. For at times he even fears that he is forsaken by God and will perish.

paras.t: Deinde Dominus consolatur eumdem, prænuntians ei, quod semen suum futurum sit peregrinum in terra non sua, et affligendum. Electi namque et boni sunt in sæculo isto quasi in gravi exilio, in quo multipliciter tribulantur, atque nonnunquam servituti invisibilium hostium ac vitiorum subduntur ; imo ad minus servire coguntur necessitatibus miseri corporis, a pravis et reprobis affliguntur hominibus, quos judicaturus est Dominus. Deinceps electi taliter exercitati et expurgati, revertuntur cum spirituali opulentia grandi ad Dominum. Et quarta generatione, videlicet post interiorum reformationem, verborum directionem, operum debitorum exsecutionem et proximorum ædificationem, ingrediuntur triumphantis Ecclesiæ patriam eis promissam.
paras.en: Then the Lord consoles him, foretelling him that his seed [[15:13|shall be a stranger in a land not their own|futurum sit peregrinum in terra non sua]], and shall be afflicted. For the elect and the good are in this world as in a heavy exile, in which they are troubled in many ways, and are sometimes brought into bondage to invisible enemies and to vices; at the least they are forced to serve the needs of the wretched body, and are afflicted by wicked and reprobate men, whom the Lord will judge. Afterwards the elect, thus exercised and purged, return to the Lord with great spiritual wealth. And [[15:16|in the fourth generation|quarta generatione]], that is, after the reform of the inner man, the right ordering of words, the carrying out of due works and the edification of their neighbours, they enter the fatherland of the Church triumphant promised them.

paras.t: Interim vero apparet eis clibanus fumans, lampasque ignis transiens inter præfatas divisiones : quia ut ait Scriptura, Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis. Itemque: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus.
paras.en: Meanwhile there appears to them [[15:17|a smoking furnace|clibanus fumans]], [[15:17|and a lamp of fire passing between|lampasque ignis transiens inter]] the aforesaid divisions: because, as the Scripture says, [[Ecclus 27:6|The furnace trieth the potter's vessels, and the trial of affliction just men|Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis]]. And again: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace|Tanquam aurum in fornace]] the Lord [[Wis 3:6|hath proved|probavit]] his elect.

paras.t: Postremo Augustinus tangit aliam spiritualem hujus capituli intelligentiam, quam et Isidorus ac Richardus induunt, sed prolixitatem devitans, pertranseo.
paras.en: Lastly, Augustine touches on another spiritual understanding of this chapter, which Isidore and Richard also bring forward [the printed text has *induunt*, apparently for *inducunt*]; but, to avoid prolixity, I pass it over.

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam Abram figura est Christi, potest capitulum istud allegorice de Christo exponi, ita: Factus est sermo Domini ad Abram per visionem, dicens: Noli timere; id est, Verbum æternum, seu Deus Pater, aut Trinitas Deus, dixit Christo secundum suam humanam naturam, Ne timeas inter adversa, quæ tibi intulerunt aut inferre conati sunt Judæi increduli: non quod aliquis timor inordinatus potuit esse in Christo, qui secundum naturam assumptam fuit perfecte confirmatus in bono: sed ne naturali timore, quem interdum sponte assumpsit, diu immoraretur, et ne eum frequentius quam oportebat, assumeret. Unde in persona Christi cantat Ecclesia: In die qua invocavi te, Domine, dixisti, Ne timeas. Potest quoque exponi hoc verbum, Noli timere, non quasi hortando ne formidaret, sed congratulando suæ perfectioni, qua inordinate nihil pavebat, quemadmodum canimus: Laudate eum omnes angeli ejus.
paras.en: Furthermore, since Abram is a figure of Christ, this chapter can be expounded allegorically of Christ, thus: [[15:1|the word of the Lord came to Abram by a vision, saying: Fear not|Factus est sermo Domini ad Abram per visionem, dicens: Noli timere]]; that is, the eternal Word, or God the Father, or God the Trinity, said to Christ according to his human nature: Fear not amid the adversities which the unbelieving Jews have brought upon thee or have tried to bring.
